# Reading the Airport Compliance Manual: A Practitioner's Guide to FAA Order 5190.6C

How the FAA applies the Grant Assurances, the 1999 Revenue Use Policy, and the 2013 Rates and Charges Policy in live compliance matters.

DWU AI Product; June 2026

DWU AI articles are produced with rigorous AI review but may contain mistakes — we aim to link the first-hand source on every key claim, so you can click through and verify.

**Scope & Methodology**  

**Scope.** This article walks through [FAA Order 5190.6C](https://www.faa.gov/airports/resources/publications/orders/compliance_5190_6), effective February 20, 2026 — what the Airport Compliance Manual is, how it is organized, how it interacts with the 40 Sponsor Assurances, and how practitioners use it in rate negotiations, Part 16 adjudications, and revenue-use defenses.

**Methodology.** Prepared by DWU AI using exclusively publicly available sources: the FAA Order 5190.6C landing page, Foreword, Summary of Updates, and individual chapter pages; Federal Register notices of the 1996 and 2013 Rates and Charges Policies and the 1999 Revenue Use Policy; 49 U.S.C. chapter 471 provisions at Cornell Law; and publicly posted Part 16 final agency decisions, D.C. Circuit opinions, and DOT OIG audits. No confidential DWU client data was used.

The FAA's Airport Compliance Manual — reissued on February 20, 2026 as **Order 5190.6C** — is the single most consequential day-to-day compliance document for federally obligated airports and a core reference in the working library of airport CFOs, attorneys, and compliance officers. The Order is how FAA Airports District Offices and Regional Offices actually apply [49 U.S.C. § 47107](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/49/47107) Grant Assurances, [49 U.S.C. § 47133](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/49/47133), the [1999 Revenue Use Policy](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/1999/02/16/99-3529/policy-and-procedures-concerning-the-use-of-airport-revenue), and the [2013 Rates and Charges Policy](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2013/09/10/2013-21905/policy-regarding-airport-rates-and-charges) in live compliance matters. This article walks through what 5190.6C is, how it is organized, how it interacts with the 40 Sponsor Assurances, and how practitioners use it in rate negotiations, Part 16 adjudications, and revenue-use defenses.

## What FAA Order 5190.6C Is

Order 5190.6C, titled *Airport Compliance Manual*, is FAA's National Policy document providing guidance to FAA employees on implementation of the airport compliance program — the program under which FAA assures that airport sponsors comply with continuing obligations arising from grant agreements and from deeds of property conveyance for airport use. [The Order's Foreword](https://www.faa.gov/airports/resources/publications/orders/compliance_5190_6/order-5190-6c-compliance-foreword) is signed by Michael W. Helvey, Director, Airports Compliance and Management Analysis (ACO-1), with an effective date of February 20, 2026. It **cancels and replaces Order 5190.6B** (September 30, 2009), incorporating Changes 1, 2, and 3 that had been issued to 5190.6B between 2021 and 2023, and layering on further updates to reflect the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 and agency policy changes adopted since 2009.

The Order's scope is every federally obligated airport, not only airports currently receiving Airport Improvement Program (AIP) funds. Federal obligations attach through AIP grant agreements and through deeds of conveyance for surplus and non-surplus federal property, and those obligations persist for the duration specified in the underlying instrument — which for property conveyances can be perpetual. (Passenger Facility Charge (PFC) approvals carry their own assurance conditions under [49 U.S.C. § 40117](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/49/40117) and [14 CFR Part 158](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-158) — a separate program regime, not a source of the federal obligations 5190.6C administers.) 5190.6C's companion authorities are [49 U.S.C. § 47107](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/49/47107) (sponsor assurances), [49 U.S.C. § 47133](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/49/47133) (revenue-use restriction extended to any airport that is the subject of federal assistance), and [14 CFR Part 16](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-16) (the procedural vehicle for formal complaints against federally obligated airports).

**Practitioner note.** When a reader is asked *"where does FAA actually say that?"* the default answer for day-to-day compliance questions is now 5190.6C — not 5190.6B, and not the Grant Assurances document standing alone. The Grant Assurances state the obligation; 5190.6C tells FAA staff how to apply it.

## History and Evolution

The Airport Compliance Manual has a five-decade lineage that tracks the statutory and policy architecture governing federally funded airports:

| Version | Effective | Principal context |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Order 5190.6 | August 24, 1973 | Original consolidated airport compliance order, issued under the Federal Aid to Airports Program / Airport Development Aid Program era |
| Order 5190.6A | October 2, 1989 | *Airport Compliance Requirements* — post–Airport and Airway Improvement Act of 1982 (AAIA) update and the practitioner reference through the 1990s and 2000s |
| Order 5190.6B | September 30, 2009 | Reflected the 1996 Rates and Charges Policy, the 1999 Revenue Use Policy, AIR-21 (2000), and Vision 100 (2003) |
| 5190.6B Change 1 | December 3, 2021 | Updated Chapters 1, 9, 10, 11, and 23 |
| 5190.6B Change 2 | December 9, 2022 | Updated Chapters 2, 3, 4, and 5 |
| 5190.6B Change 3 | September 15, 2023 | Updated Chapters 16, 17, 18, and 19 |
| **Order 5190.6C** | **February 20, 2026** | **Incorporates Changes 1–3 and adds updates to Chapters 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14, 15, 20, 21, 22, and Appendix G to reflect the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 and post-2009 policy developments** |

The drivers of each revision track federal aviation policy: the 1996 [*Policy Regarding the Establishment of Airport Rates and Charges*](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/1996/06/21/96-15687/policy-regarding-the-establishment-of-airport-rates-and-charges) (61 Fed. Reg. 31994), the 1999 *Policy and Procedures Concerning the Use of Airport Revenue* ([64 Fed. Reg. 7696](https://www.federalregister.gov/citation/64-FR-7696)), § 804 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 1996 ([P.L. 104-264](https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/PLAW-104publ264)), which codified the revenue-use restriction as [49 U.S.C. § 47133](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/49/47133), the 2013 republication of the Rates and Charges Policy reflecting the 2008 amendment ([78 Fed. Reg. 55330](https://www.federalregister.gov/citation/78-FR-55330)), the 2014 amendment to the Revenue Use Policy addressing aviation fuel tax proceeds ([79 Fed. Reg. 66282](https://www.federalregister.gov/citation/79-FR-66282)), accumulated Part 16 docket experience, and most recently the [FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024](https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/PLAW-118publ63) ([P.L. 118-63](https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/PLAW-118publ63)) signed May 16, 2024. The 2024 Reauthorization Act made amendments to 49 U.S.C. chapter 471 that 5190.6C incorporates through updated citations and substantive references.

**Practitioner note.** Airports that still carry 5190.6B references in their airline-use agreement recitals, bond Official Statement (OS) disclosures, or internal compliance manuals typically calendar an update following a new Order issuance. Prospectively, internal policy documents citing the Order now point to 5190.6C and the February 20, 2026 effective date; historical references to 5190.6B are retained where they accurately describe the regulatory regime in effect at the time of the underlying transaction.

## Structure of the Order

5190.6C is organized into eight Parts: Parts I-VII contain 23 chapters, and Part VIII contains the eight appendices (Appendices A-H), followed by a References list and an Index. The Parts group the chapters by function:

* **Part I: Background** — Chapter 1 (*Scope and Authority*) and Chapter 2 (*Compliance Program*).
* **Part II: Types of Federal Agreements** — Chapter 3 (*Federal Obligations from Property Conveyances*) and Chapter 4 (*Federal Grant Obligations and Responsibilities*).
* **Part III: Complaint Resolution** — Chapter 5 (*Initiating, Accepting and Investigating Informal and Formal Complaints*), which houses the Part 13 informal process and the Part 16 formal complaint linkage.
* **Part IV: Airports and Aeronautical Users** — Chapters 6 through 14, covering rights and powers and good title, airport operations and maintenance, exclusive rights, unjust discrimination between aeronautical users, reasonable commercial minimum standards, self-service, review of aeronautical lease agreements, airport noise and access restrictions, and safety-and-efficiency restrictions.
* **Part V: Financial Responsibilities** — Chapters 15 through 19, covering permitted and prohibited uses of airport revenue, resolution of unlawful revenue diversion, self-sustainability, airport rates and charges, and airport financial reports.
* **Part VI: Land Use** — Chapter 20 (*Compatible Land Use*) and Chapter 21 (*Land Use Compliance Inspection*).
* **Part VII: Releases and Property Reversions** — Chapter 22 (*Land Use Changes and Releases of Federally Acquired and Federally Conveyed Land*) and Chapter 23 (*Reversions of Airport Property*).
* **Part VIII: Appendices** — Appendix A (*Airport Sponsors Assurances*), Appendix B (*SPA Reg. 16*), Appendix C (*DoD Base Realignment and Closure (BRAC)*), Appendix D (*Sample Airport Rules and Regulations*), Appendix E (*Sample Deed of Conveyance*), Appendix F (*Sample Notice of Reversion of Property and Revestment of Title to the United States*), Appendix G (*Explanation of Terms*), and Appendix H (*Acronyms*).

The Order's layered structure moves from general principles (scope, authority, compliance-program objectives) to the specific federal agreements that create obligations (grants and conveyances), to complaint and enforcement mechanics, to the substantive obligations grouped by subject matter, to land-use and release procedures, and finally to sample instruments and definitions. The **[40 Grant Assurances](https://www.faa.gov/airports/resources/publications/orders/compliance_5190_6/order-5190-6c-compliance-appendix-a) are listed in Appendix A** (Assurances 1–40, including new Assurance 40 *Access to Leaded Aviation Gasoline* added by the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024) — which sets out the assurance titles and their statutory bases, with the current authoritative copy of the Sponsor Assurances maintained separately by FAA — not in Chapter 2 — a point worth emphasizing because the assurances are the contractual spine, while the chapter text is FAA's interpretive and enforcement guidance.

**Practitioner note.** When citing 5190.6C in correspondence with an Airports District Office (ADO), specify chapter and section (for example, *5190.6C § 15.12* for prohibited uses of airport revenue). The Order's section numbering is stable within a chapter and mirrors the numbering conventions established in 5190.6B Change 3, so citations in pre-2026 Part 16 filings that referenced *5190.6B § 18.6* generally map to the same section number in 5190.6C § 18.6; FAA has published a [Section Renumbering and Retitling Chart](https://www.faa.gov/airports/resources/publications/orders/compliance_5190_6/order-5190-6c-compliance-renumbering-and-retitling-chart) for verification in the non-trivial cases.

## How the Order Interacts with the 40 Grant Assurances

The 40 Grant Assurances (Appendix A, 5190.6C — including Assurance 40 \*Access to Leaded Aviation Gasoline\*) bind the airport sponsor contractually as a condition of accepting federal airport assistance. 5190.6C does not replace them; it explains how FAA interprets and enforces them. Four assurances dominate most compliance work, and each is anchored to a specific chapter.

**Assurance 22, Economic Nondiscrimination**, prohibits unjustly discriminatory treatment among aeronautical users. Chapter 9 (*Unjust Discrimination between Aeronautical Users*) is the operative chapter, covering rental fees and charges generally (§ 9.2), types of charges (§ 9.3), terms applied to aeronautical-service tenants (§ 9.5), fixed-base operator standards (§ 9.6), and air carrier airport access (§ 9.8). Assurance 22 disputes are where FAA most frequently invokes the "fair and reasonable terms, without unjust discrimination" language — as illustrated in the [City of Santa Monica Part 16 final agency decision of July 8, 2009](https://part16.airports.faa.gov) (Docket 16-02-08), which held that Santa Monica's ordinance banning Category C and D aircraft violated Grant Assurance 22 even though it did not rise to an exclusive-rights violation under Assurance 23.

**Assurance 23, Exclusive Rights**, is operationalized through Chapter 8 (*Exclusive Rights*), including the definition of an exclusive right (§ 8.2), the legislative and statutory history (§ 8.3), the development of the prohibition into FAA policy (§ 8.4), the single-provider airport scenarios (§ 8.5), and the narrow exceptions (§ 8.8). Chapter 8 is one of the chapters updated for 5190.6C, reflecting updated FAA guidance on self-service fueling (including access to 100-octane low-lead aviation gasoline under Section 770 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024) and on proprietary exclusive rights.

## Frequently Asked Questions

What is FAA Order 5190.6C?

FAA Order 5190.6C is the Airport Compliance Manual — the FAA's consolidated interpretive guidance on how the 39 Grant Assurances, the 1999 Revenue Use Policy, and the 2013 Rates and Charges Policy are applied in live compliance matters. It superseded 5190.6B (effective February 20, 2026) and is the operative reference FAA field offices and ADO regional counsel use when evaluating sponsor behavior, processing complaints under 14 CFR Part 16, and conducting Part 13 informal reviews.

Who uses Order 5190.6C and when does it apply?

The Order is binding on FAA compliance staff and advisory for airport sponsors, tenants, and the public. It applies whenever an airport has received federal financial assistance under the Airport Improvement Program (AIP) or equivalent — which includes essentially every federally-obligated commercial-service airport. Tenants and complainants use it to understand the substantive standard FAA applies before filing Part 16 complaints.

What changed in 5190.6C compared to 5190.6B?

The Order consolidates post-2009 FAA guidance, incorporates the 2013 Rates and Charges Policy, and reflects updated interpretations on grant-assurance scope (particularly GA 22 economic nondiscrimination, GA 23 exclusive rights, GA 24 self-sustaining aggregate fee/rental, and GA 25 revenue use). It also clarifies the Part 16 informal-investigation path and the private-contract-dispute doctrine under which FAA declines to adjudicate AULA construction issues between a sponsor and a signatory carrier.

How does the Order treat airport revenue diversion?

Chapter 15 (Revenue Use) restates the four universally-recognized forms of diversion: direct transfers to the general fund, excessive indirect-cost allocation (2 CFR Part 200 methodology required with annual true-ups), PILOT payments exceeding reasonable-cost reimbursement, and land/property lease mispricing below fair market value. The grandfathered-airport exception (nine airports frozen at September 2, 1982 amounts, CPI-U escalable) is narrowly construed — any new revenue stream created after grandfathering is subject to the full revenue-use prohibition. NBAA v. Town of East Hampton (Docket 16-15-08) is the paradigmatic GA 25 enforcement case.

Is Order 5190.6C legally binding in court?

The Order itself is FAA interpretive guidance, not a regulation — federal courts give it Skidmore deference (persuasive weight in proportion to the thoroughness of the reasoning and consistency with FAA's prior positions) rather than Chevron deference. However, underlying grant assurances are enforceable contract terms, and 49 U.S.C. §§ 47107 and 47111 are statutory; the Order's principal legal effect is signaling to sponsors how FAA will apply those statutes and contracts in Part 16 proceedings and AIP grant decisions.

# FAA Airport Compliance Manual - Order 5190.6C – Airports

**February 2026**

Order 5190.6C sets forth policies and procedures for the FAA Airport Compliance Program. It provides basic guidance for FAA personnel in interpreting and administering the various continuing commitments airport owners make to the United States as a condition for the grant of federal funds or the conveyance of federal property for airport purposes. The Order discusses the obligations set forth in the standard airport sponsor assurances, addresses the application of the assurances in the operation of public-use airports, and facilitates interpretation of the assurances by FAA personnel.

Order 5190.6C cancels and replaces 5190.6B. Version C incorporates Changes 1 through 3 to 5190.6B discussed below and updates the following chapters:

Please follow these guidelines to create your summary:

1. Identify and preserve the main topic or purpose of the webpage.
2. Retain key facts, statistics, and data points that are central to the content's message.
3. Keep important quotes from credible sources or experts.
4. Maintain the chronological order of events if the content is time-sensitive or historical.
5. Preserve any lists or step-by-step instructions if present.
6. Include relevant dates, names, and locations that are crucial to understanding the content.
7. Summarize lengthy explanations while keeping the core message intact.

When handling different types of content:

- For news articles: Focus on the who, what, when, where, why, and how.
- For scientific content: Preserve methodology, results, and conclusions.
- For opinion pieces: Maintain the main arguments and supporting points.
- For product pages: Keep key features, specifications, and unique selling points.

Your summary should be significantly shorter than the original content but comprehensive enough to stand alone as a source of information. Aim for about 25-30 percent of the original length, unless the content is already concise.

args.summary:
This webpage is the official FAA (Federal Aviation Administration) landing page for "FAA Airport Compliance Manual - Order 5190.6C – Airports," dated February 2026. The Order establishes policies and procedures for the FAA Airport Compliance Program, providing guidance for FAA personnel in administering the continuing commitments airports make to the United States as a condition for federal grants or conveyance of federal property. It covers standard airport sponsor assurances, their application in public-use airport operations, and interpretation by FAA personnel.

Order 5190.6C cancels and replaces version 5190.6B, incorporating Changes 1 through 3 and updating several chapters. The Office of Airport Compliance and Management Analysis conducted a review and published these changes.

The page provides a comprehensive table of contents with links to 23 chapters including: Scope and Authority; Compliance Program; Federal Obligations from Property Conveyances; Federal Grant Obligations; Complaints (informal and formal); Rights and Powers/Good Title; Airport Operations and Maintenance; Exclusive Rights; Unjust Discrimination; Reasonable Commercial Minimum Standards; Self-Service; Aeronautical Lease Agreements; Airport Noise and Access Restrictions; Safety and Efficiency Restrictions; Permitted and Prohibited Uses of Airport Revenue; Resolution of Unlawful Revenue Diversion; Self-Sustainability; Airport Rates and Charges; Airport Financial Reports; Compatible Land Use; Land Use Compliance Inspection; Land Use Changes and Releases of Federally Acquired/Conveyed Land; and Reversions of Airport Property.

The document also includes 8 appendices (Airport Sponsor Assurances, SPA Reg. 16, DoD BRAC, Sample Airport Rules, Sample Deed of Conveyance, Sample Notice of Reversion, Explanation of Terms, and Acronyms), plus References and an Index. Users can navigate via a table of contents menu with expandable/collapsible sections.

# Passenger Boarding (Enplanement) and All-Cargo Data for U.S. Airports

Passenger boarding (enplanement) and all-cargo data is extracted from the FAA's Air Carrier Activity database. This database supports the FAA's airport categories for use in apportionment formula calculations under the [Airport Improvement Program (AIP)](/airports/aip) and [Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act programs](/iija).  
[More about the collection and use of passenger and all-cargo data »](/airports/planning_capacity/passenger_allcargo_stats/passenger/collection)

Passenger boarding and all-cargo data is collected for a full calendar year and is used in calculating airport categories and entitlements for the next full fiscal year (i.e., Calendar Year 2025 data determines Fiscal Year 2027 category and funds).

Airports can view their individual CY 2025 enplanement report on our [Airports External Portal (AEP)](https://aep.airports.faa.gov/Home.aspx). Please select "Enplanement Public Report and Form" on the AEP site.

See [Abbreviations](#abbreviations) for an explanation of the abbreviations used in the enplanements and cargo files column headings.

# Economic Impact Study

Exploring the Impact of the Gerald R. Ford International Airport on the West Michigan Regional Economy

Edit

## About the Study

Gerald R. Ford International Airport Authority (GFIAA) leadership worked closely with researchers at Grand Valley State University's Seidman College of Business to conduct a thorough analysis of the Gerald R. Ford International Airport's (GFIA) impact on the local economy.

The scope of work included measuring the economic impact of GFIA on Kent County and the West Michigan Economic Development Region, which is inclusive of 13 area counties, for the year 2022. In addition, the study measured the catalytic effect of the airport, which is inclusive of the industries that exist because of airport services, the role the airport plays in attracting business to West Michigan, and the effect it has on household incomes.

![GRR-GRAND-RAPIDS-142](https://www.grr.org/hs-fs/hubfs/GRR-GRAND-RAPIDS-142.jpg?width=2000&height=1252&name=GRR-GRAND-RAPIDS-142.jpg "GRR-GRAND-RAPIDS-142")

## Terms and Definitions

 The following terms and definitions are used throughout the report.

|  |
| --- |
| Commercial Visitors Those who arrive at GFIA on commercial airlines and are not residents of the West Michigan Economic Development Region. |

|  |
| --- |
| General Aviation Visitors General Aviation (GA) activities focus on non-commercial, non-scheduled operations, with many GA visitors arriving and departing in the same day. For those who do stay overnight, they have the same spending patterns as commercial visitors. |

|  |
| --- |
| Airport Operations GFIA is managed by the airport authority (GFIAA), which consists of a wide range of jobs that are associated with daily operations of GFIA. |

|  |
| --- |
| Airport Capital Investment The economic impact associated with capital investment only occurs when the spending associated with the project is taking place. Once the project-related spending is over, the economic impact associated with the project also ends. |

|  |
| --- |
| Airport Tenants Businesses located directly on GFIA's campus. These tenants provide aviation-related services or support for airport customers. |

|  |
| --- |
| Catalytic Effect This measurement is used to determine the value to a region of the income of residents who would live elsewhere if it were not for GFIA. |

|  |
| --- |
| Economic Modeling This economic impact study was estimated using the IMPLAN model. IMPLAN is a regional economic analysis software that estimates the ripple effect of economic activity within a specific geographic region utilizing an input-output method. |

## Economic Service Area

The Gerald R. Ford International Airport is based in Kent County, Michigan, and primarily serves the 13-county West Michigan Economic Development Region. This includes Allegan, Barry, Kent, Ionia, Lake, Mason, Mecosta, Montcalm, Muskegon, Newago, Oceana, Osceola, and Ottawa counties.

##### West Michigan Economic Region By The Numbers:

* Population: 1,627,734
* Average Annual Growth Rate *(2013-2020)*: 0.75%
* Median Household Income: $58.5K

args.summary:
This webpage from the Gerald R. Ford International Airport (GFIA) in Grand Rapids, Michigan presents its Economic Impact Study, conducted in partnership with Grand Valley State University's Seidman College of Business. The study analyzed GFIA's economic impact on Kent County and the 13-county West Michigan Economic Development Region for the year 2022, including the airport's catalytic effect on attracting business and household incomes.

Key 2022 statistics include: 3,468,156 total passengers, 85,276,304 pounds of cargo, 3,764 jobs on the GFIA campus, 6 commercial airline partners, 34 nonstop destinations, and 23,581 itinerant general aviation passengers. The study highlights include 40,000 jobs supported, $7.7 billion in economic impact, and $1.3 billion in household income.

The Western Michigan Economic Region has a population of 1,627,734, with a 0.75% average annual growth rate (2013-2020) and a median household income of $58.5K. The region includes Allegan, Barry, Kent, Ionia, Lake, Mason, Mecosta, Montcalm, Muskegon, Newago, Oceana, Osceola, and Ottawa counties. The study used the IMPLAN regional economic analysis model.

GFIA is the second busiest airport in Michigan and the 76th busiest in the country per the Bureau of Transportation. It has received accolades including USA Today's "Best Small Airport in the Country" and multiple Airports Council International World awards (best airport of 2-5 million passengers, most dedicated staff, easiest airport journey, most enjoyable airport, and cleanest airport in North America). The page also notes a rental car return location change effective July 9, directing visitors to the Ground Transportation page, and offers a downloadable PDF of the full economic impact study.

## [CHAPTER 4](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/1#content-toc_AKjd)

## [The Role of the Airport in the Local Economy](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/1#content-toc_AKjd)

[Chapter 2](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/3#6) discusses how population and economic growth drive both economic activity and higher aviation emissions if they are not otherwise abated. This chapter focuses on new research that may help airports supplement their own economic impact studies to better explain to stakeholders and the community the important role that both commercial service and GA airports play in the local economy. The results developed will help airports address one of the important questions growing out of the climate change discussion: Since aviation climate effects are so expensive to abate, what benefits would be lost by curtailing aviation activity?

**The Community Values a Local Airport When Planning Travel**

The International Air Transport Association’s (IATA) 2022 Global Passenger Survey found that passengers want convenience when they plan travel. Seventy-five percent of those surveyed “prioritized proximity to airport when choosing where to fly from” (*[52](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/13#backmatter05_ref-52)*). This chapter documents the value consumers place on being able to fly by air and from a local airport.

During the case studies conducted for this engagement (described in [Chapter 7](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/8#57) and in detail in [Appendix B](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/10#87)), some airports expressed reluctance to link economic activity with climate discussions. In general, the more the local community was engaged in the climate change issue, the less willing the airport was to make the linkage. Instead, airports often choose to say that they “will accommodate growth in aviation in the most responsible and climate-friendly manner.” However, the positive economic consequences of growth may still play an important internal role in setting airport policies and goals. A different interpretation of the previous statement is that “the economic impact is why it is important (and perhaps even cost-beneficial) for a community to invest in mitigation so that aviation can continue to grow.”

### [Summary of Economic Impacts](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/1#content-toc_pz9-17)

Airports produce very impressive economic impact results. For example, ACI recently published an economic impact study on the national impacts of commercial airports. The following is an excerpt from that study.

Airports are more than runways and terminals. Airports are powerful engines of economic growth and possibility for local communities across the United States. In Taking America Beyond the Horizon: The Economic Impact of Commercial Service Airports in 2017, we are pleased to announce the total economic output of U.S. commercial airports now exceeds $1.4 trillion, supporting more than 11.5 million jobs with a payroll of more than $428 billion. The study, which summarizes the economic benefits that the 493 commercial airports in the United States make to the national economy, also found that America’s airports account for more than 7 percent of U.S. GDP (*[53](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/13#backmatter05_ref-53)*).

Many states and larger commercial service airports have also produced economic impact studies. It is important to define terms before discussing how the results of these studies can contribute to airport communications.

#### How Do Economic Impact Studies Work?

Economic impact studies measure three kinds of impacts:

The larger and more integrated the local and regional economies are, the less “leakage” there is when counting the indirect and induced impacts. Leakage refers to dollars that are re-spent outside of the region. For example, leakage would occur if a law firm hired by an airport contractor employed lawyers who resided outside of the region.

There are examples of national, state, and local airport economic impact studies. The main methodological distinction between them is the definition of the economy affected by indirect and induced impacts.

Most economic impact studies developed by airports have a local or regional focus. ACRP published an excellent synthesis of these models, which provides more details on the general methodologies (*[54](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/13#backmatter05_ref-54)*).

### [New Research to Supplement Airport Economic Impact Studies](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/1#content-toc_pz9-19)

This section describes three new measures of economic impacts that were developed from research done for this project. All three economic measures address the question raised earlier: What benefits would be lost by curtailing aviation activity?

These three measures directly address statements some organizations have made (see [Chapter 5](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/6#44)) to curtail aviation activity in order to address climate change:

Details on how these measures were estimated can be found in [Appendix A](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/9#77) of the Guide. [Appendix A](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/9#77) also discusses how to update the models. In this section, the focus is on interpreting the results.

#### Expected Additional Economic Impacts Due to Growth in Activity

[Chapter 5](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/6#44) discusses statements made by some organizations that because abatement costs for aviation are so high, the only way to reduce emissions is to reduce activity—that is, flights and passengers. This section describes a way to estimate the costs to the local economy of losing projected future growth.

The following estimates of economic benefits use a model to estimate how jobs, household income, and total expenditures will grow in the region as a result of activity growth. The model also provides separate estimates of the benefits of new types of air service at commercial service airports. Details on the methodology can be found in [Appendix A](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/9#77).

[Figure 4-1](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz46-2) shows an estimate of the average annual jobs, household income, and local expenditures gained or forgone due to additional or reduced enplanements at a commercial airport with more than 2,500 enplanements per year.

On average,

It is important to note that the values in [Figure 4-1](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz46-2) are annual. The net added job(s), income, and output will remain in the region so long as enplanements remain.

[Figure 4-2](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz47-2) provides a different set of economic benefits that an airport would gain (or lose) due to changes in air services. They are based on the connectivity benefits estimated in *ACRP Report 132* (*[55](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/13#backmatter05_ref-55)*). This type of analysis is relevant to provide information on the consequences if the airport stops promoting new air services or loses air services to some areas. The example is for Austin, Texas, and is based on its January 2023 Official Airline Guide (OAG) schedule.

![Average economic impact per incremental enplanement](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/assets/images/img-46.jpg)

Looking at [Figure 4-2](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz47-2), the first row says that adding nonstop service to one more domestic city (column c) would add $72.7 million (column e) annually to Austin’s GDP. The second row says that adding nonstop service at least once per week to an international city would add $341.3 million to the regional GDP. These estimates depend importantly on existing levels of air service and the size of the local economy. For example, Austin already has nonstop service to all the major connecting hubs in the United States, so there is a 0% change in the GDP from trying to add service to another domestic hub city. The details on how to apply this methodology are contained in [Appendix A](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/9#77).

[Figure 4-3](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz48-2) provides information on the average regional economic benefits due to the growth in activity and growth in based jet aircraft for a GA airport. The economic impacts of each are separately reported in the figure.

[Figure 4-3](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz48-2) illustrates that, on average,

**Interpreting Results in [Figures 4-1](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz46-2), [4-2](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz47-2), and [4-3](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz48-2)**

It is important to interpret the results in these figures correctly. The reported impacts for an airport are “marginal,” meaning that the changes in jobs, income, and regional output are best understood as resulting from relatively small changes in enplanements, activity, or based jet aircraft.

Airports may wish to compare the results from [Figures 4-1](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz46-2), [4-2](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz47-2), and [4-3](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz48-2) to their existing economic impact estimates. The results from the figures are not the same as average impacts that might be derived from an existing economic impact study for the airport, e.g., by taking estimates of total jobs created by an airport from an existing study and dividing it by enplanements. In general, one would expect the marginal impacts reported in [Figures 4-1](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz46-2), [4-2](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz47-2), and [4-3](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz48-2) to be smaller than the average impacts calculated from an airport’s own economic impact study. When this is the case, the airport can be more confident in the results from the figures. When this is not the case, the airport may wish to report results based on the calculated averages from their own economic study, with the caveat that averages can sometimes overstate marginal impacts.

![Benefits of incremental air service changes at Austin, Texas](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/assets/images/img-47.jpg)
![Annual economic benefits of additional activity in operations (a) and per based jet aircraft at a GA airport (b)](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/assets/images/img-48.jpg)

#### Costs to Consumers If They Made the Same Trip Using Another Mode of Transportation

The values shown in [Figures 4-1](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz46-2), [4-2](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz47-2), and [4-3](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz48-2) focus on the contribution of the airport to the local and regional economy. They demonstrate that airports are an important driver of local economic activity, household income, and jobs. If activity were to slow down for whatever reason, some of this economic activity could be lost to the community (unless something else took its place).

The discussion now turns to the costs to consumers if they opted or were forced to travel via different modes of transportation. There would be two impacts to focus on:

The sum of these two items is called the full price of travel (FPT) and usually includes higher out-of-pocket costs and higher time-related costs. The higher FPT would cause consumers to change where they travel or even whether they travel at all. The project team does not try to estimate this impact here. Instead, the team wanted to identify how much more efficient air transportation is than available alternatives for the same trips consumers have already taken. In effect, consumers would be poorer by the increase in the FPT if the air mode were not available.

Details on how these estimates are made can be found in [Appendix A](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/9#77).

[Table 4-1](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz48-11) shows the average results for large, medium, small, and nonhub airports broken down by the changes in out-of-pocket and time-related costs as well as the change in the FPT.

**Table 4-1. Average increase in FPT via alternate mode by type of hub.**

| **FAA Hub** | **Time-Related Costs** | **Out-of-Pocket Costs** | **FPT** | **Avg. Annual Increase in GHGs (tons)** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Large | 426% | 157% | 289% | 70% |
| Medium | 360% | 125% | 241% | 56% |
| Small | 317% | 101% | 206% | 56% |
| Nonhub | 283% | 73% | 172% | 51% |

The increases in out-of-pocket costs make intuitive sense. Most trips made by air are to distant places. For example, taking a car to a domestic destination or a boat overseas will be more expensive than flying when taking into account the life cycle cost of the automobile, assuming two passengers per trip, and the added expense of accessing a second mode for intercontinental trips.

To understand the time-related costs, it is important to understand how they were derived. Two explanations are provided:

##### Example of the Advantage of Aviation Versus an Alternative Mode

Take a simple example of a trip from the East Coast of the United States to Europe. Via commercial aviation, the trip might take 8 hours and cost about $800. The FPT would be the fare plus the value of consumer time, which, using the U.S. DOT value of time of $47.10 per hour, would be $377; in this example, the FPT via aviation would be $1,177 ($800 in out-of-pocket costs + $377 in time-related costs).

If aviation was not available, the trip would be taken by ocean liner. Assume the consumer resides in a port city and incurs no additional costs to get to the ship. The typical time to cross the Atlantic would be 6 days or 144 hours. A consumer would be devoting 6 days to make the Atlantic crossing instead of 8 hours. Using the U.S. DOT’s value of time of $47.10 and assuming a passenger would use 8 hours a day to sleep and 8 hours a day for personal time whether they were traveling on an ocean liner or at home, they would invest at least 48 hours (8 hours x 6 days) traveling on a cruise ship, which would be worth $2,261. A typical cost on the Queen Mary would be $1,600 one way. So, the FPT for the trip (money plus the value of time) would be $3,861.

In this example, aviation would save the consumer: $2,684 each way ($3,861 via ocean liner minus $1,177 via commercial aviation) or $5,368 for the round trip. This example illustrates the vast increase in travel productivity made possible by aviation, especially for long-distance trips.

These alternative mode estimates are not available for GA airports because the trips from GA airports are not as well documented in terms of aircraft type, origins, destinations, and the number of passengers.

[Table 4-1](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz48-11) also reports the estimated percentage change in CO2 emissions that would occur by traveling via alternative modes. The results are based on the travel distances for the trips made from the airport, and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) measures of CO2 emissions by mode and other source material reported in [Table 4-2](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz50-1) and [Figure 4-4](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz50-5). The large increases in emissions reported in [Table 4-1](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz48-11) are due primarily to the assumed reliance on ocean liners as an alternative to air transportation for intercontinental trips (except within the Americas). Per-passenger mile, ocean liners emit twice as much GHG emissions on long-haul trips (over 2,300 miles) than the average commercial aircraft (see [Table 4-2](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz50-1)).

The conclusion from [Table 4-1](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz48-11) is that aviation is less costly for consumers and produces fewer emissions than alternative modes of transportation for trips typically taken from the airport.

**Table 4-2. Unit measures of CO2 emissions by mode.**

| **Vehicle Type** | **Tank-to-Wake CO2 Factor (kg/unit)** | **Well-to-Tank CO2 Factor (kg/unit)** | **Total: Well-to-Wake CO2 Factor (kg/unit)** | **Units** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Air Travel: Short-Haul (< 300 miles) | 0.207 | 0.045 | 0.252 | Passenger mile |
| Air Travel: Medium-Haul (≥ 300 miles, < 2,300 miles) | 0.129 | 0.028 | 0.157 | Passenger mile |
| Air Travel: Long-Haul (≥ 2,300 miles) | 0.163 | 0.035 | 0.198 | Passenger mile |
| Air Travel: Short-Haul (< 300 miles) | 2.151 | 0.464 | 2.615 | Freight-ton mile |
| Air Travel: Medium-Haul (≥ 300 miles, < 2,300 miles) | 1.340 | 0.289 | 1.629 | Freight-ton mile |
| Air Travel: Long-Haul (≥ 2,300 miles) | 1.694 | 0.366 | 2.060 | Freight-ton mile |
| Passenger Car: 2 Passengers | 0.166 | 0.038 | 0.204 | Passenger mile |
| Passenger: Intercity Rail | 0.113 | 0.029 | 0.142 | Passenger mile |
| Passenger: Ocean | — | — | 0.402 | Passenger mile |
| Medium- and Heavy-Duty Truck | 0.211 | 0.054 | 0.265 | Freight-ton mile |
| Rail | 0.022 | 0.006 | 0.028 | Freight-ton mile |

SOURCE: EPA 2022 GHG emission-factors-hub.xls; NREL Annual Technology Baseline: <https://atb.nrel.gov/transportation/2020/jet_fuel>; <https://airinsight.com/the-pending-newfaa-weight-balance-rules/>; ICCT: [https://theicct.org/marine-cruisingflyingmay22/#.~.text=So%2C%20if%20one%20person%20goes,2%/20on%20an%20average%20airline](https://theicct.org/marine-cruisingflyingmay22/#.~.text=So%252C%20if%20one%20person%20goes,2%25/20on%20an%20average%20airline).

![GHG emissions by mileage block and mode](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/assets/images/img-50.jpg)

#### Costs to Consumers If They Made the Same Trip Using Another Airport

It is also important for each airport to communicate the efficiency their community gains by using the local airport instead of the closest alternative airport with approximately the same service level. This is relevant because in some communities there may be movements to curtail operations or even shutter the local airport because of concerns about climate change, noise, or other issues. It is important for the community to understand how much more costly it is (both in terms of FPT and emissions) when local passengers choose to fly from a nearby, larger airport—a form of leakage as previously discussed that is an air service problem often encountered by small and nonhub airports.

Preserving or improving the level of service would be an important criterion consumers would consider when selecting an alternative airport in the event their local airport closed or its operations were curtailed. For example:

The measures presented here consider the out-of-pocket costs of driving or otherwise accessing a more distant alternative airport plus the value of the time required to access the alternative. The cost also takes account of whether consumers would enjoy more nonstop services (fewer connections) at the alternative airport, in which case they would save the time that would have been spent making those connections if they had flown via their local airport. These changes in costs are then compared to the actual consumer out-of-pocket (fare) and time-related costs for trips taken from the airport.

[Table 4-3](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz51-10) shows the results by FAA large, medium, small, and nonhub airports. The table reports the percentage of change in the time-related costs, out-of-pocket (cash) costs, and FPT when using the closest airport with at least comparable service (same FAA hub-type or better).

[Table 4-3](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz51-10) also reports the estimated increases in the tons of GHG emissions due to driving to a more distant airport.

The results reported in [Table 4-3](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz51-10) demonstrate that local consumers would spend on average 19% to 29% more (on an FPT basis) when flying from an alternative airport. This is made up of 10% to 15% higher out-of-pocket costs and 29% to 45% higher time-related costs. The time-related costs account for the offsetting benefit that some domestic passengers gain by using the alternate airport; even accounting for that, local passengers incur net out-of-pocket and time-related costs.

**Table 4-3. Average increase in FPT via alternate airport by hub-type.**

| **FAA Hub** | **Time-Related Costs** | **Out-of-Pocket Costs** | **FPT** | **Avg. Annual Increase in GHGs (tons)** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Large | 45% | 15% | 29% | 13.6% |
| Medium | 39% | 13% | 26% | 14.3% |
| Small | 35% | 12% | 23% | 14.4% |
| Nonhub | 29% | 10% | 19% | 13.9% |

**Table 4-4. Increase in FPT due to using an alternate airport.**

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | **FAA Hub Classification of Alternate** | | |
| **Hub-Type** | **Higher** | **Same** | **Lower** |
| Large | — | 35% | 13% |
| Medium | 21% | 38% | 26% |
| Small | 24% | 25% | 25% |
| Nonhub | 22% | 20% | — |

[Tables 4-4](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz52-1), [4-5](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz52-11), and [4-6](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz53-1) look behind these findings to add color to the commentary.

First, the cost of using an alternative airport depends in part on the quality of service available at the alternative versus the subject airport. [Table 4-4](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz52-1) uses FAA hub classifications for both the subject airport and the alternative used in the analysis. For example, if the subject airport is a medium hub and the alternative airport is a large hub, then on average the FPT from the alternate would be 21% higher.

In most but not all cases, when the alternate airport has a higher hub classification than the subject airport, the cost of using the alternate is lower than otherwise. This makes sense because better service at the alternate likely includes more nonstops to more places, which will offset some of the penalty of added airport access cost and time.

[Table 4-5](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz52-11) shows that in most cases, even when an alternate airport has many more nonstop services, consumers usually save time overall by flying locally. This means that in almost all cases, the added access time needed to reach an alternative airport exceeds the time savings due to having more nonstops at an alternate.

Finally, it is interesting to look at the dispersion of the results of the analysis by breaking them into quintiles from the smallest increase in the FPT to the largest. This is shown in [Table 4-6](https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5#chapter04_pz53-1).

The dispersion of results is greatest for large-hub airports. This is attributable to the assumption that the alternate for a large hub is (in most cases) another large hub. As a result, for example, using Newark Liberty International Airport as the alternate for JFK International Airport only a few miles away would result in a relatively small increase in the FPT. But it is far more difficult to replace the quality of service in Las Vegas, which is 283 miles from Los Angeles. Of course, different assumptions about alternatives would yield different results.

The dispersion across other hub-types is more muted simply because there are more likely to be closer alternate airports that provide comparable service. However, the trend is clear that replacing the service at a more isolated airport will be more costly in terms of out-of-pocket costs, time, and GHG emissions.

Again, alternative airport measures are not available for GA airports because of a lack of comparable information.

**Table 4-5. Airports where passengers save time by flying locally.**

| **Hub-Type** | **Domestic Markets** | **International Markets** | **All Markets** |

In Taking America Beyond the Horizon: The Economic Impact of Commercial Service Airports in 2017, we are pleased to announce the total economic output of U.S. commercial airports now exceeds $1.4 trillion, supporting more than 11.5 million jobs with a payroll of more than $428 billion."
args.summary:
This is Chapter 4 ("The Role of the Airport in the Local Economy") of a 2025 National Academies publication titled "Communicating a Balanced Look at Local Airport Activity and Climate Change." The chapter provides new research to help airports supplement their own economic impact studies when communicating with stakeholders about the tension between economic benefits and climate change concerns. It addresses the question: "Since aviation climate effects are so expensive to abate, what benefits would be lost by curtailing aviation activity?"

Key content includes:
- IATA's 2022 Global Passenger Survey found 75% of passengers "prioritized proximity to airport when choosing where to fly from."
- ACI's national study reports U.S. commercial airports produce total economic output exceeding $1.4 trillion, supporting more than 11.5 million jobs with a payroll exceeding $428 billion, and account for more than 7% of U.S. GDP.
- Economic impact studies measure three types of impacts: direct, indirect, and induced. "Leakage" refers to dollars re-spent outside the region.

Three new measures of economic impacts are presented:
1. Expected additional economic impacts due to growth in activity (marginal jobs, income, and output per additional enplanement at commercial airports; and per additional operation/based jet aircraft at GA airports).
2. Costs to consumers if they made the same trip using another mode of transportation (Full Price of Travel - FPT).
3. Costs to consumers if they made the same trip using another airport.

Key data tables:
- Table 4-1 shows average increase in FPT via alternate mode by hub type: Large hub = 426% time-related, 157% out-of-pocket, 289% FPT, 70% GHG increase; Medium = 360%/125%/241%/56%; Small = 317%/101%/206%/56%; Nonhub = 283%/73%/172%/51%.
- An example: East Coast to Europe via air costs about $800 fare plus $377 time value = $1,177 FPT; via ocean liner = $3,861 FPT, saving $2,684 each way via aviation.
- Table 4-2 lists CO2 emissions factors by mode (well-to-wake), including air travel (short/medium/long-haul for passengers and freight), passenger car, intercity rail, ocean (0.402 kg/passenger mile), truck, and rail.
- Table 4-3 shows FPT increases using an alternate airport: Large hub = 45% time, 15% out-of-pocket, 29% FPT, 13.6% GHG; Medium = 39%/13%/26%/14.3%; Small = 35%/12%/23%/14.4%; Nonhub = 29%/10%/19%/13.9%. Conclusion: local consumers spend on average 19-29% more on FPT basis flying from an alternative airport.
- Table 4-4 shows FPT increases based on alternate airport's hub classification relative to subject airport.
- Table 4-5 shows passengers almost always save time flying locally (e.g., 29 of 29 large hub domestic markets).
- Table 4-6 shows quintile dispersion of FPT increases, greatest for large hubs.

Methodological notes: results are "marginal" impacts not average impacts; marginal impacts typically smaller than average impacts from existing economic impact studies. Alternative mode and alternate airport measures are not available for GA airports due to lack of comparable data. The chapter includes case study examples (Austin, Texas) and notes that airports sometimes are reluctant to link economic activity with climate discussions in communications.

# The Value of My Airport

Airports, state departments of transportation, and others involved in the aviation community will commonly undertake or commission (from consultants or universities) economic impact studies as a way of communicating the economic role and importance of airports. Generally, economic impact analyses begin with an inventory of the direct effects of the airport. Direct impacts are those effects within the economy that are directly related to the provision of aviation services at your airport. Most commonly, the direct impacts evaluated for an airport study include:

1. On-airport jobs, wages, and revenue (see [Inside my Fence](/acrpwebresource1/inside-my-fence/) for guidance on how to collect this type of data)
2. Jobs, wages, and revenue associated with visitor spending (see [Visitor Spending](/acrpwebresource1/visitor-spending/))
3. Jobs, wages, and revenue at airport-reliant businesses (see [My Airport’s Business Constituency](/acrpwebresource1/my-airports-business-constituency/))

Direct effects can then be translated into broader spinoff (multiplier) effects in your regional economy. According to economics parlance, spinoff effects are broken down into two categories: indirect and induced impacts. Indirect impacts are the effect of increased economic activity for businesses that supply goods or services to businesses that directly benefit from the airport. For example, if an electronics manufacturer sells components to an airline doing business at an airport, the sales by the manufacturer represent an indirect impact. Moreover, this manufacturer creates additional indirect impacts on a regional economy when it purchases materials or services from other businesses in the airport area. Induced impacts are the effect of consumer spending by wage earners employed at businesses that directly or indirectly benefit from the airport. Spending by wage earners creates induced impacts within housing, retail, and service sectors.

Multiplier effects can be estimated (based on direct effects) using regional input-output models that use region-specific economic data to trace inter-industry relationships. Under tools you will find a list of modeling systems commonly used in economic impact analyses. Because economic impacts depend on a definition of what is “local” within a community, the determination of spinoff effects will depend on your selection of an impact area. Impact areas are generally defined to coincide either with the market area of an airport, or with an entire state if an assessment is being prepared for an agency or group interested in economic development from this broader perspective.

Preparing a full economic impact study may not be necessary or feasible in all cases. If you are interested in communicating the economic value of your airport, without engaging in a full impact study, a number of options are available:

1. See if your airport has already been evaluated within a larger-scale study. Reach out to your state’s department of aviation, or conduct a search online.
2. Present only direct impacts and then use qualitative descriptions or information obtained directly through interviews to discuss the types of spinoff effects likely to be accruing within your community.
3. Contact local planning agencies, chambers of commerce, or business and tourism associations in your region to see if a potential partner organization already has economic data or models for describing multiplier effects.

Because the terminology used to describe economic impact studies can sometimes be unclear, there are two diagrams under the tools section, below, that can be used to help explain the process and outcomes of economic impact evaluations.

#### Resources

* [ACRP Synthesis 7 *Airport Economic Impact Methods and Models*](http://onlinepubs.trb.org/onlinepubs/acrp/acrp_syn_007.pdf)

  Discusses various analysis methods, models, and tools available for assessing airport economic impacts.
* [ACRP Web-Only Document 20 *Guidebook for Estimating the Economic Impact of Air Cargo Operations at Airports*](http://onlinepubs.trb.org/onlinepubs/acrp/acrp_webdoc_020.pdf)

  Discusses a number of economic models, air cargo data sets, and methodologies that can be used to describe the economic impact of air cargo operations.
* [ACRP Report 87 *Procuring and Managing Professional Services for Airports*](http://onlinepubs.trb.org/onlinepubs/acrp/acrp_rpt_087.pdf)

  A handbook that provides guidance for procuring and managing professional services at airports, including guidance for consultant selection and firm engagement.
* [ACI-NA – Airport Economic Impact Studies](http://www.aci-na.org/content/airport-economic-impact-studies)

  A catalogue of links to national and regional airport economic impact studies.
* [National Association of State Aviation Officials – Economic Impact Library](http://www.nasao.org/resources/economic-impact-library/)

  A library of economic impact studies.

Example Studies:

* [ATL 2013 Economic Impact Study Executive Summary](http://www.atlanta-airport.com/docs/Airport/ATL%20EIS%20Exec%20Summary%20Brochure%20-%20Final.pdf)

  Pages 9 and 10, *Flow of Economic Impacts* explain the flow of economic impacts from direct on-airport activity to indirect and induced impacts elsewhere in the economy.
* [Economic, Fiscal, and Developmental Impacts of DFW International Airport](http://cedr.unt.edu/sites/cedr.unt.edu/files/users/lgg0003/DFW_Airport_Impact_Report_Sept2013_Final.pdf)

  The findings of these reports show that DFW International Airport continues to generate a tremendous impact on the region throughout airport operations.
* [2013 Economic Impact Study of Colorado Airports](https://www.codot.gov/programs/aeronautics/Economic%20Impact%20Study)

  This report summarizes that airports in Colorado are responsible for generating billions of dollars in economic benefit and supporting hundreds of thousands of jobs.
* [2014 Oregon Aviation Plan Economic Impact Statement for NPIAS Airports](http://www.oregon.gov/aviation/docs/system_plan/2014_Oregon_Aviation_Economic_Update_Executive_Summary.pdf)

  This impact study discusses how airports are a key asset to Oregon commerce, providing transportation, employment and real estate for commercial and industrial development, in addition to being infrastructure essential to emergency response, medical evacuation, fire protection, and freight transport.
* [South Dakota State Aviation System Plan 2010-2030](http://www.sddot.com/transportation/aviation/docs/FinalReport.pdf)

  Chapter 6, *Economic Impact* takes a look at the economic contributions of airports and the aviation industry to both the state economy and local economies. These economic activities include on-airport economic activities, off-airport spending by visitors, and air cargo services required by South Dakota businesses.

#### Tools

* [Economic Measures](/acrp0331/wp-content/uploads/sites/7/2016/10/A1_Tool1-EconomicMeasuresTool.pdf)

  This diagram explains the relationship between jobs, wages, output, and value added as measures of economic activity.
* [Anatomy of an Impact Study](/acrp0331/wp-content/uploads/sites/7/2016/10/A1_Tool2-AnatomyOfAnImpactStudyTool.pdf)

  This diagram explains the relationship between direct, indirect, and induced economic impacts.
* [U.S. Department of Commerce Bureau of Economic Analysis Regional Input-Output Modeling System](http://www.bea.gov/regional/rims/index.cfm)

  This regional economic model is a tool used by investors, planners, and elected officials to objectively assess the potential economic impacts of various projects.
* [IMPLAN® Economic Impact Modeling System](http://implan.com/index.php?option=com_virtuemart&Itemid=195)

  IMPLAN® is an economic modeling system that provides tools, data, and outstanding support to do in-depth examinations of state, county, or multi-county regions.
* [REMI Economic Modeling System](http://www.remi.com/products)

  REMI has developed a set of complex tools that can help measure and predict future economic, demographic, and transportation changes. The modeling approach builds on the strengths of input-output, general equilibrium, econometric, and economic geography.
* [ACRP Report 132 *The Role of U.S. Airports in the National Economy*](http://onlinepubs.trb.org/Onlinepubs/acrp/acrp_rpt_132.pdf)

  Section 3.1, *National Studies and Regression Analyses* reviews and compares available national economic data sets and models.

# Global Impact of Investor Home Country Bias

By [Larry Swedroe](https://alphaarchitect.com/author/larryswedroe/ "Posts by Larry Swedroe")|Published On: December 5th, 2019|Categories: [Research Insights](https://alphaarchitect.com/category/architect-academic-insights/), [Larry Swedroe](https://alphaarchitect.com/category/other-insights/larry-swedroe/), [Macroeconomics Research](https://alphaarchitect.com/category/architect-academic-insights/macro/)|

A large body of research demonstrates that “familiarity breeds investment.” For example, a [study](https://www0.gsb.columbia.edu/mygsb/faculty/research/pubfiles/1554/Huberman-familiarity-breeds.investment.pdf) by Gur Huberman found that shortly after AT&T was broken up and shareholders were given shares in each of what were called the Baby Bells, the residents of each region held a disproportionate number of shares of their regional Bell. Each group of regional investors was confident their regional Baby Bell would outperform the others. How else can you explain each investor having most of their eggs in one baby basket? This is not Lake Wobegon where all Baby Bells can outperform the average of the group.

Other examples of familiarity breeding investment are Georgia residents who own a disproportionate share of Coca-Cola stock, and people in Rochester, New York, who tended to own disproportionate shares in local companies such as Kodak, Xerox and Bausch & Lomb. This story is a good analogy for the way domestic investors view nondomestic assets.

Research documents that familiarity breeding investment (leading to a home country bias) is a global phenomenon, as most investors hold the vast majority of their wealth in the form of domestic assets. In a 2017 [study](https://www.vanguard.com/pdf/ISGGEB.pdf), Vanguard found that in each case they examined, investors exhibited a strong home-country bias.

U.S.U.K.Japan Canada Australia
Percent of Global Market Capitalization 50 7 7 3 2
Percent Allocated to Domestic Equities 79 26 55 59 67

Note that the countries with a smaller market share tend to have larger gaps between the share of assets allocated to domestic markets and their share of global market capitalization. For example, the home country bias in the U.S., with at the time a 50 percent share of global market capitalization, results in U.S. investors overweighting domestic assets by 29 percentage points. The gap for Japan, with just a 7 percent share of global market capitalization, is 48 percentage points. For the even smaller Canadian and Australian markets, the gaps are 56 percentage points and 65 percentage points, respectively. U.K. investors appear to be _relatively_ less subject to this bias, with a gap of just 19 percentage points.

Even supposedly sophisticated professional money managers are subject to home country bias. Moritz Maier and Hendrik Scholz, authors of the January 2019 study “[Determinants of Home Bias: Evidence from European Equity Funds](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3354503),” examined the holdings of 699 actively managed equity funds, domiciled in 15 European countries, that broadly invested in European stocks over the period January 2003 to December 2016. Following is a summary of their findings:

*   More than 90 percent of funds show, on average, a home bias.
*   The home bias was present in all 15 markets. France had the highest overweighting (30 percentage points), followed by the U.K. (24 percentage points) and Germany (21 percentage points).
*   On average, funds overweight their domestic stocks by about 16 percentage points. At the 90th percentile, the overweight was about 36 percentage points. 
*   The home bias across funds is quite stable over time. 
*   The home bias of individual funds is, on average, positively related to the relative size of the stock market, the cumulative 12-month lagged domestic stock market return in excess of the European stock market return, real GNP growth and the country’s credit rating.
*   Informational advantages do not seem to be a reason for the observed home bias. 
*   The differences between future returns of the stocks bought and sold by funds are essentially zero.

The results are hypothetical results and are NOT an indicator of future results and do NOT represent returns that any investor actually attained. Indexes are unmanaged, do not reflect management or trading fees, and one cannot invest directly in an index.

## **Does Home Country Bias Impact Stock Prices?**

An interesting question: If investors all around the globe exhibit a home country bias, does it affect stock prices? In other words, if everyone equally overweights their domestic market, does it all essentially wash out, with the overweights canceling out the underweights? Victor Haghani and James White of Elm Partners sought to [answer](https://elmfunds.com/home-biased-more-indexing/) this intriguing question.

They developed the following thought experiment. They began by assuming a simple world with no home bias, and eleven national markets with a total value of $100: the big U.S. market, weighing in at 50 percent of the total, and ten small markets (Japan, United Kingdom, China, Canada, France, Switzerland, Germany, Australia, South Korea and Taiwan), representing 5 percent each.In line with the findings from the aforementioned Vanguard study, Haghani and White then assumed that U.S (the big market) investors now want to be 80 percent invested in their domestic market, 30 percentage points above the market cap weight of 50. The 10 small markets exhibit even stronger home bias, wanting to be 50 percent invested in their home market, 45 percentage points above their 5 percent weight.

They found that by flipping the home bias switch, they created a supply-and-demand problem: the U.S. market isn’t currently big enough to take on the extra demand created by the home bias of domestic investors plus the demand from global investors—the demand is greater than the supply in terms of market capitalization. On the other hand, the smaller markets have a shortfall, as demand is less than the market capitalization.

Haghani and White note:

> “Ultimately, this conundrum must be resolved by market values changing: specifically, the big market going up in value relative to the small markets. All else equal it would have to go up quite a lot: 60%, from $50 to $80 if we hold the small markets constant. The increase in big market value could be accomplished either through rising prices or through new issuance. If prices rise, this would mean a reduction in the long-term expected return of the big relative to the small market of around 1.5% , a very sizable impact assuming both markets had expected returns around 4% without the home bias distortion. If instead there’s new issuance, such issuance would represent less attractive investment opportunities at the margin than previously outstanding equity, resulting again in lower expected returns for big market equities.”  Haghani and White, ” [Home Biased: A Case for More Indexing](https://elmfunds.com/home-biased-more-indexing/),” 2019

Their findings lead to an interesting conclusion. While active investors have been claiming that passive investing is leading to distortions in market prices, Haghani and White demonstrate that, at least in terms of relative valuations between U.S. and international markets, it seems the reverse is more likely the case. The active decisions of investors (influenced by a home country bias) leads them to overweight, not market-cap weight, their home country. And because of the large size of the U.S. market relative to all other markets, that bias can lead to distortions in markets.

> “If there were less home bias and more passive investing in line with global market-value proportions, US equity investors would likely enjoy lower relative valuations and higher expected returns.”  Haghani and White, ” [Home Biased: A Case for More Indexing](https://elmfunds.com/home-biased-more-indexing/),” 2019

Keep this in mind as you consider your global equity allocation. Are you market-cap weighting? Or, perhaps influenced by another well-documented bias, recency, are you overweighting U.S. equities? As you consider these questions, remember that behavioral biases have a tendency to destroy investment returns. As legendary investor Pogo stated, **“We have met the enemy and he is us!”**

Finally, I add this note of caution, one that might help you avoid home country bias. If a belief in relatively high market efficiency has led you to conclude that you should be a passive investor—accepting market prices as the best estimate of the right prices—you should also accept the idea that all risky assets have similar risk-adjusted returns. If that were not the case, capital would flow from assets with lower expected risk-adjusted returns to the assets with higher expected risk-adjusted returns until equilibrium was reached. If all risky assets have similar risk-adjusted returns, there is no reason to have a home country bias—other than perhaps a small bias to take into account that investing in U.S. stocks is a bit cheaper than investing in international stocks. On the other hand, if you are still employed, it is likely your labor capital is more exposed to the economic cycle risks of the U.S. than to foreign market risks. If that is the case, once you include your labor capital as part of your portfolio, you should consider overweighting foreign markets to offset your labor capital risk.

This article by Larry Swedroe (published December 5, 2019 on Alpha Architect) explores the global phenomenon of home country bias in investing—the tendency of investors to overweight domestic assets relative to their share of global market capitalization. The article draws on multiple research studies including:
- A Gur Huberman study showing how AT&T breakup led shareholders to disproportionately hold their regional "Baby Bell" shares.
- A 2017 Vanguard study showing strong home country bias across countries. Data showed: US (50% of global market cap, 79% allocated to domestic equities), UK (7% market share, 26% domestic allocation), Japan (7% share, 55% domestic), Canada (3% share, 59% domestic), and Australia (2% share, 67% domestic). Smaller countries show larger gaps—the home bias gap for Australia reached 65 percentage points.
- A January 2019 study by Moritz Maier and Hendrik Scholz examining 699 actively managed European equity funds (2003-2016) found: over 90% of funds showed home bias; France had the highest overweight (30 percentage points), followed by UK (24) and Germany (21); funds average around 16 percentage points overweight domestic stocks; informational advantages do not explain the bias.

The article's central question asks whether home country bias affects stock prices. Victor Haghani and James White of Elm Partners conducted a thought experiment with one large market (US at 50%) and ten small markets (5% each), assuming US investors want 80% domestic allocation and small market investors want 50% domestic allocation. They concluded that home bias creates excess demand for the large US market (pushing it up as much as 60%, from $50 to $80) and a shortfall in smaller markets, reducing expected returns for US equities by about 1.5%. This contradicts active investors' claims that passive investing distorts prices—rather, active home-bias decisions drive the distortion.

Swedroe concludes by noting behavioral biases destroy returns and suggests that believers in market efficiency should accept that all risky assets have similar risk-adjusted returns, eliminating the rationale for home bias. He also notes that US investors whose labor capital is tied to the US economy should consider overweighting foreign markets to offset labor capital risk.
