--- SOURCE 2: Understanding the ICAO Aerodrome... - Aviation-knowledge ---
URL: https://www.facebook.com/AVIO.KNOWLEDGE/posts/understanding-the-icao-aerodrome-reference-code-%EF%B8%8Fever-wondered-how-airports-are-/1681363800696769

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an informational Facebook post by the page Aviation-knowledge (August 8) explaining the ICAO Aerodrome Reference Code, a two-element classification system defined in Annex 14, Volume I, Clause 1.6 of the Chicago Convention. The system links airport design requirements to the physical characteristics of aircraft they serve.

Element 1 – Code Number (1 to 4) is based on the aeroplane reference field length (minimum runway length required for take-off at maximum certified take-off mass, sea level, standard conditions):
- Code 1: Less than 800 m
- Code 2: 800 m to <1,200 m
- Code 3: 1,200 m to <1,800 m
- Code 4: 1,800 m and over

Element 2 – Code Letter (A to F) is based on the greatest wingspan of the aircraft the facility is intended to serve:
- Code A: Up to 15 m (e.g., Cessna 404)
- Code B: 15 m to <24 m (e.g., CRJ-200)
- Code C: 24 m to <36 m (e.g., Boeing 737-700)
- Code D: 36 m to <52 m (e.g., Airbus A310)
- Code E: 52 m to <65 m (e.g., Boeing 787-8/9)
- Code F: 65 m to <80 m (e.g., Airbus A380-800)

The code letter is also used in AIS publications to specify aircraft usage restrictions (e.g., "Code F aircraft subject to special permission"). This classification determines critical airport design parameters including runway width, taxiway clearances, and obstacle-free zones. The example shown in the image is Code 4-F with an 80m wingspan and >1800m runway length, representing the largest aircraft category (Airbus A380) and longest runway requirements.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"This code is a two-element classification system that links airport design requirements to the physical characteristics of the aircraft they serve."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the ICAO postal history collection provides a detailed overview of Annex 14 – Aerodromes, one of the technical annexes to the Chicago Convention developed by ICAO. Key historical facts: the Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs) for Aerodromes were first adopted by the ICAO Council on 29 May 1951, comprising 61 pages at that time. From 9 March 1990, Annex 14 was issued in two volumes: Volume I (Aerodrome Design and Operations) and Volume II (Heliports). Volume I prescribes physical characteristics, obstacle limitation surfaces, and facilities including visual aids and rescue and fire fighting services, and also classifies airports into 10 categories based on movements, aircraft length and fuselage width. Volume II covers Standards for heliport planning, design and operations. The page also details the history of bird strike management: ICAO began collecting bird strike data in 1965, introduced the IBIS (ICAO Bird Strike Information System) reporting system, and introduced a Bird Strike Reporting Form in November 1979. In September 1969, Amendment 23 to Annex 14 recommended bird reduction actions, which became Standards in 2003. Related publications include the Aerodrome Design Manual, Airport Services Manual, Heliport Manual (Doc 9261), and Manual on Certification of Aerodromes. The page also shows related philatelic items from the ICAO collection, including stamps from Gabon (1967), Libya (1984), Botswana, Swaziland, Nauru, and Maldives (all 1994 for ICAO's 50th anniversary), a badge of Italy's National Fire Corps (CNVVF), souvenir covers from the 2011 Global Runway Safety Symposium in Montréal, and a 2019 Kyrgyzstan sheetlet featuring five international airports for ICAO's 75th anniversary.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Aerodromes are one of the most important links in the civil aviation network. They are the key interface between the passengers and the aircraft, and the location where every flight begins and ends."

URL: https://www.aci-europe.org/press-release/537-european-passenger-traffic-finally-exceeds-pre-covid-levels-in-2026.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 12 February 2025, ACI EUROPE released its Full Year 2024 traffic report showing that Europe's airports finally surpassed pre-Covid (2019) passenger volumes, welcoming over 2.5 billion passengers in 2024 — a +7.4% increase over 2023 and +1.8% above 2019 levels. Growth was driven primarily by international traffic (+8.8% vs 2023) rather than domestic (+2.5%, which remained -6.3% below 2019), and was more pronounced in H1 (+8.9%) than H2 (+6%). This reflects structural aviation market changes including partial modal shift to rail, strong EU Single Market cross-border mobility, and growing demand in emerging non-EU markets.

The report highlights a "multi-speed" European airport market: EU+ market airports grew +7.8% versus +4.8% in the rest of Europe, where geopolitics hit Israel (-33.3%), Russia (-13.5%), and Ukraine (no traffic). Nearly half of Europe's airports (47%) remain below pre-pandemic volumes. Small airports (under 1 million passengers) remain -34.5% below 2019 levels, growing at just +5% — the slowest segment. Twenty national markets have not recovered pre-pandemic levels, including Ukraine (-100%), Israel (-41.5%), Finland (-25.1%), and Sweden (-23.5%). In contrast, Albania (+220.8%) and Uzbekistan (+185.9%) led growth versus 2019.

TOP 5 airports by passenger volume in 2024: 1) London Heathrow (83.9M, +5.9% vs 2023, +3.7% vs 2019), 2) Istanbul (80.1M, +5.3%, +16.9% vs 2019), 3) Paris CDG (70.3M, +4.3%, -7.7% vs 2019 — hampered by Olympic Games), 4) Amsterdam Schiphol (66.8M, +8%, -6.8% vs 2019), 5) Madrid (66.1M, +9.9%, +7.2% vs 2019). Rome Fiumicino notably grew +20.7% over 2023. Among major national markets, Türkiye (+9.1%), Italy (+12.6%) and Spain (+12.5%) exceeded pre-pandemic levels, unlike the UK (-0.1%), France (-3.3%), and Germany (-16.6%).

Freight traffic grew strongly at +13.2% in 2024 (+11.8% vs 2019), with Istanbul (1.97M tons, +39.6% vs 2019) replacing Frankfurt as Europe's busiest freight airport, followed by Paris CDG, London Heathrow, Amsterdam Schiphol, and Liège. Aircraft movements rose +5.1% but remained -3.3% below 2019 levels. ACI EUROPE forecasts +4% passenger growth for 2025, subject to review given global political and economic uncertainties, with downside risks from airlines' fleet management issues, ATM capacity shortages, aviation policy, and geopolitics. The report is based on preliminary data from approximately 450 airports. The article is from ACI EUROPE, representing over 600 airports in 55 countries that facilitate over 95% of European commercial air traffic.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Europe's airports welcomed an additional 200 million passengers last year, with many surpassing their previous historic records. This was achieved despite much inflated air fares, continued supply pressures, mostly tepid economic growth and geopolitical tensions. That clearly speaks volumes about how consumers are now prioritising experiences and travel in particular." - Olivier Jankovec, Director General of ACI EUROPE, "But 2024 also confirmed major structural post-Covid shifts, with leisure & Visiting Friends and Relatives (VFR) demand and Low-Cost Carriers largely defining traffic performance – along with airline consolidation, changing air connectivity dynamics and geopolitics. This means that beyond our positive headline results, nearly half of Europe's airports remained below their pre-pandemic traffic levels last year. We are now in a multi-speed European airport market where competitive pressures just keep rising." - Olivier Jankovec, "Looking at the months ahead, we expect demand for air travel to remain resilient – defying fragile consumer confidence and generally sluggish European economies. This webpage is the Eurostat Reference Metadata (ESMS) document for the "Air transport measurement - passengers" (avia_pa) domain, detailing the statistical concepts, methodologies, and quality processes for air transport data collection and dissemination in the EU.

**Data Overview:** The Air transport domain contains national and international intra/extra-EU data, covering passengers (number of passengers), freight and mail (in 1,000 tonnes), and air traffic data on airports, airlines, and aircraft. Data is collected at airport level and compiled under Regulation (EC) N°1358/2003, implementing Regulation N°437/2003. Airports handling less than 15,000 passenger units annually are excluded. Data is transmitted by EU Member States, EFTA countries, and other reporting countries. Statistics based on Regulation 437/2003 are disseminated from reference year 2003 (with some partial data from 1993 onwards).

- Three datasets: Flight Stage (A), On Flight Origin/Destination (B), Airport (C)
- Passengers on board: all passengers landing/taking off, including direct transit passengers (counted at arrivals and departures)
- Passengers carried: passengers counted once per flight, excludes direct transit passengers
- Direct transit passengers: continue on same aircraft and same flight number
- Flight Stage vs. OFOD concepts are not directly comparable due to direct transit passenger treatment (illustrated with a New York-London-Paris example)

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is Version 17 (July 2024) of the "Reference Manual on Air Transport Statistics," the fifteenth version, published by Eurostat. It provides comprehensive methodological, definitional, and procedural guidance for implementing EU Regulation (EC) 437/2003 on statistical returns for the carriage of passengers, freight, and mail by air, along with implementing Regulations 1358/2003, 546/2005, and 158/2007.

The manual is organized into three main parts:
- **Part I (Methodology, Definitions, Classifications):** Describes three core datasets: A1 (Flight Stage data by airport-to-airport routes, including passengers on board, freight/mail on board, commercial air flights, and passenger seats available, reported monthly since 2004); B1 (On Flight Origin/Destination data including passengers carried and freight/mail loaded or unloaded, reported monthly since 2004); and C1 (Airport data including total passengers carried, direct transit passengers, transfer passengers, freight/mail, commercial aircraft movements, and total aircraft movements, with at least annual data required). Key coding standards include ICAO 4-letter airport codes (Document 7910), ICAO airline codes (Document 8585), and ICAO aircraft type designators (Document 8643). Special codes include ZZZ (unknown airline), 888 (confidential), and 999 (all airlines). The manual provides specific guidance on reporting diverted flights, zero traffic (requiring 8 records for A1/B1 datasets per month), and flight type codification (passenger service, all-freight/mail service, or non-commercial). URL: https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/Annexes/avia_paodis_esms_an_2.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the fifteenth version (March 2021) of the "Reference Manual on Air Transport Statistics" produced by Eurostat. It provides comprehensive guidance for implementing Regulation (EC) 437/2003 on statistical returns for the carriage of passengers, freight, and mail by air, along with implementing Commission Regulations 1358/2003, 546/2005, and 158/2007.

The manual is organized into three main parts:
- **Part I**: Methodology, definitions, and classifications
- **Part II**: National methodologies (revised to incorporate individual country metadata accessible via Eurobase and the ESS Metadata Handler)
- **Part III**: Procedures for data treatment and dissemination

**Key Datasets** (per Regulation 1358/2003):
1. **A1 (Flight Stage)**: Airport-to-airport route data broken down by arrivals/departures, scheduled/non-scheduled, passenger/all-freight services, airline, and aircraft type. Includes passengers on board, freight/mail on board, commercial air flights, and passenger seats available.
2. **B1 (On Flight Origin/Destination)**: Data on traffic identified by unique flight number, subdivided by airport pairs based on embarkation/disembarkation points. Includes passengers carried and freight/mail loaded or unloaded.
3. **C1 (Airports)**: Airport-level data including total passengers carried, direct transit passengers, transfer passengers, freight/mail loaded/unloaded, total commercial aircraft movements, and total aircraft movements.

**Important Definitions**:
- Air passenger: any person excluding on-duty crew; infants in arms included
- Aircraft movement: take-off or landing; one arrival + one departure = two movements
- Passenger unit: one passenger OR 100 kg of freight/mail (used for airport classification thresholds)
- Direct transit passengers: passengers continuing on the same aircraft with the same flight number (counted once)
- Transfer/indirect transit passengers: passengers arriving and departing on different aircraft within 24 hours or same aircraft with different flight numbers (counted twice)

**Airport Categories**:
- Category 3 (>1.5M passenger units/year): must report A1, B1, and C1
- Category 2 (150,000–1.5M): must report A1, B1, and C1 (may have had derogations 2003-2005)
- Category 1 (15,000–150,000): must report C1 only
- Category 0 (<15,000): no reporting obligation, but data may be provided

**Coding Systems**:
- Country codes: 2-letter codes based on ICAO nationality prefixes (e.g., EB=Belgium, LF=France, ED=Germany)
- Airport codes: 4-letter ICAO codes per Document 7910; "ZZZZ" for unknown partner airports
- Airline codes: 3-letter ICAO codes per Document 8585, with alternatives including "1+ISO" (EU licensed), "2+ISO" (non-EU), 1EU, or 1NE; special codes ZZZ (unknown), 888 (confidential), 999 (all airlines)
- Aircraft codes: 4-letter ICAO per Document 8643; "ZZZZ" for unknown types

**Transmission Requirements**:
- Data must be transmitted no later than six months after the reference period (e.g., January data by July of the same year)
- Acceptable formats: CSV (semicolon-separated) and SDMX-ML
- STRUVAL replaced EVE as the EDAMIS validation engine in Q2 2019; Genedi was phased out
- Reporting countries should provide airline information at the highest level of detail available

**Type of Flight Codification Guideline**:
- If flight has at least one passenger: "Passenger service flight" (Code 1)
- If no passengers but freight/mail: "All-freight and mail service flight" (Code 2)
- If no passengers, freight, or mail: non-commercial flight, should not be reported

**Diverted Flight Reporting** (flights returning to departure airport due to weather/technical issues):
- Recommended: treat as non-commercial, exclude from A1 and B1, report only in C1 aircraft movements
- Alternative: report in A1/C1 with specific rules (all passengers as direct transit in A1, transfer passengers in C1), but never in B1

- EU air passenger numbers increased by 8.3% in 2024 compared to 2023, reaching 1.1 billion passengers—higher than pre-pandemic 2019 levels (1.0 billion). All EU countries recorded growth.
- Hungary had the highest increase (+19.2%), followed by Czechia (+18.9%). Sweden (+3.8%) and Bulgaria (+1.3%) had the lowest growth.
- Among EFTA and candidate countries, Norway and Montenegro both grew 15.2%, followed by Switzerland (+8.8%) and Türkiye (+8.4%).
- Monthly data showed growth every month in 2024, with the largest increase in February (+13.0%), followed by March (+12.1%) and May (+10.0%).

**Transport by type (2024):**
- Extra-EU transport dominated at 49.3% of total air passenger transport, followed by intra-EU (36.4%) and domestic (14.3%).
- National transport's share fell 0.7 pp to benefit extra-EU (+0.3 pp) and intra-EU (+0.4 pp).
- International transport rose in all EFTA/candidate countries, highest in Norway (+18.2%). National transport declined in Iceland (-1.8%) and Serbia (-3.0%).

**Top routes and airports:**
- Spain was involved in 6 of the top 10 intra-EU country-to-country flows; Spain-Germany represented 21.4% of the top 10 routes and 7.6% of all intra-EU transport.
- Paris Charles de Gaulle was the largest EU airport with 70.3 million passengers, followed by Amsterdam Schiphol (66.8M), Madrid Barajas (66.1M), Frankfurt Main (61.5M), Barcelona El Prat (54.9M), Roma Fiumicino (46.7M), and München (41.5M).
- Amsterdam Schiphol led in passenger flights with 456,000.
- All top EU airports grew in passengers; Roma Fiumicino (+20.8%) had the highest growth.
- Barcelona El Prat - Palma de Mallorca was the top intra-EU airport pair (2.3 million travelers); 7 of top 10 routes were domestic.

**Distance bands:**
- For distances over 2,000 km, extra-EU transport represented 80.5% in 2023-2024.
- Intra-EU dominated distances between 500-1,499 km.
- National transport dominated distances under 500 km (74.3% for under 300 km).
- Shares remained relatively stable 2022-2024.

**Extra-EU markets:**
- Europe (except EU) was the main extra-EU destination with 56.7% of total extra-EU transport.
- Eastern Asia saw the highest relative growth (+43.0%); Central Asia and Oceania each had only 0.1% shares.

**Data sources:** Statistics derived from Eurostat aviation database, with definitions per Regulation (EC) No 1358/2003 implementing Regulation (EC) No 437/2003.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: World's Busiest Airports: Atlanta Holds, Asia Climbs. Strong Demand while Asia-Pacific Growth Reshape the Rankings | ACI World ---
URL: https://aci.aero/2026/07/15/worlds-busiest-airports-atlanta-holds-asia-climbs-strong-demand-while-asia-pacific-growth-reshape-the-rankings

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 15 July 2026, ACI World released the 2026 ACI World Airport Traffic Dataset, confirming global air travel reached 9.8 billion passengers in 2025, approaching the 10 billion threshold. The dataset covers 2,817 airports across more than 180 countries and territories, showing global passenger traffic rose 3.7% over 2024 and 6.5% above 2019 levels. The world's 20 busiest airports handled 1.59 billion passengers (16% of global travelers).

Asia-Pacific airports led ranking shifts. Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KUL) was the biggest mover, rising from 26th to 20th place with 63.4 million passengers (+11% YoY). Shanghai Pudong (PVG) climbed from 10th to 5th with 84.9 million passengers (+10.7%), driven by visa policy easing and China's aviation market reopening. Guangzhou Baiyun (CAN) fell to 57th in 2022 after topping the table in 2020, but returned to 9th in 2025.

Atlanta (ATL) retained the No. 1 position with 106.3 million passengers despite a 1.6% decline. Dubai (DXB, 95.2 million, +3.1%) held second and Tokyo Haneda (HND, 91.7 million, +6.7%) third, both closing the gap on Atlanta. Five of the top 20 airports are US-based, mostly domestic hubs (80-95% domestic traffic), with LAX the exception at 68% domestic.

Global air cargo exceeded 131 million metric tonnes in 2025, up 3.3% YoY and 7.4% above 2019, driven by e-commerce and supply chain restructuring. The top 20 cargo airports handled nearly 41% of global volumes. Hong Kong (HKG) retained the top cargo ranking with 5.1 million metric tonnes. Memphis (MEM) dropped from 3rd to 6th after losing the US Postal Service contract, with volumes falling 20.9%.

Global aircraft movements exceeded 103.1 million in 2025, up 2.0%, nearing pre-2019 levels. Chicago O'Hare (ORD) claimed the top spot with 857,000 movements (+10.5%), displacing Atlanta (ATL) which had led since 2020. Dallas/Fort Worth (DFW) held 3rd with 743,000 movements.

ACI World Director General Justin Erbacci commented: "Global air travel is approaching a historic milestone, but record demand is also exposing growing pressures on capacity. The planning and investment decisions made today will determine whether aviation can meet the demands of the next generation of travellers."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Global air travel is approaching a historic milestone, but record demand is also exposing growing pressures on capacity. The planning and investment decisions made today will determine whether aviation can meet the demands of the next generation of travellers." — ACI World Director General Justin Erbacci, "In 2025, global air travel reached 9.8 billion passengers, bringing the industry closer than ever to the 10 billion-passenger threshold", "Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KUL) was the biggest mover in the top 20, rising six places from 26th in 2024 to 20th in 2025", "Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) retained the No. 1 position with 106.3 million passengers in 2025, despite a year-on-year decline of 1.6%", "Memphis International Airport (MEM) dropped from 3rd to 6th after losing the US Postal Service contract in late 2024, with volumes falling 20.9%"

URL: https://aci.aero/2026/01/28/aci-world-releases-global-airport-traffic-forecasts-as-long-term-demand-growth-continues-to-reshape-aviation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 28 January 2026, from Montreal, Airports Council International (ACI) World released its World Airport Traffic Forecasts (WATF) 2025–2054, described as the industry's most comprehensive and authoritative outlook on global airport traffic. Key forecast figures include 10.2 billion passengers in 2026 and 18.8 billion by 2045.

Sustained Growth Outlook: The long-term outlook is firmly positive, with global passenger traffic demand projected to more than double by the mid-2040s, driven primarily by emerging and developing markets. However, this growth is increasingly accompanied by challenges including capacity constraints and insufficient investment risks.

Call for Collective Action: ACI World Director General Justin Erbacci warned that long-term growth is not guaranteed without coordinated action. He called for accelerated investment in airport infrastructure, airspace capacity, and operational resilience, along with strengthened collaboration across airports, airlines, governments, regulators, and industry partners. Erbacci noted that capacity constraints could create operational bottlenecks affecting passenger journey quality, while insufficient investment would result in missed economic development opportunities—noting aviation contributes 3.9% of global GDP (per ATAG).

About the WATF: The WATF 2025–2054 provides a comprehensive 30-year outlook covering passenger traffic, air cargo, and aircraft movements across 176 markets. It uses advanced machine-learning models to deliver highly accurate, transparent forecasts to support data-driven planning and investment decisions.

About ACI: ACI is the trade association of the world's airports, a federated organization comprising ACI World, ACI Africa, ACI Asia-Pacific and Middle East, ACI EUROPE, ACI Latin America and the Caribbean, and ACI North America. As of January 2025, ACI serves 830 members operating 2,181 airports in 170 countries. The Executive Summary of the forecast is available for download.

Contact details: Sabrina Guerrieri, Director of Communications at ACI World, is the media contact (mediarelations@aci.aero, +1 514 373 1254). ACI World is headquartered at 1500-800 rue du Square Victoria, Montréal, Québec H3C 0B4, Canada.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The forecast sends a clear signal to the global aviation community: long-term growth is not guaranteed without coordinated action," said ACI World Director General Justin Erbacci. "To accommodate rising demand, the industry must accelerate investment in airport infrastructure, airspace capacity, and operational resilience, while strengthening collaboration across airports, airlines, governments, regulators, and industry partners.", "Ensuring the sector can sustainably absorb future demand growth is therefore not only an industry priority, but a global economic imperative.", "Without collective action, capacity constraints jeopardize the industry's ability to meet the projected demand and create operational bottlenecks, directly affecting the quality and reliability of the passenger journey."

# Report: Tri-Cities Airport contributed $233 million to region’s economy in 2019

by: [Slater Teague](https://www.wjhl.com/author/slater-teague/ "Posts by Slater Teague")

233-million-to-regions-economy-in-2019%2F)

NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WJHL) — The Tri-Cities Airport had an economic impact of more than $233 million and brought in more than 80,000 visitors in 2019, according to a new report by the Tennessee Department of Transportation.

[The report](https://www.tn.gov/content/dam/tn/tdot/aeronautics/TASP-Economic%20Impact%20Brochure%20FINAL.pdf) says the airport contributed $233,294,000 to the region’s economy, including $80.6 million through payroll and $109.2 million in visitor spending.

Tri-Cities Airport supported 1,661 jobs in 2019 as well, according to the report.

The airport says it is also home to 28 companies that employ more than 400 people.

args.summary:
Published by WJHL on February 4, 2021, this news article reports that the Tri-Cities Airport had an economic impact of more than $233 million and brought in more than 80,000 visitors in 2019, according to a report by the Tennessee Department of Transportation. The airport contributed $233,294,000 to the region's economy, including $80.6 million through payroll and $109.2 million in visitor spending. Tri-Cities Airport supported 1,661 jobs in 2019 and is home to 28 companies employing more than 400 people.

The article also breaks down the economic contributions of five smaller airports in the Tennessee portion of News Channel 11's viewing area, which collectively contributed nearly $35.7 million to the region's economy and supported 278 jobs:
- Elizabethton Municipal Airport: 74 jobs, $4,071,000 payroll, $1,756,000 visitor spending, $9,651,000 total economic impact
- Greeneville Municipal Airport: 180 jobs, $8,414,000 payroll, $3,789,000 visitor spending, $23,323,000 total economic impact
- Hawkins County Airport (Rogersville): 11 jobs, $595,000 payroll, $9,000 visitor spending, $1,421,000 total economic impact
- Johnson City Airport: 5 jobs, $131,000 payroll, <$1,000 visitor spending, $292,000 total economic impact
- Johnson County Airport (Mountain City): 8 jobs, $374,000 payroll, $39,000 visitor spending, $1,004,000 total economic impact

The article was written by Slater Teague.

# Economic impact study: MEM supports 67,550 jobs and $10.7 billion in economic output in TN

Memphis International Airport

[blog](https://flymemphis.com/news/blog/), [news](https://flymemphis.com/news/news/)

![](https://i0.wp.com/flymemphis.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/MEM-Economic-Impact-Study-2024-FINAL-REPORT-16Jan2026_Page_01-scaled.png?fit=1024%2C1455&ssl=1)

MEMPHIS, TENN. (February 23, 2026) – The Tennessee Association of Air Carrier Airports (TAACA), representing the state’s five primary commercial service airports in Chattanooga, Knoxville, Memphis, Nashville, and the Tri-Cities, released the findings of its 2025 Economic Impact Study – based on calendar year 2024 data. The study affirms the aviation industry’s significant and expanding role as a driver of economic growth across Tennessee.

Memphis International Airport (MEM) is highlighted as a major economic engine for Tennessee’s economy according to the study, with data revealing that MEM supports 67,550 local jobs and generates $10.7 billion in statewide economic output.

The study was conducted by InterVISTAS Consulting, an internationally recognized aviation and transportation consulting firm with a proven record of delivering comprehensive economic impact analyses, air service development initiatives, strategic and business plans, market assessments, and economic recovery strategies for airports, transportation systems, tourism organizations, business associations, and government clients.

The study evaluated the economic contributions generated by aviation activity at Tennessee’s commercial airports, including job creation, personal income, business revenue, and tax generation. The findings demonstrate the far-reaching economic value of commercial aviation to communities across the state, supporting thousands of jobs, enabling tourism and commerce, and generating substantial federal, state, and local tax revenues.

**Tennessee’s Five Primary Commercial Service Airports impact is as follows:**

* $28.3 billion in total economic impact for Tennessee.
* Over 171,000 Tennessee jobs are facilitated by airport activity.
* Contributes to $4.1 billion in total taxes which includes $2.5 billion in federal, $1.08 billion in state and $548 million in local taxes.
* This represents an $8.8 billion, 45%, increase in economic impact since the State of Tennessee sponsored CY19 study.

**Key findings for MEM:**

* $10.7 billion in statewide economic impact
* Of the $10.7 billion, $8.34 billion came from on-airport activities, $1.9 billion from visitor spending, and $402 million from capital improvements.
* Contributes to $1.5 billion in total taxes which includes $1.1 billion in federal, $300 million in state and $100 million in local taxes.

In reference to MEM, the report stated, “The airport’s economic benefits are reflected not only in the employment and income it supports directly, but also in its broader contributions to the regional economy through GDP and economic output.”

The study also underscores the need for continued investment in terminal facilities, airfield infrastructure, and roads to meet future demand and remain competitive. These findings will support collaboration among Airport Authority leadership, the business community, and elected stakeholders to advance projects at the airport to strengthen the region’s economy and workforce.

MEM’s economic impact report can be found [here](https://flymemphis.com/reports/mem-economic-impact-study-2024-final-report-16jan2026/).

“This recent study demonstrates MEM’s role as a significant economic engine within the state of Tennessee,” said Terry Blue, President and CEO of the Memphis Shelby County Airport Authority. “MEM takes great pride in its integral role not only locally and statewide, but across the Mid-South region by connecting people and commerce to the world.”

This is the Tri-Cities Local News page (hvbcgroup.com/news) for late August 2026, covering local news for the Tri-Cities area (Tennessee/Virginia). The page lists news from stations WTFM, WVEK, WRZK, WKPT, WOPI, and WKTP.

Top breaking news stories (August 21, 2026):
- Hard Rock Hotel and Casino Bristol donated over $15,000 to fund a new Police K-9 for the Bristol Virginia Police Department.
- A Damascus, Virginia man faces multiple gun and drug charges; firearms, methamphetamine, and ammunition were seized from his home, and he remains in Southwest Virginia Jail.
- East Tennessee State University (ETSU) officially opened its new 67,000-square-foot academic building featuring 27 classrooms, 22 collaboration spaces, and four recording studios.
- More than 130 bronze cemetery vases stolen from cemeteries across Northeast Tennessee and Southwest Virginia were recovered after an anonymous tip.
- Sullivan County Commission voted not to renew its contract with Flock Safety, ending the county's license plate reader (flock camera) use.

Other stories from August 20-21, 2026:
- ETSU announced BigXthaPlug and Shelailai will perform at its fall SGA concert October 7 at Freedom Hall.
- The American Eagle Foundation and Dollywood are moving non-releasable bald eagles from Eagle Mountain Sanctuary to the foundation's 50-acre campus in Kodak.
- A new economic impact study shows Tri-Cities Airport supported about 2,100 Tennessee jobs and $289 million in economic activity in 2024, with ~130,000 visitors.
- A man accused of stabbing three women in Blountville on Highland Drive is in custody and expected to be arraigned.
- The suspect in the fatal Milligan Cycling team crash, John Benfield (69, of Newland, NC), was freed on bond after a judge set his bond, later doubled to $300,000; he faces two counts of reckless vehicular charges.
- Former Kingsport doctor Scott McLain was arrested again on charges of domestic assault, false imprisonment, and retaliation following a dispute with his fiancée.
- Tennessee hunters can hunt without a license this Saturday for Free Hunting Day (TWRA).
- Greeneville's Municipal Airport Authority is finalizing a long-range improvement plan with the state outlining projects through 2032.
- TBI issued an Endangered Child Alert for 15-year-old Gabriella Carpenter at the request of the Washington County Sheriff's Office.
- Washington County deputies arrested 28-year-old Bailey Dalton Williams after reports of an armed man firing shots on Antioch Road.
- Networks Sullivan Partnership received a 2026 Silver Award from the International Economic Development Council for its redesigned website.
- Johnson City Water and Sewer Services to install a new waterline connection near North Roan Street and West Springbrook Drive.
- Washington County deputies arrested 40-year-old Tyrone Jackson of Bristol after a traffic stop on Apache Drive (stolen handgun).
- Food City distributed $800,000 to more than 1,000 schools through its School Bucks program for the 2025-26 year.
- A precautionary boil water advisory is in effect for parts of Bristol, Virginia, while the Washington County Service Authority repairs a water line.
- A North Carolina man accused in the fatal crash involving the Milligan University Cycling team was arraigned in Carter County General Sessions Court.

Massad Boulous, the US’s senior advisor for Africa, stated the US International Development Finance Corporation DFC will be involved in the project. The new airport aims to relieve congestion at Bole International Airport and support the expansion of Ethiopian Airlines, ultimately planning to handle over 100 million passengers and nearly 4 million tonnes of cargo annually by 2029. African aviation expert Sean Mendis and African aviation analyst Sindy Foster highlight both strategic and commercial motivations behind the US decision. Mendis notes the current Bole Airport's high altitude restricts non-stop flights to North America, an issue the lower-altitude Bishoftu Airport will resolve, benefiting Ethiopian Airlines and potentially allowing Boeing to sell more planes. Foster suggests this move helps anchor US influence and offers an alternative financing model in a critical corridor. The project also strengthens the relationship between Ethiopian Airlines, a major Boeing customer, and the US. Some analysts also see this as an effort to counter China's influence in the region, though Mendis is skeptical it will significantly diminish China's construction dominance. The investment is also considered a safe decision with potential for high returns due to Ethiopian Airlines' success and the Ethiopian market's stability.   ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL IDENTITY IN AVIATION ⛳ Ahead of Zambia's 61st Independence Day Celebrations, let's take a trip down memory lane in order for us to understand the history of civil aviation activities and the formation of some of the cornerstone bodies in Zambia. Zambia inherited Northern Rhodesia’s aviation infrastructure after gaining independence on 24th October 1964. This included aerodromes, air traffic services, and control facilities previously managed under the British colonial administration. The new government sought to assert national sovereignty by developing its own civil aviation authority and aviation policies separate from the Central African Federation system. FORMATION OF ZAMBIA AIRWAYS ✈️ The creation of Zambia Airways (initially Zambia Airways Corporation) was one of the most significant achievements shortly after independence. It was established as a national flag carrier in December 1964, symbolizing Zambia’s freedom to operate its own international air services. The airline began operations using aircraft inherited from Central African Airways and later expanded regional and international routes, promoting trade and tourism. DEVELOPMENT OF KEY AERODROMES AND AIRPORT INFRASTRUCTURE 🏗️ Lusaka Airport (later Kenneth Kaunda International Airport) became the main international gateway, replacing Salisbury (now Harare) as Zambia’s hub after the breakup of the Federation. The government prioritized upgrading runways, terminal facilities, and navigation aids to meet ICAO standards and accommodate larger aircraft. Ndola and Livingstone Airports were also modernized to handle increasing domestic and regional air traffic. ESTABLISHMENT OF INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS THROUGH AVIATION 🔗 Zambia joined the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) soon after independence, aligning its civil aviation framework with international standards. Bilateral air service agreements were signed with countries like the United Kingdom, Kenya, and South Africa to facilitate air connectivity and diplomacy. SYMBOL OF NATIONAL UNITY AND PROGRESS 🕊️ During the 1964 Independence Day celebrations, aircraft flyovers and air displays were featured as part of the national festivities, symbolizing technological progress and national pride. Aviation was presented as a gateway to modernization, linking Zambia’s provinces and neighboring countries to promote unity and economic development. LAYING THE FOUNDATION FOR CIVIL AVIATION REGULATION 🏛️ The independence period also saw the groundwork for what would become the Department of Civil Aviation, later evolving into the Zambia Civil Aviation Authority (ZCAA). The new department began developing policies on air safety, licensing, and infrastructure oversight, ensuring compliance with international aviation safety standards.

args.summary:
This LinkedIn feed page contains multiple posts about global aviation economics and infrastructure developments, with a heavy focus on Africa.

1. **Graham Webb's Post (Pratt & Whitney VP)**: Highlights the ATAG "Aviation Benefits Beyond Borders" report showing aviation's global economic impact: 4.4 billion passengers in 2023 served by 1,138 commercial airlines and 4,072 airports; civil aviation supports 86.5 million jobs and contributes $4.1 trillion (3.9% of global GDP); nearly 61.4 million tonnes of air cargo represents 33% of global trade by value (~$8 trillion). The report projects aviation will account for $8.5 trillion in economic activity by 2043.

2. **US-Ethiopia $10B Airport Project** (covered by multiple posts including Baobab Pulse, POA English, and CA Rohit Upadhyaya): The US has pledged support — via the International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) and other institutions — for Ethiopia's new $10 billion Bishoftu International Airport, located 40km south of Addis Ababa. Expected to become Africa's largest by 2030, the airport aims to relieve congestion at Bole International Airport, handle over 100 million passengers and nearly 4 million tonnes of cargo annually by 2029, and support Ethiopian Airlines expansion. Analysts note the lower altitude resolves altitude-related restrictions on non-stop flights to North America, strengthens US-Ethiopian/Boeing ties, counters China's Belt & Road influence, and represents US infrastructure diplomacy in the Horn of Africa.

3. **Latin American Aviation (Abogados Sierra)**: Aviation accounts for 3.6% of Latin America's GDP, contributing ~$240 billion through direct, indirect, and induced effects.

4. **African Aviation (Bernard Onguso)**: Fuel accounts for up to 51% of Direct Operating Costs for African airlines; producing Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) locally could unlock a revenue stream worth 3-5x the value of conventional jet fuel, though the "Africa Risk Premium" deters global capital.

5. **DSKAFOS Africa Aviation & Maritime Update (Sept 2025)**: Nigeria evaluating COMAC C919 certification; African states won 8 ICAO Council seats; Tanzania-Zambia aviation partnership renewal; Cairo remains Africa's busiest airport (1.6M seats, October 2025); Astral Aviation launched Haikou-Johannesburg cargo route; new Mogadishu International Airport under construction; maritime items include Red Sea security risks and BlackRock/GIP interest in Nigerian aviation and port infrastructure.

6. **Zambia Aviation History (Michael Malobeka)**: Zambia inherited Northern Rhodesia's aviation infrastructure after independence on October 24, 1964, established flag carrier Zambia Airways in December 1964, developed key airports (Lusaka/Kenneth Kaunda International became the main international gateway), joined ICAO after independence, and laid groundwork for what became the Zambia Civil Aviation Authority.

7. **SAF Collaboration (Christopher Surgenor/GreenAir)**: The African Development Bank and Japanese engineering group JGC signed a letter of intent at TICAD9 in Yokohama to collaborate on SAF production in Africa; an AFRAA survey found low SAF access for African carriers but strong support for cooperation.

8. **Incheon Airport (Modalis)**: South Korea's Incheon Airport secured $407M abroad, but nearly two in three overseas projects lost money.

args.summary:
This webpage from ATAG (Air Transport Action Group) highlights the economic and social benefits of air transport globally. Air transport supports 86.5 million jobs worldwide (11.6 million direct jobs) and generates $4.1 trillion in total global economic impact. If aviation were a country, it would rank 20th in GDP. Aviation facilitates tourism (58% of international tourists travel by air), trade, connectivity, poverty alleviation, and disaster response. In December 2024, ATAG published its flagship report "Aviation: Benefits Beyond Borders," which provides global and regional analyses.

Key regional data from the report:
- Africa: 8.1 million jobs and $75 billion GDP; forecast to reach 16 million jobs and $190 billion GDP by 2043
- Asia-Pacific: 34.7% share of global passenger traffic (1.4 billion passengers in 2023), 42 million jobs, $890 billion GDP; forecast to reach 62 million jobs and $2.3 trillion GDP by 2043
- Europe: 25.9% share of global passenger traffic (988 million passengers in 2023), 15 million jobs, $1.2 trillion in economic activity; forecast to reach 21 million jobs and $2.1 trillion GDP by 2043
- Latin America and the Caribbean: 8.3 million jobs and $240 billion in economic activity
- Middle East: 4 million jobs and $290 billion in GDP
- North America: 8.4 million jobs and $1.4 trillion in economic activity

The report also provides detailed regional summaries for Africa, Asia-Pacific, Europe, Latin America and the Caribbean, the Middle East, North America, APEC economies, EU, ASEAN member states, small island states, developing countries, OECD countries, least-developed countries, and landlocked developing countries. The full report is available free of charge at aviationbenefits.org.

# Policy Brief: Taxation of International Air Transport and Airports – Economic Benefits and Costs

#### Service Area

Policy Analysis & Regulations

![Orange plan waiting at gate during sunrise.](https://www.intervistas.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/lucas-silva-pinheiro-santos-_sN2I7lsvZs-unsplash-1920x1080.jpg)

## Project Brief

InterVISTAS was commissioned by ACI World to prepare a policy brief on the impacts of taxation on aviation. The analysis included quantifying the current levels of taxation globally, and calculating the economic impacts associated with the travel demand suppressed by that taxation. The brief also discussed important policy implications associated with taxation and provides guidance for policy makers on issues to consider when taxing aviation. A series of case studies on taxation were also completed for each of the ACI World regions.

## Approach

To obtain the necessary information to complete the study, InterVISTAS relied on a number of different sources, techniques and applications. This included using a variety of data sources to collect information on taxes globally, including ACI sources as well as other industry data.

Using multiplier analysis, direct, indirect and induced economic impacts were assessed, both on a global and regional level. Estimates of demand elasticities were also used to calculate the suppressed demand levels due to taxation levels.

## Results

### The key findings of the report are:

* There is a common misconception between charges and taxes in aviation
* Estimated taxes on aviation equate to US $90 billion globally
* The removal of the tax burden could lead to additional passenger traffic (750 million passengers) and resulting GDP and jobs impacts (US$ 93 billion direct GDP and 2.2 million aviation jobs)

The report also covered a number of policy recommendations for countries globally, including the need to remove complicated tax regimes.

InterVISTAS-ga2 would like to thank the sponsors, listed above, for their support in this study. The study results further illustrate the benefits to communities that have liberalized, or plan to liberalize and expand their air services agreements.
2 Liberalizing only 320 bilateral agreements of the existing thousands would create 24.1 million full-time jobs and generate an additional $490 billion in Gross Domestic Product. This corresponds to an economy almost the size of Brazil.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY This study found extensive and significant evidence that supports the generally accepted “conventional wisdom” that liberalization of air services between countries generates significant additional opportunities for consumers, shippers, and the numerous direct and indirect entities and individuals affected by such liberalization. Conversely, it is also evident that restrictive bilateral air services agreements between countries stifle air travel, tourism and business, and, consequently, economic growth and job creation. Prominent findings of the study are: x Traffic growth subsequent to liberalization of air services agreements between countries typically averaged between 12% and 35%, significantly greater than during years preceding liberalization. In a number of situations, growth was at rates exceeding 50%, and in some cases reached almost 100% of the pre-liberalization rates. x A simulation of the likely results of liberalizing 320 country pair markets that are not today in an Open Skies (deregulated) mode indicate traffic growth, on average, of almost 63%. This is substantially higher than typical world traffic growth of around 6%-8%. Liberalizing only these 320 bilateral agreements of the 2,000 in our database would create 24.1 million full-time jobs and generate an additional $490 billion in Gross Domestic Product. This corresponds to an economy almost the size of Brazil. x The creation of the Single European Aviation Market in 1993 led to an average annual growth rate in traffic between 1995 and 2004 that was almost double the rate of growth in the years 1990 to 1994. This produced about 1.4 million new jobs. x A simulation of full liberalization of the United States-United Kingdom market under a Comprehensive First Step Air Service Agreement (ASA) between the United States and the European Union would produce an almost 29% increase in traffic. Some of the increase results from the impact of lower fares, while the remainder would result from allowing any U.S. city to obtain nonstop service to London’s Heathrow or Gatwick airports. The economic benefits of this liberalization would be substantial. There would be an additional 117,000 new jobs generated, and the incremental GDP impact to both the U.S. and to the UK would be roughly $7.8 billion. x An examination of 190 countries and 2,000 bilateral air service agreements suggests that there are still a number of countries that place a priority on protecting their flag carrier(s), rather than enhancing the overall welfare of the broader public interest. 3 A. BACKGROUND Commercial aviation owes its existence to the rapid development and application of technology. Modern aerospace technology allows aircraft to operate efficiently and safely under a very wide range of conditions, to areas and climates throughout the world. Air service is widely available, and allows even the poorest nations access to the most advanced products. The new, ultra-long range aircraft can operate nonstop flights to points so distant that airlines must decide whether to fly east, over the Atlantic and northern Europe, or west across the Pacific and the Far East, to reach their destination. But the most important contribution of technology has been to lower the cost of air travel. Fuel-efficient engines and aerodynamic surfaces, low maintenance and modular components, and improved materials have progressively allowed airlines to lower air fares, thereby allowing more and more people to use air transportation on a routine basis. This diffusion has permitted commercial aviation to play a far more important role in peoples’ lives. However, commercial aviation still faces a challenge common to many of the newer and more technically advanced areas of our society. Our transportation political and trade institutions have not kept pace with the evolution of technology or the needs of the public. Commercial aviation remains encumbered by well meaning but outmoded and arcane rules, principles and institutions. These rules and regulations often prevent fit, willing and able airlines from fully serving passengers and shippers who are completely willing and able to pay. They also impose protective machinery that frustrates innovation, and has in the past directed the evolution of the industry into a contrived and artificial structure. By sheltering airlines from market forces, they reduce the incentives for them to pass the benefits of improved technologies on to passengers, shippers and investors. International air commerce today is still, in many respects, governed by a framework of rules laid down in the post World War II era. Despite today’s trend toward global markets, free trade, the internet, and the economic integration of entire continents, one of the most globalized, technology-intensive industries remains encumbered by rules that stifle competition and prevent airlines, communities, passengers, and shippers from benefiting to the fullest. The “bilateral air service agreements” (ASAs) that continue to govern much of world trade in aviation define the terms under which airlines will link their two home territories. These ASAs often frustrate market growth, force users to pay a price premium, and create a series of vested interests. The proponents of continuing protection are often large, powerful vested interests, who consider that they have much to lose from its abolition. The beneficiaries are often small and fragmented. They include actual and would-be passengers and shippers, hotel operators, airports, and the huge numbers of people who could or might be employed in the tourism, transportation, or manufacturing industries. The collective benefits, while very large, are so widely distributed that few persons or organizations perceive that they have a major interest in reform. The benefits, permeating throughout the economy, are 4 often so difficult to trace that many are not even aware that they could benefit. Often, even those who oppose liberalization could gain, but would face certain transitional risks, and would have to modify their business methods. This imbalance has fostered a “comfortable status quo,” in which the wide but diffuse benefits of air liberalization are subordinated to the interests of the minority. A society that is unaware of the magnitude of the benefits, whose individuals are unaware that a change could help them, and cannot estimate the payoffs in any meaningful way, is unlikely to be able to reap the full rewards of liberalization. These factors suggest that a key to reforming the regulatory environment surrounding international air travel is education. Specifically, a society can only make a rational choice between protectionism and competition if it knows: x That the incremental benefits can be very large; x That the benefits are widely diffused among many individuals and organizations; x That many sectors could benefit, such as the tourism industry, trade/transportation and manufacturing; x That many persons who may not perceive themselves as actually benefiting could in fact be made better off; x That even those most opposed to the change could benefit if they can change their behavior accordingly; and x That these benefits can often be gained at minimal public expenditure. B. OBJECTIVES OF THE STUDY The broad objective of this study is to attempt to quantify the results of both historical and prospective bilateral air service agreement (ASA) liberalization. In order to accomplish that objective, a number of subsidiary programs have been pursued. Thus, InterVISTAS-ga2 examined the economic consequences of the liberalization of air transport throughout the world. Specific subsidiary objectives were: x To examine recent instances of air service liberalization, or lack thereof, and identify their most important consequences on competition, traffic growth, carrier behavior and national economic benefits; x To develop a flexible and robust analytical model, with all associated databases, so that the benefits of liberalization can be quantified prospectively for any arbitrary country-pair, or groups of country-pairs; and 5 This report summarizes the development of a methodology to quantify the benefits of international air service liberalization. x To promote a more informed public debate on the historical and potential benefits of liberalization of air services agreements between countries.
This study summarizes the research performed in pursuit of these objectives. This project has created a mathematical framework of worldwide applicability. While the model is unique in its sophistication and versatility, the project is still but one of a large group of analyses of the consequences of liberalization. While the assumptions, methodologies and results vary widely, the models clearly demonstrate the importance of high quality and reasonably priced air service to world economic development and job growth. C.
FINDINGS & CONCLUSIONS This study demonstrates that air service liberalization can promote traffic growth, with an accompanying growth in non-aviation sectors. The sheer scale of the largest airports, and the global reach of the industry, and its technological innovation, support the often cited statistic that the travel and tourism industry drive 12% to 15% of the world output of goods and services. 1. THE ECONOMIC IMPACT OF AIR SERVICES – CURRENT EVIDENCE This report summarizes the development of a methodology to quantify the benefits of international air service liberalization. The approach developed is unique in that it can apply to any arbitrary country-pair and any level of liberalization. Extensive research attests to the importance of commercial aviation to nations in all states of development. Air service liberalization, which replaces a set of strict and arcane rules with the primacy of the market, has repeatedly proven a decisive influence in expanding the industry, and making its benefits available to more people. Many airports, airlines, academic institutions, governments and private organizations have documented the relationship between liberalization and economic growth. These efforts have contributed greatly to our knowledge of liberalization. However, most research has been narrowly focused in one or a very few specific markets. Most of the work has been ex poste and retrospective; contrasting a situation before and after liberalization. The data and models have been very situation-specific, and could not be quickly and simply applied to other markets. This study describes a framework to assess the economic benefits of international air service liberalization in any market, anywhere in the world. Its approach is ex ante; it estimates the impact of liberalization on any market that is presently restrictive. Its global applicability depends on the use of data generated throughout the world, involving over 190 nations and 1,400 country-pairs. The various statistical relationships that form the model not merely accommodate, but, indeed, require this diversity. The model has a wider 6 applicability, greater robustness, and better statistical properties than those developed from more limited and homogeneous sets of data. In keeping with the worldwide focus of the research, the study draws on, to the fullest extent possible, experience obtained throughout the world. The United States, because of its size, and the relatively lengthy period since its domestic market was deregulated, offers among the best examples of market liberalization. Furthermore, American communities and airports have been most active in pursuing new services, and in evaluating the economic impacts of aviation. Section III of this study examines recent evidence on air service liberalization. It does not purport to provide a detailed review of the literature. Rather, it summarizes the highlights of recent research, and establishes a point of departure for the approach to developing the model and related framework. This study, and most others, is based on a causal chain that links changes in air service regulation to changes in the broader economy (Figure 1). Figure 1: The Causal Relationship Between Air Service Liberalization and Economic Growth The failure of any one link can halt the process of expansion. Sometimes, the current regulations, however restrictive, may not constrain market behavior. Policy makers may authorize new services, but if airlines do not wish to operate it, the liberalization would be irrelevant. Many bilateral agreements are rife with “unused authority”; services that are allowed but that have no commercial value. The logical and empirical link between better air services and traffic growth is much stronger, and all evidence suggests that the market responds to improved service. The link between traffic growth and economic growth depends on the level of employment, the propensity to import, and whether the increased air travel diverts expenditures from other forms of consumption, savings and investment. 2. AIR SERVICE LIBERALIZATION AND TRAFFIC GROWTH Airlines are continually fine-tuning their routes to accommodate traffic growth, changes in aircraft technology, airport congestion and other factors. In a mature market, this results in a never-ending “trickle” of schedule changes. When the market fundamentals experience a sudden and dramatic change, a “torrent” of new routes often results. Such Liberalization New and better air services Traffic growth Economic growth Job growth 7 events can include rapid economic growth of the type being experienced in China and India, the availability of new air routes, and, most importantly, market liberalization. As of 2006, many nations have allowed market forces to govern their domestic routes, while a slow, erratic process of “creeping liberalization” has prevailed on many international air corridors. Liberalization has promoted many new services around the world, as testified by Table 1. Table 1: Liberalization and Air Service Growth Event Results U.S. deregulation, 1978 Emergence of hub and spoke systems, low cost carriers with nationwide route networks, new entrants and integrated cargo carriers. Domestic deregulation in Brazil Growth of low cost carrier Gol and others. Single European Market Growth of low cost carriers. Ryanair, Easyjet, etc. New services, traffic growth, new gateways throughout European Union. Published aviation statistics testify to the ability of new air service to stimulate traffic. Table 2 portrays how new services have stimulated traffic. It compares traffic levels in the year immediately preceding inauguration of the new service to volumes in the first full calendar year of operation. Most of the examples result from changes in bilateral air service agreements, or from specific governmental decisions to relax the restrictive provisions of current agreements. 8 Table 2: New International Services and Traffic Growth Passengers/Year City-Pair Service Liberalization Event Before After Gain Vancouver-Phoenix America West 1995 Canada-U.S. Bilateral 31,216* 76,910 146.4% Toronto-Minneapolis Air Canada 1995, Northwest 1995 Canada-U.S. Bilateral 53,020 82,320 55.3% Toronto-New Orleans Air Canada 1998 1995 Canada-U.S. Bilateral 31,390 44,320 41.2% Ottawa-Chicago Air Canada/ American 1995 1995 Canada-U.S. Bilateral 14,720 30,870 109.7% Montreal-Atlanta Delta 1995 1995 Canada-U.S. Bilateral 39,690 61,730 55.5% Atlanta-San Jose CR Delta 1998 1997 U.S.-Costa Rica --118.5% Dallas/Fort Worth-Santiago American 1996 --336.6% Chicago-Hong Kong United 1996 (not daily) U.S.-Hong Kong Bilateral --21.1% Chicago-London United 1995 U.S.-U.K Mini Deal, 1995 545,152+ 774,504+ 42.1% Chicago-Sao Paulo United 1997 --80.4% Chicago-Buenos Aires United 1998 --41.1% Houston-Sao Paulo Continental 1999 --120.5% Atlanta-Guadalajara Delta 1999 --169.5% Washington-Buenos Aires United 2002 Reassignment of routes --208.7% Washington-Sao Paulo United 2002 Reassignment of routes --88.4% Detroit-Beijing Northwest 1996 --174.3% Dallas/Fort Worth-Lima American 1996 --482.0% Houston-Tokyo Continental 1998 1998 U.S.-Japan --116.6% Atlanta-Rome Delta 1999 1998 U.S.-Italy --110.8% Dallas/Fort Worth-Zurich American 2000 1995 Open Skies --115.3% Sources: United States Department of Transportation Databases 1B and 28IS; Statistics Canada Report 51-205, “Air Passenger Origin and Destination, Canada-United States Report.” The U.S. Department of Transport provides public disclosure of raw international origin-destination traffic statistics. Traffic usually requires several years to adjust fully to a new service. Despite the conservative approach, nonstop international services can often cause international traffic to double in only a year, even for city-pairs that already have a profusion of one-stop connecting services. Any mechanism that allows international services to proliferate to non-traditional gateways can be a powerful stimulus to traffic. Restrictive bilateral agreements, through confining service to a few named points, can thwart the growth. They also exacerbate the airside and groundside congestion at the largest gateways. 9 Figure 2: Growth of United States-Canada Traffic, 1990-2004 Passengers (in Millions) Source: United States Department of Transportation Database 28DM Figure 2 depicts United States-Canada passenger flows. Until 1995, this market was governed by a very restrictive bilateral, negotiated in 1966 and updated in 1975. It prohibited nonstop scheduled services on a large number of routes, including Toronto-Washington, Atlanta-Montreal and Vancouver-Denver. Notwithstanding that the two countries had concluded a free trade agreement in 1988, extended to Mexico in 1994, aviation functioned under a constrained bilateral air services agreement. The liberalization of air service in 1995 allowed carriers of either nation to serve any route desired, at commercially determined prices. As shown by the graph, the previously stagnant traffic saw rapid growth after liberalization. 3. AIR TRAFFIC AND ECONOMIC GROWTH Tables 1 and 2 indicate a strong causal relationship between liberalization, air service improvement, and international traffic. Table 3 explores the final step of the causal chain; the relationship between traffic and economic development. Many airports have prepared “economic impact statements” to quantify their influence on their communities. Several measures are used, including Gross Domestic Product, output, employment, investment, and tax revenues. Several methods are available, and assumptions vary widely between each such project. Despite the methodological differences, the studies have reached a worldwide consensus that airports and civil aviation can have an enormous and positive 20 18 16 14 12 10 8 6 4 2 0 Liberalization 1995 2004 1990 1992 1994 1996 1998 2000 2002 10 impact on regional prosperity. Table 3 summarizes economic impact statements for a cross-section of airports and civil aviation activities throughout the world. A further refinement involves measuring the incremental impact of a specific improvement in air service. 4. CATALYTIC EFFECTS FROM AIR SERVICE DEVELOPMENT The relationships explored in Table 3 view the various impacts as the response of a pre-existing economy to incremental changes in civil aviation. It assumes that there will be no changes to the underlying structure of the regional economy. Growing evidence indicates that new air services can lead to changes in the underlying structure of the regional economy by creating new capabilities, and forming a different set of transactor expectations. These reactions can literally create new industries in a region, and allow the area to compete for economic opportunities throughout the world. These “catalytic 11 impacts” are the most difficult to quantify. Although most evidence is anecdotal, there is growing evidence that these effects can be large: x A 10 percent increase in the supply of intercontinental flights creates around a 4 percent increase in the number of headquarters of large firms located in the corresponding urban area … headquarters of knowledge-intensive sectors are much more influenced by the supply of direct intercontinental flights than are those of non-knowledge-intensive sectors.1 x Nine foreign-owned companies in Northern Kentucky cited air service as an important factor in their choice of location. The nine firms collectively employ 1,470 persons.2 x In 2003, Kenya exported 50,000 tonnes of flowers by air freight.3 x The growth of European air transport since 1995 has boosted European Union GDP by 4 percent. The expected growth to 2025 will boost GDP of the 25 European Union nations by a further 1.8 percent.4 x Air service liberalization in Egypt could increase the GDP of the Travel and Tourism industry by 12 percent by 2011, adding 260,000 full time jobs. Furthermore, the total GDP for all sectors would increase by 1.8 percent.5 The evidence cited demonstrates a strong causal link between air service liberalization, traffic growth and economic development. It lends further strength to the need for air service liberalization by illustrating the benefits of successful efforts, and the harmful consequences that have resulted from retaining the status quo. 5. THE ENVIRONMENT Commercial aviation industries are driven by the business realities of competitive market forces that drive continuous innovations in technology that increase airplane efficiencies and minimize environmental impacts. The aviation industry also recognizes that its members must share the leadership required to minimize environmental impacts resulting from air travel growth. 1 Germà Bel and Xavier Fegeda, “Getting There Fast: Globalization, Intercontinental Flights and Location of Headquarters”, Unpublished.
