--- SOURCE 1: [PDF] The Development of a Web-Based Small Airport Economic Impact Model ---
URL: https://static.tti.tamu.edu/tti.tamu.edu/documents/0-7066-R1.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This technical report (Report 0-7066-R1) from the Texas A&M Transportation Institute (TTI), published November 2020, documents the development of a web-based Small Airport Economic Impact Estimator tool, created in cooperation with the Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) and the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA). The project (Project 0-7066) was conducted from November 2019 to October 2020.

**Purpose:** While TxDOT periodically commissions statewide economic impact studies (typically every 5-7 years), airports need more frequent and precise economic impact estimates. Local officials frequently use these numbers to justify airport investments, grant-matching funds, and capital improvements. The tool addresses gaps including airports omitted from statewide studies, privacy concerns with single-tenant data, and changes in activity levels between studies.

**Model Development:** Researchers built an input/output (I/O) model using IMPLAN multipliers, visitor spending data from the Texas Governor's Office, Terminal Area Forecast data from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and data from the recently completed 2018 Texas Aviation Economic Impact Study. The I/O model was selected as the best methodology for small airports due to its practicality, lower data requirements compared to econometric analysis, and verifiable numbers compared to expert surveys.

**Tool Features:** The Small Airport Economic Impact Estimator provides an interface for users to calculate economic impact using default data or new inputs based on current conditions. Users select their airport (from 264 general aviation airports and 15 non-hub commercial service airports in Texas) and calculate impacts across three activity types:
- Airport activity (employment/expenses for airport functioning)
- Visitor activity (visitor spending impacts)
- Tenant/business activity (on-airport business employment/expenses)

It also calculates annual impacts of capital expenditures based on a 3-year average. Outputs include direct, indirect, and induced impacts measured as Employment, Payroll Expenditures, and Output. The tool is designed for airport managers, planners, and local officials, supporting grant applications, local funding matches, new development attraction, and scenario planning for improvements.

**Validation:** The model was tested against results from the 2018 Texas study (for airport activity, general aviation visitor activity, and capital expenses) and validated against CDM Smith study comparisons at five airports: South Texas Regional Airport at Hondo, Sugar Land Regional Airport, Littlefield Taylor Brown Municipal Airport, San Marcos Regional Airport, and Fox Stephens Field–Gilmer Municipal Airport. The tool builds on prior work including the Minnesota DOT's web-based calculator (first developed 2005, updated 2011).

**Key authors:** Jeffrey D. Borowiec, Brianne Glover, Jacqueline Kuzio, Tengxi Wang, Maxwell Steadman, Chris Bratlien, and Bill Prieto. Report is unclassified, 82 pages, accessible through NTIS.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: The Role of Aviation in Supporting Local Economic Activity - CRP ---
URL: https://crp.trb.org/acrpwebresource12/understanding-air-service-and-regional-economic-activity/the-role-of-aviation-in-supporting-local-economic-activity

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage, part of TRB's Cooperative Research Programs (ACRP), examines the role of aviation and air service in supporting local and regional economic activity, particularly employment. The central challenge discussed is causality: whether new air service attracts economic activity or whether growing metropolitan areas cause airlines to add service. Definitive proof is difficult due to proprietary airline contract data, but emerging research using innovative statistical methods supports a consensus that air travel can be a positive, causal trigger for generating additional employment and income in metropolitan economies.

Key research findings highlighted include:
- Bruekner (2003): A 10% increase in passenger traffic raises total employment by 0.9% and service employment by 1.1%.
- McGraw (2020): Airports in midsized/smaller cities contributed to an average 3.9% growth in total employment (and 3.4% population growth) per decade (1950-2010).
- ACRP Research Report 218: Each departing seat at small-hub airports is associated with 0.005 jobs (5 jobs per 1,000 departing seats; a daily 100-seat aircraft departure supports 182.5 jobs). Non-hub airports show 0.0114 jobs per departing seat—over twice the impact of small hubs.

Air service is linked most strongly to particular industries: professional/scientific/technical fields, finance, corporate management/headquarters, IT, and advanced manufacturing. Notable studies include Button and Taylor (2000) on international air service and "new economy" employment; Alkaabi and Debbage (2007) on passenger demand and professional/scientific/technical employment; Sheard (2014) finding a 10% increase in air traffic generates 1,650 additional service jobs in an MSA of 1 million residents; and Blonigen and Cristea (2015) finding a 50% increase in passenger growth leads to a 3.2% increase in annual per-capita income growth and 5.5% increase in employment growth.

The page also explains Input-Output (I-O) models as a way to quantify air service usage by industry sectors. According to BEA data, 53% of air travel purchases are for personal reasons, 16% are exported (international travelers), and 31% is used by industry as an input to goods/services production—this 31% is tied to regional economic activity.

Improved connectivity is shown to strengthen economic activity. Bilotkach (2015) found that connecting an MSA with an extra nonstop destination created 223 jobs and 15 new business establishments on average. Connectivity increases through more capacity, more connecting opportunities, more nonstop destinations (especially hubs), and higher "quality" of destinations. The page describes the IATA connectivity index and MIT's Airport Connectivity Quality Index (ACQI), which weight connections to major hubs and international gateways more heavily than service to small regional destinations.
</summary>

A 10 percent increase in passenger traffic raises total employment by 0.9 percent and service employment by 1.1 percent, suggesting employment gains far beyond the airport. (McGraw 2020), For the non-hubs studied, there was an estimate of 0.0114 jobs per departing seat. This is an average regional impact that is over twice as strong as that shown for small hub airports. (Ballard et al. 2020), A 50 percent increase in the air passenger growth rate leads to an average 3.2 percent increase in the annual growth of per-capita income and an average 5.5 percent increase in the annual rate of employment. --- SOURCE 5: Chapter 4 The Role of the Airport in the Local Economy ---
URL: https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is Chapter 4 ("The Role of the Airport in the Local Economy") of a 2025 National Academies publication titled "Communicating a Balanced Look at Local Airport Activity and Climate Change." The chapter presents new research to help airports supplement their own economic impact studies to better explain to stakeholders and communities the important role that commercial service and general aviation (GA) airports play in the local economy. The central question addressed: Since aviation climate effects are so expensive to abate, what benefits would be lost by curtailing aviation activity?

**Key Economic Impact Data:**
- According to ACI's study (Taking America Beyond the Horizon), total economic output of U.S. commercial airports exceeds $1.4 trillion, supporting more than 11.5 million jobs with payroll exceeding $428 billion, accounting for more than 7 percent of U.S. GDP (based on 2017 data covering 493 commercial airports).
- IATA's 2022 Global Passenger Survey found 75% of passengers "prioritized proximity to airport when choosing where to fly from."

**Three New Economic Measures Developed by the Research:**
1. **Expected additional economic impacts due to growth in activity** - Models estimate jobs, household income, and total expenditures that grow in a region due to activity growth at commercial airports (Figure 4-1). For Austin, Texas (based on January 2023 OAG schedule): adding nonstop service to one more domestic city would add $72.7 million annually to Austin's GDP; adding nonstop service to one international city would add $341.3 million to regional GDP (Figure 4-2).
2. **Costs to consumers if they made the same trip using another mode of transportation** - Calculates the "full price of travel" (FPT), combining out-of-pocket and time-related costs. Using the U.S. DOT value of time of $47.10/hour, a sample East Coast-to-Europe trip costing $800 by air (8 hours) has an FPT of $1,177, versus $3,861 via ocean liner (144 hours), saving the consumer $2,684 each way or $5,368 round trip (Table 4-1).
3. **Costs to consumers if they made the same trip using another airport** - Local consumers would spend on average 19% to 29% more (on an FPT basis) when flying from an alternative airport, consisting of 10% to 15% higher out-of-pocket costs and 29% to 45% higher time-related costs (Table 4-3).

**Emissions Comparison Data (Table 4-2):** Per-passenger mile CO2 factors (well-to-wake): Air short-haul 0.252 kg, medium-haul 0.157, long-haul 0.198; Passenger car (2 passengers) 0.204; Intercity rail 0.142; Ocean passenger 0.402. Alternative modes increase GHG emissions by 51%-70% depending on hub type. Ocean liners emit twice as much GHG per passenger-mile on long-haul trips (over 2,300 miles) than the average commercial aircraft.

**Key Methodology Notes:**
- Economic impact studies measure direct, indirect, and induced impacts; "leakage" refers to dollars re-spent outside the region.
- Results in Figures 4-1, 4-2, and 4-3 are "marginal" impacts (from relatively small changes), which are generally smaller than average impacts from existing airport economic studies.
- Alternative mode and alternative airport measures are not available for GA airports because trips from GA airports are not well documented in terms of aircraft type, origins, destinations, and passenger numbers.

**Key Findings/Conclusions:**
- Aviation is less costly for consumers and produces fewer emissions than alternative transportation modes for trips typically taken from airports.
- Passengers almost always save time by flying locally - even when an alternate airport has many more nonstop services, the added access time to reach the alternate airport exceeds time savings from more nonstops (Table 4-5: 29 of 29 large hub markets, 195 of 197 nonhub markets).
- Some airports expressed reluctance to link economic activity with climate discussions, especially where the community is engaged in climate change issues; such airports often say they will "accommodate growth in aviation in the most responsible and climate-friendly manner."
- A different interpretation offered: "the economic impact is why it is important (and perhaps even cost-beneficial) for a community to invest in mitigation so that aviation can continue to grow."

The chapter notes that materials can be used to develop effective airport communications, including in response to organizations concerned about aviation activity because of climate effects. Appendix A outlines how airports can undertake similar studies with updated information.
</summary>

DHL shipments per day in Canada increased by an average of 40% since 2019.
- Passenger activity (Passenger Operations, Visitor Spending, Concession Spending) generated ~1,190 jobs and $393.0 million in industry activity in 2021. - DHL opened a new 238,000 sq ft facility in September 2021 following a $100 million CAD investment, capable of processing up to 28,000 packages per hour and bringing ~150 new jobs.

Since IMPLAN lacks a Hamilton-specific model, Ontario results were downscaled based on the assumption that Hamilton accounts for approximately 5% of the Ontario economy. Impacts were classified as direct (~65% of operational impacts; ~50% of capital impacts), indirect, and induced. Output metrics include Employment, Labor Income, Value Added (GRP), and Industry Activity.

--- SOURCE 1: The Role of Aviation in Supporting Local Economic Activity - CRP ---
URL: https://crp.trb.org/acrpwebresource12/understanding-air-service-and-regional-economic-activity/the-role-of-aviation-in-supporting-local-economic-activity

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from TRB's Cooperative Research Programs (ACRP Product Line) examines the role of aviation and air service in supporting local and regional economic activity. The central challenge discussed is establishing causality—whether air service attracts economic activity or whether growing metropolitan areas cause airlines to add service—a "chicken or egg" conundrum complicated by proprietary airline-firm contract data. Despite this, a consensus is emerging from recent research using innovative statistical methods that air travel can be a positive, causal trigger for additional employment and income in metropolitan economies.

Key research findings cited include: Bruekner (2003) found a 10% increase in passenger traffic raises total employment by 0.9% and service employment by 1.1%. McGraw (2020) studied midsized and smaller city airports from 1950-2010, finding airports contributed to 3.9% growth in total employment and 3.4% growth in population per decade. ACRP Research Report 218 found each departing seat at small hub airports was associated with 0.005 jobs (5 jobs per 1,000 seats; one daily 100-seat aircraft supporting 182.5 jobs), while non-hub airports showed a stronger 0.0114 jobs per departing seat. ACRP Report 132 examined airports' role in the national economy.

Stronger links were found between air service and particular industries: professional/scientific/technical fields, finance, corporate headquarters, IT, and advanced manufacturing. Sheard (2014) found a 10% increase in air traffic generates 1,650 additional service jobs in an MSA with 1 million residents but no measurable effect on manufacturing or non-tradable services. Blonigen and Cristea (2015) found a 50% increase in air passenger growth rate leads to 3.2% increase in annual per-capita income growth and 5.5% increase in annual employment growth, plus positive effects on local business growth.

The page explains input-output (I-O) models as a way to measure how air service is consumed by different sectors. According to BEA I-O tables, 53% of air travel purchases are personal, 16% is exported (international travelers), and the key 31% is used by industry as an input to production—this portion is associated with regional economic activity.

Connectivity is highlighted as critical to businesses. Bilotkach (2015) showed adding flights to a new destination generated more economic effects than adding capacity to existing destinations, creating on average 223 jobs and 15 new business establishments per extra destination. Connectivity improves through more capacity, increased connecting opportunities, more nonstop destinations, and higher "quality" destinations (especially hubs and international gateways). The page discusses the IATA connectivity index and MIT's Airport Connectivity Quality Index (AQCI), noting the IATA model focuses on international markets while the AQCI rates "quality" of destinations served.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Bruekner (2003) found a correlation between air service and total employment in metropolitan areas, reporting that a 10 percent increase in passenger traffic raises total employment by 0.9 percent and service employment by 1.1 percent." "McGraw (2020) found that the presence of airports in these communities contributed to an average of 3.9 percent growth in total employment (and 3.4 percent growth in population) per decade." "For areas served by small hub airports, each departing seat was associated with 0.005 jobs. In other words, for every 1,000 departing seats, there were 5 associated jobs in the area." "A 50 percent increase in the air passenger growth rate leads to an average 3.2 percent increase in the annual growth of per-capita income and an average 5.5 percent increase in the annual rate of employment." "It is this 31 percent that is associated with regional economic activity; 53 percent of travel purchases is for personal reasons, 16 percent is exported, and the remaining 31 percent is used by industry as an input."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] The Development of a Web-Based Small Airport Economic Impact Model ---
URL: https://static.tti.tamu.edu/tti.tamu.edu/documents/0-7066-R1.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This technical report (Report 0-7066-R1, published November 2020) documents the development of a Web-Based Small Airport Economic Impact Model by the Texas A&M Transportation Institute, in cooperation with the Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) and the Federal Highway Administration. The project created the Small Airport Economic Impact Estimator, a web-based tool that allows airport managers, planners, and local officials to calculate the economic impact of their airport.

**Purpose and Need:** TxDOT conducts statewide economic impact studies every five to seven years, but airports need more frequent, up-to-date economic impact data. Local officials use these numbers to justify airport investment, grant-applications, and local funding matches. Key reasons for more frequent examination include airports being omitted from statewide studies, privacy concerns with single-tenant airports, changes in activity levels since the last study, and the desire for more detailed analysis.

**Methodology:** The research team reviewed airport economic impact modeling and determined that a traditional input/output (I/O) model would provide the best estimates for small airports. The model was built using:
- IMPLAN multipliers (region-specific)
- Visitor spending data from the Texas Governor's Office
- Terminal Area Forecast data from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)
- Latest data from the 2018 statewide Texas Aviation Economic Impact Study

**Model Components:** The Estimator generates economic impact outputs for three types of activity:
1. Aircraft/Airport activity (employment and expenses related to airport functioning)
2. Visitor activity (impact of visitor spending on the region)
3. Tenant/business activity (employment/expenses of on-airport businesses)

It also calculates the annual impact of capital expenditures (based on an average of the past three years). Users can calculate using default data or provide new inputs based on current conditions.

**Economic Impact Measures and Categories:** The I/O model provides three measures of economic impact: employment, payroll expenditures, and output. These cannot be summed (would cause double counting). The model evaluates four categories: on-airport activity, capital projects, commercial service visitors, and general aviation visitors. Impacts are categorized as direct, indirect, and induced (multiplier) effects.

**Context on Texas Airports:** Texas has 264 general aviation airports and 15 non-hub commercial service airports. Small airports were defined as all general aviation airports and non-hub commercial service airports in the Texas Airport System Plan.

**Data Requirements:** The research team collected airport sponsor data (operations, employment, payroll, operating and capital expenditures, enplanements, visitor spending, operations mix, aircraft occupancy) and tenant/business data (employment by industry, operating expenditures, payroll, gross sales, capital expenditures). They identified 16 different types of businesses typically located on airports.

**Model Validation:** The model was validated by comparing results against the 2018 Texas Aviation Economic Impact Study and a CDM Smith study for selected airports (including South Texas Regional Airport at Hondo, Sugar Land Regional Airport, Littlefield Taylor Brown Municipal Airport, San Marcos Regional Airport, and Fox Stephens Field–Gilmer Municipal Airport).

**Prior Work:** The report references a similar web-based calculator developed by the Minnesota Department of Transportation in 2005 and updated in 2011 as a precedent for this approach.
</summary>

"Knowing the current economic impact of an airport is critical to both airport sponsors and the Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT)... Having updated and current numbers is important because many local officials use the airport's economic impact values to justify airport investment."

--- SOURCE 5: GAO-24-106681, Commercial Aviation: Trends in Air Service to Small Communities ---
URL: https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-24-106681/index.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This GAO report (GAO-24-106681, published September 25, 2024) examines trends in air service to small communities in the contiguous U.S. from 2018 through 2023. The report was requested by Congress and addresses three objectives: (1) changes in air service to small communities from 2018-2023; (2) factors contributing to those changes and their effects on federal air service programs; and (3) options to improve air service to small communities.

**Methodology:** GAO identified 218 "small communities" using U.S. Census Bureau population data (the 218 least populous communities with commercial airports). GAO analyzed flight data reported by airlines to DOT from 2018-2023, and conducted semi-structured interviews with 33 aviation stakeholders, including 16 small airports, 5 airlines, industry associations, academic researchers, and DOT officials.

**Key Findings:**
- From 2018 to 2023, mean total departures from small communities decreased 14% (from 2,235 to 1,919 flights annually), with a steep drop at the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. About half of the 218 small communities saw modest change in passengers; 8% declined more than 50% in onboards, while 14% increased by 50% or more.
- Mean seats per departure increased 26% (from 60 to 76 seats), reflecting airline "upgauging" to larger aircraft. Airlines are retiring smaller 50-seat-or-fewer aircraft as they become uneconomical.
- Mean total onboards increased 11% (from 102,241 to 113,291), though from a low baseline.
- Mean connectivity index (a measure of access to the aviation system) decreased 8% (from 5.1 to 4.7) for small communities, remaining far lower than large communities (which had a score of about 402 in 2023).
- EAS small communities lost less air service (−12% departures vs. −15% for non-EAS) and gained more seats per departure (+34% vs. +26%), and had smaller connectivity declines. EAS communities had an average of 896 departures in 2023 vs. 2,786 for non-EAS small communities.

**Factors Affecting Air Service:** Stakeholders cited (1) pilot shortages (including a regional airline captain shortage exacerbated by mainline airlines hiring regional pilots), with the 1,500 flight hour requirement, cost of training, and infrastructure constraints as barriers; (2) aviation maintenance worker shortages; (3) increased airline operating costs—operating costs for eight regional airlines increased from almost $0.12 per available seat mile in 2018 to $0.16 in 2023 (in real 2023 dollars); and (4) travelers choosing to drive or use larger nearby airports.

**Federal Programs:**
- The Essential Air Service (EAS) program, created in 1978, provides subsidies to airlines serving eligible communities. As of March 2024, 107 communities in the contiguous 48 states received EAS service. EAS subsidy costs increased approximately 31% from 2018 through 2023. Eligibility requires subsidy per passenger under $650 (unless 175+ miles from nearest large/medium hub), under $1,000 (lowered to $850 in Oct 2026), and average 10+ enplanements per service day unless exemptions apply.
- The Small Community Air Service Development Program (SCASDP), established in 2000, provides discretionary grants for strategies to improve small airport air service. DOT awarded an average grant of $767,000 to 19 communities in its most recent cycle, often used for minimum revenue guarantees. Higher airline operating costs limited the impact of SCASDP grants.
- Airport incentives such as fee waivers and marketing assistance are common: 67% of small hub and 48% of nonhub airports offer marketing assistance; 75% of small hub and 40% of nonhub airports offer fee waivers.

**Options to Improve Air Service:** Stakeholders and recent studies identified options including increasing pilot supply, addressing operating costs through electric aircraft or bus service, focusing EAS eligibility on more remote communities or expanding EAS, and modifying SCASDP in response to rising costs.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"From 2018 to 2023, small communities in the contiguous U.S. generally experienced a decrease in departing flights, with a steep drop at the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, but an increase in the average number of seats per departure."
</key_excerpts>

The chapter provides new research to help airports supplement their own economic impact studies when communicating with stakeholders about the tension between economic benefits and climate change concerns. It addresses the question: "Since aviation climate effects are so expensive to abate, what benefits would be lost by curtailing aviation activity?"

Key content includes:
- IATA's 2022 Global Passenger Survey found 75% of passengers "prioritized proximity to airport when choosing where to fly from."

Three new measures of economic impacts are presented:
1. Expected additional economic impacts due to growth in activity (marginal jobs, income, and output per additional enplanement at commercial airports; and per additional operation/based jet aircraft at GA airports).
2. Costs to consumers if they made the same trip using another mode of transportation (Full Price of Travel - FPT).
3. Costs to consumers if they made the same trip using another airport.

Key data tables:
- Table 4-1 shows average increase in FPT via alternate mode by hub type: Large hub = 426% time-related, 157% out-of-pocket, 289% FPT, 70% GHG increase; Medium = 360%/125%/241%/56%; Small = 317%/101%/206%/56%; Nonhub = 283%/73%/172%/51%.

--- SOURCE 6: [PDF] The Development of a Web-Based Small Airport Economic Impact Model ---
URL: https://static.tti.tamu.edu/tti.tamu.edu/documents/0-7066-R1.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This technical report (Report 0-7066-R1, published November 2020) documents the development of a Web-Based Small Airport Economic Impact Model by the Texas A&M Transportation Institute, in cooperation with the Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) and the Federal Highway Administration. The project created the Small Airport Economic Impact Estimator, a web-based tool that allows airport managers, planners, and local officials to calculate the economic impact of their airport.

**Purpose and Need:** TxDOT conducts statewide economic impact studies every five to seven years, but airports need more frequent, up-to-date economic impact data. Local officials use these numbers to justify airport investment, grant-applications, and local funding matches. Key reasons for more frequent examination include airports being omitted from statewide studies, privacy concerns with single-tenant airports, changes in activity levels since the last study, and the desire for more detailed analysis.

**Methodology:** The research team reviewed airport economic impact modeling and determined that a traditional input/output (I/O) model would provide the best estimates for small airports. The model was built using:
- IMPLAN multipliers (region-specific)
- Visitor spending data from the Texas Governor's Office
- Terminal Area Forecast data from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)
- Latest data from the 2018 statewide Texas Aviation Economic Impact Study

**Model Components:** The Estimator generates economic impact outputs for three types of activity:
1. Aircraft/Airport activity (employment and expenses related to airport functioning)
2. Visitor activity (impact of visitor spending on the region)
3. Tenant/business activity (employment/expenses of on-airport businesses)

It also calculates the annual impact of capital expenditures (based on an average of the past three years). Users can calculate using default data or provide new inputs based on current conditions.

**Economic Impact Measures and Categories:** The I/O model provides three measures of economic impact: employment, payroll expenditures, and output. These cannot be summed (would cause double counting). The model evaluates four categories: on-airport activity, capital projects, commercial service visitors, and general aviation visitors. Impacts are categorized as direct, indirect, and induced (multiplier) effects.

**Context on Texas Airports:** Texas has 264 general aviation airports and 15 non-hub commercial service airports. Small airports were defined as all general aviation airports and non-hub commercial service airports in the Texas Airport System Plan.

--- SOURCE 16: Comparing Enhanced Models for Evaluating the Economic ... ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2673-7590/3/3/62

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in Future Transportation (Volume 3, Issue 3, 2023, pages 1124-1146, DOI: 10.3390/futuretransp3030062), addresses the challenge of evaluating the economic impact of airports when multiple airports operate in the same region, where the standard input-output (IO) model fails to distinguish individual airport contributions.

**Objective:** The paper compares three approaches to determine individual airport economic contributions and identify their social and economic benefits. The study considers three weight factors for the input-output basic model recommended by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO).

**Methodology:** The three distribution models used as weights for IO analysis were:
1. **Circular Buffer Model** - deterministic model based on Euclidean (straight-line) distance within a 200 km radius of each airport
2. **Travel/Displacement Time Model** - deterministic model using minimum travel time (calculated via Google Maps) instead of straight-line distance
3. **Huff's Gravitational Model** - probabilistic model considering airport attractiveness (e.g., passenger numbers) and distance decay

The analysis was applied to the three largest airports in São Paulo state, Brazil, due to their proximity: Viracopos International Airport (SBKP), Governador André Franco Montoro Airport (SBGR), and Deputado Freitas Nobre Airport (SBSP). Municipalities within a 200 km radius were included in the analysis.

**Key methodological details:**
- The IO model uses three matrices: intersectoral flows (S-table), technical coefficients (A-table), and the Leontief matrix (L-table)
- Data sources included NEREUS (Center for Regional and Urban Economics of the University of São Paulo) IO matrices and Brazilian federal employment/wage microdata
- A noted limitation was that the most recent Brazilian IO matrix available was from 2015 (2018 via NEREUS updates), a common global delay issue

**Authors:** Ivaciane de Quadra Magalhães, Anderson Ribeiro Correia, Michelle Carvalho Galvão da Silva Pinto Bandeira (corresponding author), Mauro Zackiewicz (all from Brazilian institutions), and Luiz Antonio Tozi.

The study fills a gap in literature by proposing improvements to methods for evaluating airports' economic and social benefits, enabling better prediction of returns on airport infrastructure investments for government and private sector decision-makers, particularly regarding correlations between airport infrastructure investments and GDP, employment, and added value generation.

**Literature review context:** Prior studies reviewed include Tveter's difference-in-difference IO model (Norway regional airports), Nasution et al. (Indonesia air transport–GDP relationship), Bandeira et al. (Viracopos Airport, Brazil), Hakfoort et al. (Amsterdam Schiphol Airport, employment multiplier of 2), Zhao et al. (China, 2007-2020), and others on IO models in transportation impact assessment.
</summary>

Key findings include:

- **Historical cases:** Average traffic growth post-liberalization was nearly 63%, compared to typical world traffic growth of 6%-8%.

- **US-UK scenario:** Full liberalization under a Comprehensive First Step Air Service Agreement with the EU would produce a 29% traffic increase, creating 117,000 new jobs and roughly $7.8 billion in incremental GDP for the US and UK combined.

**Background:** Commercial aviation remains governed by post-World War II bilateral ASAs that often frustrate market growth, force price premiums, and create vested interests. The study argues that education is key to reform, since benefits are large but widely diffused, and beneficiaries (passengers, shippers, hotels, airports) are fragmented.

**Methodology:** The study developed a globally applicable ex ante analytical model using data from over 190 nations and 1,400 country-pairs, examining the causal chain: liberalization → new/better air services → traffic growth → economic growth → job growth.

# Small Communities' Air Service Declines Despite Federal Support

By Legis1 Editorial· Edited by Joanne Levine

Friday, August 21, 2026

## Why It Matters

Smaller communities are facing a severe decline in commercial flights. A [June 2026 Government Accountability Office (GAO) report](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-26-109182) reveals that nonhub airports, which handle more than 10,000 annual passenger boardings but represent less than 0.05% of total U.S. commercial traffic, saw average daily departures per route plummet 19% between 2018 and 2024.

Over 70% of nonhub airports that do not receive Essential Air Service (EAS) support suffered departure losses. Meanwhile, the cost to maintain flights in subsidized areas skyrocketed, with EAS subsidy costs rising 31% from 2018 to 2023.

## The Big Picture

The decline reflects structural pressures in the regional aviation market. Stakeholders cited pilot and maintenance workforce supply challenges as a market factor contributing to changes in air service to small communities. Stakeholders also cited increased airline operating costs and heightened airline expectations for revenue guarantees as market factors affecting air service to small communities.

The Small Community Air Service Development Program (SCASDP), which provides grants to help airlines establish or restore service to underserved communities, has become less effective as operating costs have risen faster than grant amounts can offset.

## Solutions Under Consideration

Stakeholders and recent studies identified increasing aviation workforce supply as an option to improve air service to small communities. Stakeholders and recent studies identified supporting other transportation modes, such as bus service, as an option to improve air service to small communities. Stakeholders and recent studies identified supporting new technologies, such as electric aircraft, as an option to improve air service to small communities.

Stakeholders identified options to change EAS, such as focusing EAS assistance on more remote communities. Others suggested expanding EAS to better ensure small airports do not lose air service. A third group advocated for modifying the Small Community Air Service Development Program (SCASDP) in response to rising airline operating costs.

## The Bottom Line

args.summary:
A June 2026 Government Accountability Office (GAO) report reveals that smaller communities (nonhub airports, handling more than 10,000 annual passenger boardings but less than 0.05% of total U.S. commercial traffic) experienced a 19% decline in average daily departures per route between 2018 and 2024. Over 70% of nonhub airports not receiving Essential Air Service (EAS) support suffered departure losses, while EAS subsidy costs rose 31% from 2018 to 2023.

The decline stems from structural pressures in regional aviation, including pilot and maintenance workforce supply challenges, increased airline operating costs, and heightened airline expectations for revenue guarantees. The Small Community Air Service Development Program (SCASDP) has become less effective as operating costs rise faster than grant amounts can offset.

Stakeholders identified several potential solutions: increasing the aviation workforce supply, supporting other transportation modes (e.g., bus service), supporting new technologies (e.g., electric aircraft), focusing EAS assistance on more remote communities, expanding EAS, and modifying SCASDP. In April 2026, the GAO recommended that the FAA establish and publicly communicate timelines for finalizing two pilot training initiatives provided for in statute; the Department of Transportation agreed with these recommendations. The DOT administers federal programs providing subsidies and grants to help eligible small communities retain a link to the national aviation system.

APPENDIX B NATIONAL PLAN OF INTEGRATED AIRPORT SYSTEMS Pocatello Regional Airport Airport Master Plan Appendix B B-1 Final 2012 APPENDIX B NATIONAL PLAN OF INTEGRATED AIRPORT SYSTEMS The Airport and Airway Improvement Act of 1982 directed the Secretary of Transportation to prepare, publish, and revise every two years a national airport system plan – the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS) - for the development of pubic-use airports in the United States. The NPIAS is a system that emphasizes system planning and development to meet current and future aviation needs; it includes development considered necessary to provide a safe, efficient, and integrated airport system meeting the needs of civil aviation, national defense, and the United States Postal Service. It takes into account, amongst other things, the relationship of each airport to the rest of the transportation system in a particular area, the forecast of technological developments in aeronautics, and the development forecast in other modes of transportation. Projects eligible for funding under the Airport Improvement Program (AIP) must be included in the NPIAS. The NPIAS currently includes 3,364 of the 5,314 airports open to the public. Approximately 1,000 publicly owned, public use airports are not included because they do not meet the minimum entry criteria of ten based aircraft, are within 20 miles of a NPIAS airport, or are located at inadequate sites and cannot be expanded and improved to provide safe and efficient airport facilities. The remaining airports that are excluded from the NPIAS are privately owned, public use airports that are not included because they are located at inadequate sites, are redundant to publicly owned airports, or have too little activity to qualify for inclusion. In addition, nearly 14,000 civil landing areas are not open to the general public and are not included in the NPIAS. Airport facilities included in the NPIAS are classified under two different categories: service level and airport role. B.1 SERVICE LEVEL The airport service level reflects the type of public use the airport provides to the community and the funding categories established by Congress to assist in airport development. The following list defines the different types of service levels:  Commercial service airports are public airports that enplane in excess of 2,500 or more annual passengers and receive aircraft offering scheduled passenger service.  Primary airports are commercial service airports that have more than 10,000 annual enplaned passengers.  Large hub airports are those primary airports that enplane at least one percent of total U.S. passenger enplanements.  Medium hub airports are those primary airports that enplane between 0.25 percent and one percent of total U.S. passenger enplanements. Pocatello Regional Airport Airport Master Plan Appendix B B-2 Final 2012  Small hub airports are those primary airports that enplane between 0.05 percent and 0.25 percent of the total U.S. passenger enplanements.  Non-hub primary service airports are those primary airports that enplane less than 0.05 percent of all commercial passenger enplanements but more than 10,000 annual enplanements.  Cargo service airports are served by aircraft providing air transportation of property only, including mail, with an aggregate annual aircraft landing weight in excess of 100,000 thousand pounds.  Reliever airports provide substantial capacity or instrument training relief to a commercial service airport that serves a metropolitan statistical area with a population of at least 250,000 persons or has at least 250,000 annual enplaned passengers and operates at 60 percent of its capacity; or would be operated at such a level before being relieved by one or more reliever airports; or is subject to restrictions that limit activity that would otherwise reach 60 percent of capacity. An airport not meeting these criteria may be included in the NPIAS as a reliever airport if it is so designed in a state, regional, or metropolitan system plan and the FAA concurs with that portion of the plan.  General aviation airports that receive U.S. mail services, are listed as a scheduled stop by an air carrier transporting mail pursuant to a current contract with the U.S. Postal Service, or area otherwise designated by USPS and served through a public airport are included in the plan. A general aviation airport can also be listed if it is included in a state system plan, serves a community more than 30 minutes from the nearest existing or proposed airport included in the NPIAS, is forecasted to have 10 based aircraft during the short-term planning period, and has an eligible sponsor willing to undertake ownership and development of the airport.  Public use heliports that do not meet other service level criteria but are included in the plan if they make significant contributions to public transportation. Helicopter landing areas are included in the plan if they have at least four based rotorcrafts or 800 annual itinerant operations, or 400 itinerant operations by air taxi rotorcraft. There are currently 546 commercial service airports included in the NPIAS; of these, 422 have more than 10,000 enplanements and are classified as primary airports. Primary airports receive an annual apportionment of at least one million dollars in AIP funding, when funding levels meet or exceed $3.2 billion, with the exact amount determined by the number of enplaned passengers. Of these, 31 are classified as large hub commercial airports and account for nearly 70 percent of all passenger enplanements. Large hub airports tend to focus on airline passenger and freight operations and have limited general aviation activity. Reliever airports are typically high capacity general aviation airports in major metropolitan areas. These specialized airports provide pilots with attractive alternatives to using the congested hub airports. There are 260 reliever airports that average 228 based aircraft and together account for 27 percent of the Nation’s general aviation fleet. General aviation airports are typically located in communities that do not have commercial service and account for enough activity, usually at least ten based aircraft, and are located a minimum of 20 miles from the nearest NPIAS airport. There are 2,558 general aviation airports included in the NPIAS and tend to be distributed on a one-per-county basis in rural areas. These airports average 32-based aircraft and account for nearly 38 percent of the Nation’s general aviation fleet. These airports tend to be of particular importance to rural areas. Pocatello Regional Airport Airport Master Plan Appendix B B-3 Final 2012 B.2 ROLE An airport included in the NPIAS is further classified into one of four basic service levels, which describe the type of service that the airport currently provides to the community and is anticipated to provide to the community at the end of the five-year planning period. The four roles include:  PR – primary commercial service  CM – non-primary commercial service  RL – reliever  GA – general aviation airport

This document is Appendix B of the Pocatello Regional Airport Master Plan (2012), explaining the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS). The NPIAS was established by the Airport and Airway Improvement Act of 1982 and is revised every two years by the Secretary of Transportation. It includes development needed to provide a safe, efficient, integrated airport system meeting civil aviation, national defense, and USPS needs. Projects must be included in the NPIAS to be eligible for Airport Improvement Program (AIP) funding.

The NPIAS includes 3,364 of the 5,314 public airports. Approximately 1,000 public airports are excluded for failing minimum entry criteria (fewer than ten based aircraft, being within 20 miles of an NPIAS airport, or being at inadequate sites). Nearly 14,000 civil landing areas are not open to the public and are excluded.

Airports are classified by service level: Commercial service airports (2,500+ annual enplanements with scheduled passenger service); Primary airports (commercial service with 10,000+ annual enplanements); Large hubs (at least 1% of U.S. enplanements); Medium hubs (0.25%-1%); Small hubs (0.05%-0.25%); Non-hub primary (less than 0.05% but more than 10,000 enplanements); Cargo service airports (excess of 100,000 thousand pounds landing weight); Reliever airports (capacity/instrument training relief to commercial service airports); General aviation airports; and Public use heliports.

Current statistics: 546 commercial service airports are in the NPIAS, of which 422 are primary airports (receiving at least $1 million in AIP funding annually when funding meets or exceeds $3.2 billion). There are 31 large hub commercial airports accounting for nearly 70% of all passenger enplanements. There are 260 reliever airports averaging 228 based aircraft, accounting for 27% of the nation's general aviation fleet. There are 2,558 general aviation airports averaging 32 based aircraft, accounting for nearly 38% of the fleet, typically distributed on a one-per-county basis in rural areas.

Airports are further classified into four roles: PR (primary commercial service), CM (non-primary commercial service), RL (reliever), and GA (general aviation), describing the type of service provided currently and anticipated at the end of the five-year planning period.

# Airport Roles According to NPIAS

The NPIAS is updated and published by the FAA every two years. This report uses predetermined evaluation criteria to identify airports that are of national importance to the air transportation system and inclusion in the NPIAS makes an airport eligible for AIP funding. The evaluation criteria consider important airport metrics such as commercial service enplanements, proximity to other airports and the number of based aircraft at an airport, making the NPIAS an excellent resource when understanding the role of the airport. Identifying if an airport is included in the NPIAS, followed by determining its classification within the NPIAS, provides insight into what role an airport plays within the larger regional and national aviation context.

As of January 2016, there are over 19,300 aviation facilities in the United States. However, almost three-quarters of these facilities are for private use only and not open to the general public, and therefore not eligible for the NPIAS. Of the roughly 5,100 remaining eligible public-use airports and other aviation facilities, over 3,300 airports, heliports, and seaplane bases are identified in the most recent NPIAS. A majority of the airports in the NPIAS are publicly owned, while a small number of airports are privately owned, but open for public use, and therefore also included in the plan. To learn more about the criteria used to classify NPIAS airports see the [Changing NPIAS Classification](./changing-npias-classification/) section.

The NPIAS airports are generally categorized as either primary (commercial service) or nonprimary (GA) airports based on the number of commercial service enplanements, number of based aircraft, location or proximity to other airports, or a combination of the three. All primary and commercial service airports are in the NPIAS, while only select GA airports are included. Although most of the annual enplanements occur at primary airports, these airports account for only a small portion of the overall airports in the NPIAS. Out of the over 3,300 NPIAS airports, just less than 400 airports are considered primary. The remainder of the airports are nonprimary and mainly serve GA aircraft. Due to the large number of airports classified as GA, the FAA in 2012 and 2014 developed two additional reports to further classify these airports. See [General Aviation Airports: National Assets](./general-aviation-airports-a-national-asset/) for further information.

Click below to read about each category of NPIAS airports:

* **Primary Airports**

Airports are included in this category based on their role as commercial service airports. Less than 15 percent of the airports in the NPIAS are primary airports. To be included in this category the airport must be a public-use airport with scheduled commercial airline service and have more than 10,000 annual passenger enplanements. Primary airports are further broken into four subcategories of large, medium, small, and nonhub airports based on the percentage of enplanements an airport has each year as compared to the total national enplanements.

* **Nonprimary Airports**

A majority of the NPIAS airports fall into the nonprimary category. Airports considered and classified with this designation are mostly used for GA aircraft operations. There are three service levels of non-primary airports: nonprimary commercial service, reliever airports and GA airports. Nonprimary commercial service airports mostly serve GA aircraft, but do have limited commercial service as the name implies. Reliever airports are often found in large metropolitan areas, and provide additional regional capacity where nearby airports primarily serve larger commercial air service aircraft. The last service level, GA airports, is the largest segment of the NPIAS airports.

#### Resources

* [NPIAS](http://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/npias/)

  The NPIAS report identifies over 3,300 public-use airports that are of significance to the national air transportation system. The NPIAS narrative provides a chart showing the breakdown of NPIAS airports. Appendix B: State and Territory Maps of NPIAS Airports includes national and state maps of NPIAS airports.
* [Field Formulation of the NPIAS](http://www.faa.gov/airports/resources/publications/orders/media/planning_5090_3C.pdf)

  This FAA Order (Order 5090.3C) provides guidance and sets forth policies and procedures for the continuous formulation, maintenance, and periodic publication of the NPIAS.

# Beginners’ Guide to Public-Use Airport Classification

## 

[Press Release](https://www.globalair.com/articles/press-releases)   
**Published:** Sep. 1, 2016 at 08:00 PM EST   
**Updated:** Mar. 10, 2021 at 04:30 PM EST

![](https://resources.globalair.com/images/article/jwj-Airport-0681.jpg) 

One of the best college courses I have ever taken is Airport Management. It is truly fascinating to learn about the breakdown of just how exactly airports are classified, owned, funded, and managed. Pilots would not fly without airports, and airports would not be necessary without pilots, so I believe that any good pilot should have a working knowledge of the different types of airports and how they are categorized.

I could make a whole series of articles just based on who owns what type of airport, the types of regulations they have to follow, and the different ways airports are managed. However, today I would simply like to introduce the rules behind how airports are generally classified in the US.

The FAA has been recognizing public-use airports that are eligible for federal funding since 1970. They created the National Airport Systems Plan (NASP) which included approximately 3,200 such airports that were shown to be serving public needs. In 1982, with the passage of the Airport and Airway Act, the FAA was asked to prepare a new version of the NASP, to be called the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS). This updated version included a total of 3,411 airports in 2008.

With the new NPIAS system came a new way of classifying airports for federal funding. Here are the basic parts and a quick definition for each.

**1. Primary Airports**

These are categorized in the NPIAS as those public-use airports enplaning at least 10,000 passengers annually. This accounts for less than 3 percent of the nation’s total airports, with only 383 airports falling into this category in 2008.

**2. Commercial Service Airports**

This is any airport that accommodates scheduled air carrier service by a certified airline. Of the 770 million passengers that flew domestically or internationally in the United States in 2009, practically all of them went by way of a commercial service airport. The FAA recognized 522 of these such airports in 2008.

**3. General Aviation Airports**

Airports with fewer than 2,500 annual enplaned passengers are covered by this classification, as well as airports that are used exclusively by private business aircraft not providing commercial passenger air carrier service. This category gets a little more tricky, as there are over 13,000 airports that technically fit the description. However, not all of these are included in the NPIAS. There is usually at least one GA airport in the NPIAS per county, and any airport with more than 10 aircraft based there and more than 20 miles away from the next nearest NPIAS is also included. In 2008, a total of 2,564 airports held this classification in the NPIAS.

**4. Reliever Airports**

Perhaps the most unique of the classifications, relieved airports are specifically designated as "general aviation airports that provide relief to congested major airports." In order to qualify as a reliever airport, the airport must have at least 100 airplanes based at the field or handle 25,000 itinerate operations.

Primary Airports also have a special subsection to include the different sizes of primary airport operations. It is important to note that the NPIAS definition of a hub is different than that in the airline industry, and they are simply referring to the number of annual enplaned passengers that use the airport. These are as follows:

**1. Large hubs**

These airports account for at least 1 percent of the total annual passenger enplanements. Of the 30 large hub airports that were classified in 2008, they handled 70 percent of all passenger enplanements in the US.

**2. Medium hubs**

These airports handle between .25 and 1 percent of the annual enplanements. There were 37 airports that held this designation in 2008.

**3. Small hubs**

These airports handle between 0.05 and 0.25 percent of annual passenger enplanements. The NPIAS reported 72 of these in 2008.

**4. Nonhubs**

These airports handle more than 10,000 annual enplanements, but less than 0.05 of the annual total enplanements.

I hope that I have helped to break down a little more just how airports are classified by the FAA. I would recommend looking up your favorite airports to see what type of hub they fall under, and if they are considered primary or just commercial service.

# The National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS), Airports Capital Improvement Plan (ACIP), Next Generation Air Transportation System (NextGen), and AWOS

## In September of 2019 the Federal government combined The National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS) and the Airports Capital Improvement Plan (ACIP) into one single order NPIAS-ACIP.

The order reduced redundancy and streamlined two federal programs essential to airport development.   
  
The two programs, which originated individually in the year 2000, are now joined under Order 5090.5 which made the ACIP a subset of NPIAS and the primary financial planning tool for management of the Airport Improvement Program (AIP).

## Weather is one of the greatest challenges facing airports in the 21st century.

As air traffic increases with modern airplanes becoming bigger, faster, and more technologically complex, airports must stay one step ahead in managing them and keeping the flow of air traffic seamless and orderly.  
  
This task become extremely challenging during periods of inclement weather at an airport where high air traffic levels have already placed stress on the system. Accurate weather data is crucial to an airport and air traffic control, as a single adverse weather event can cause havoc and mounting delays.

Between the years 2008 and 2013 over 69% of delays lasting longer than 15 minutes were caused by weather, amounting to more than 10 million lost minutes in 2013 alone. These delays not only have a ripple effect on the air traffic flow throughout the global airspace, but cost thousands of dollars in lost revenues. An hour-long delay costs air carrier operators between $1,400 and $4,500 depending upon the class of aircraft and whether the delay was on the ground or in the air when it occurred, and that’s not the end of it. Travelers also suffer the added expenses of delays when the value of travel time is included, a personal travel passenger adds an addition $35 per hour loss and $63 for a business travel passenger.  
  
Airports can do nothing to control the weather, but they can do something to understand, gather data, and disseminate accurate information to pilots and air traffic control, giving them the best chance of keeping an airport running safely and as efficient as possible. When it comes to gathering and disseminating meteorological reports at an airport, an AWOS system is indispensable. AWOS offer automatic minute-by-minute updates of the weather conditions around them. Their readings can help lower minimums and allow for better management of air traffic which means more aircraft are able to safely land and take off from your airport during periods of inclement weather as well as handle redirected overflow traffic from neighboring airports impacted by serious weather incidents.

## An AWOS system can be expensive to purchase and maintain, and many airports seek out support from the Federal government through the AIP.

When applying for a grant from the AIP, it is important to know both whether your airport is listed in the most recent publication of [NPIAS (2023-2027)](https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/npias/current/) as well as whether the grant you are applying for qualifies under the current five-year plan which is updated and published every two years.

As part of the current five-year plan the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://www.faa.gov/) is in the final phase of implementing an ambitious modernization program of America’s air transportation system.   
  
This program is known as the [Next Generation Air Transportation System](https://www.faa.gov/nextgen/this_is_nextgen/), or NextGen. One of the many goals of NextGen is improving the weather architecture of America’s airports and dissemination of weather data into the National Airspace System (NAS). As part of this sweeping program, Automated Weather Observing Systems (AWOS) play a key role.

## The National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS)

The first step in applying for a grant from the [Airport Improvement Program](https://www.faa.gov/airports/aip/) (AIP) is to verify that your airport is listed in the most recent publication of NPIAS. The [National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems](https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/npias/) identifies over 3,000 existing and proposed airports which are included in the NAS as well as the roles which they currently serve.   
  
NPIAS includes all commercial service airports and all reliever airports. NPIAS also includes select publicly owned general aviation airports so long as they meet certain criteria, as well as a very small number of private airports. Only airports which are listed in NPIAS qualify for grants from the AIP.

To qualify for recognition from NPIAS an airport must be both open to the public and publicly owned. If an airport is privately owned it must either be designated by the FAA as a reliever or have scheduled service and at least 2,500 annual enplanements.  
  
Through the ACIP, NPIAS also identifies the types of development eligible for Federal funding under the AIP over the next 5 years as well as the amount of development which will need to take place. Estimates of these findings are published every 2 years. Since many of America’s airports were built to accommodate older, relatively small and slow aircraft by comparison to today, many upgrades are now required to bring an airport into compliance with modern design criteria from the FAA.   
  
Many additional factors beyond upgrades, repairs, and additions to an airport are considered when composing the ACIP. An airport’s capital development needs are driven by current and forecasted traffic, use and age of facilities, and changing aircraft technology, all of which require airports to update or replace equipment and infrastructure.  
  
Modernizing America’s airports is crucial to national transportation demands. According to the 2020 census, over 95% of the US population live within 30 miles of a primary airport. When you include general aviation airports into that statistic, 99.7% of the population live within 30 miles of a NPIAS airport. This means that for over 60 million rural Americans, an airport is the only method of providing critical access to National transportation they have.

## The Airports Capital Improvement Plan (ACIP)

The [Airports Capital Improvement Plan](https://www.faa.gov/airports/aip/acip/) (ACIP) is the internal document produced by the FAA every year. This document serves as the primary planning tool for identifying and prioritizing critical airport development within the NPIAS. As a result, the plan also serves as the criteria for distribution of grant funds under the AIP.  
  
Since the demands on infrastructure, technology, and weather elements vary drastically from region to region, the National ACIP is produced annually by the FAA Airport Improvement Program Branch based upon the reported information of the nine [Regional Offices](https://www.faa.gov/airports/news_information/contact_info/regional/).   
  
Each of the nine offices prepares their report based off individual airports or state airport planning agencies anticipated developmental needs over the next 3 to 5 years.

The nine FAA Regional Airport Offices include:

➤ New England Region  
➤ Eastern Region  
➤ Southern Region  
➤ Great Lakes Region  
➤ Southwest Region  
➤ Northwest Mountain Region  
➤ Western-Pacific Region  
➤ Alaskan Region

Since demand for AIP grants is so great, the ACIP must find a way to prioritize requests both throughout the individual regions as well as the long-term national goals of the FAA. Therefore, emphasis is placed on funding highest priority projects identified throughout the country.

### This means that while something may be eligible for an AIP grant by AIP guidelines, a project must also qualify under NPIAS-ACIP criteria to be considered for one. So, while an AWOS system is eligible for funding under the AIP guidelines, how do you know if it is covered by the current ACIP and therefore eligible under NPIAS for an AIP grant?

# NPIAS 2023-2027

The most recent NPIAS publication was released on September 30, 2022, for the years 2023 through 2027. It includes 3,287 existing airports, 8 proposed airports anticipated to open by 2027, and estimates 62.4 billion in AIP eligible and justified projects, an increase of almost $19 billion (43%) from the NPIAS issued 2 years ago.   
  
Of the listed airports, 98% of them (3,232) are owned by public entities while less than 2% (55) are privately owned. 1,782 public use airports were not included because they do not meet the entry criteria of NPIAS.

Given the crucial role which NPIAS airports serve in connecting Americans with national transportation, it is important to keep them operational and functional. To that end, the FAA has a series of design standards many aging airports no longer meet as aircraft have improved and air traffic increased. Making these upgrades and bringing airports up to modern standards currently accounts for 20% of NPIAS anticipated funding needs and roughly $12.4 billion, an increase of from the previous NPIAS years.   
These developments include:

➤ Strengthening, widening, narrowing, relocating, or extending runways and taxiways and their associated lighting to provide greater clearance for aircraft with larger wingspans and improve confusing taxiway layout areas.

➤ Expansion of existing or construction of new aprons to accommodate wider aircraft.

➤ Acquiring equipment including snow removal, deicing, weather reporting *– Including AWOS for compliance with NextGen, and approach lighting and guidance systems.*

➤ Constructing buildings for equipment primarily for snow removal equipment or aircraft hangars.

Since an AWOS system is part of the FAA design standards for the modern airport, those included in the NPIAS should have a working system. Purchasing a new AWOS or upgrading/replacing an older system meets the development category criteria for the 2023-2027 NPIAS.

# Next Generation Air Transportation System (NextGen)

Work began in 2007 on one of the most ambitious infrastructure and modernization projects in U.S transportation history.   
  
Led by the FAA, the Next Generation Air Transportation System (NextGen) is a series of interlinked programs, portfolios, systems, polices, and procedures which are designed to upgrade and make improvements to the operation of the NAS.

With America’s 20th century airports feeling the burden of 21st century technology and aircraft, the plan was rather than make minor upgrades to aging infrastructure, it would be better to implement major new technologies and revitalize America’s interaction with the NAS in one sweeping revitalization program.

## The goals of the NextGen project include:

➤ Increase the safety, efficiency, capacity, access, flexibility, predictability, and resilience of the NAS.  
  
➤ Examine, understand, and reduce the environmental effect of aviation.  
  
➤ Manage air traffic through Trajectory Based Operations (TBO) with strategic planning, managing, and optimizing of flights.  
  
NextGen plans to have all major components in place by the year 2025. One of the key programs of NextGen is NextGen Weather Program whose aim is to reduce the impact of weather on aviation as it is predicted that more accurate and timely weather data could help prevent as many as 2/3rd of weather delays and cancellations.

NextGen plans to have all major components in place by the year 2025. One of the key programs of NextGen is NextGen Weather Program whose aim is to reduce the impact of weather on aviation as it is predicted that more accurate and timely weather data could help prevent as many as 2/3rd of weather delays and cancellations.

# Common Support Services – Weather (CSS-Wx)

Part of the new [Weather Architecture](https://www.faa.gov/nextgen/programs/weather/architecture/) being implemented under NextGen is the [Common Support Services – Weather](https://www.faa.gov/nextgen/programs/weather/csswx/) (CSS-Wx) which will be the single provider of weather data, products, and imagery within the NAS.   
  
The program aims to improve the quality of traffic management decisions and reduce controller workload during severe weather occurrences.  
  
With America’s 20th century airports feeling the burden of 21st century technology and aircraft, the plan was rather than make minor upgrades to aging infrastructure, it would be better to implement major new technologies and revitalize America’s interaction with the NAS in one sweeping revitalization program.

Sensors input data in CSS-Wx from AWOS and ASOS systems via the Weather Messaging Switching Center Replacement (WMSCR) and the AWOS Data Acquisition System. The data will then be sent to the NextGen Weather Processor (NWP) which centrally produces domain-wide weather products for dissemination to NAS consumers. The program is scheduled for operation in 2023.

CSS-Wx uses internationally recognized data access and data format standard and offers many improvements going forward:

➤ Facilitates consistent weather information.  
➤ Increases NAS weather access.  
➤ Reduces interface development costs.  
➤ Reduces infrastructure and bandwidth costs.

args.summary:
This article from Mesotech International, a manufacturer of Automated Weather Observing Systems (AWOS), explains how airports can secure Federal funding for AWOS systems by understanding federal programs. In September 2019, the Federal government combined the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS) and the Airports Capital Improvement Plan (ACIP) into a single order (Order 5090.5), making ACIP a subset of NPIAS and the primary financial planning tool for the Airport Improvement Program (AIP).

Key context: Weather caused over 69% of delays exceeding 15 minutes between 2008-2013, totaling over 10 million lost minutes in 2013 alone. An hour-long delay costs air carriers between $1,400 and $4,500 depending on aircraft class, plus $35/hour for personal travelers and $63/hour for business travelers.

**NPIAS**: Identifies over 3,000 existing and proposed airports in the National Airspace System. Only airports listed in NPIAS qualify for AIP grants. To qualify, airports must be open to the public and publicly owned, or privately owned but designated as a reliever or with scheduled service and at least 2,500 annual enplanements. The most recent NPIAS publication (released September 30, 2022, covering 2023-2027) includes 3,287 existing airports and 8 proposed airports, with $62.4 billion in AIP-eligible projects (a 43% increase, or nearly $19 billion, from two years prior). Of these, 98% (3,232) are publicly owned. Bringing aging airports up to modern FAA design standards accounts for 20% of anticipated funding needs (~$12.4 billion), including weather reporting equipment like AWOS for NextGen compliance.

**ACIP**: An internal FAA document produced annually by the Airport Improvement Program Branch, based on reports from nine Regional Offices (New England, Eastern, Southern, Great Lakes, Southwest, Northwest Mountain, Western-Pacific, and Alaskan Regions). It prioritizes critical airport development and serves as the criteria for AIP grant distribution. Projects must qualify under both AIP guidelines and NPIAS-ACIP criteria.

**NextGen**: Initiated in 2007 by the FAA, this modernization program aims to increase safety, efficiency, capacity, and resilience of the NAS, reduce aviation's environmental impact, and manage air traffic through Trajectory Based Operations. All major components are planned to be in place by 2025. The NextGen Weather Program predicts that more accurate weather data could prevent as many as 2/3 of weather delays and cancellations.

**CSS-Wx**: The Common Support Services – Weather program will be the single provider of weather data within the NAS, with sensors inputting data from AWOS and ASOS systems via the Weather Messaging Switching Center Replacement (WMSCR). The NextGen Weather Processor centrally produces weather products for dissemination. The program was scheduled for operation in 2023 and offers benefits including consistent weather information, increased NAS weather access, and reduced interface/development/infrastructure costs.

The article concludes that purchasing, upgrading, or replacing an AWOS system meets the development category criteria for the 2023-2027 NPIAS and is eligible for AIP grants. Mesotech's Airport Weather Advisor® product has over 25 years of experience and services all USAF fixed weather base systems.

# Publications

ACI produces a range of [publications](http://store.aci.aero/product-category/economics-statistics/) in relation to airport traffic and airport economics that provide airport operators, stakeholders and business partners with the information and tools they need to better understand aviation trends and best practices.

## Global Reports and Data

* **World Annual Traffic Reports (WATR)**  
   This [annual report](http://store.aci.aero/product-category/economics-statistics/world-annual-traffic-reports-watr/) includes regional commentary, in-depth analyses of historical trends, drivers and risks affecting air transport demand. In addition, it gives access to the most comprehensive airport statistics dataset in the aviation industry provides a view of air transport demand across the world’s airports, covering over 2,500 airports in 180 countries.
* **World Airport Traffic Forecasts (WATF)**  
   The [World Airport Traffic Forecasts (WATF)](http://store.aci.aero/product-category/economics-statistics/world-annual-traffic-forecasts-watf/) provides insights into the future evolution of air transport demand across the world. This annual forecast provides projections that extend to 2040 and are presented on a global, regional and national level. The excel dataset includes forecasts for total passengers (international and domestic), air cargo volumes (in metric tonnes) and aircraft movements for over 100 countries.
* **Airport Economics Report**  
   The annual [ACI Airport Economics Report](http://store.aci.aero/product-category/economics-statistics/economics-report/) presents global analyses of airport activities based on the data collected in the financial year prior to each publication. Airport samples collectively represent around 80% of worldwide passenger traffic. As in previous years, the report consists of in-depth analyses, summaries and commentary on industry revenues (aeronautical and non-aeronautical) by source, costs (operating and capital) and their evolution over time.

* **The Airport Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)**  
  [Airport Key Performance Indicators](http://store.aci.aero/product-category/economics-statistics/key-performance-indicators-kpis/) provide insight into areas such as financial and employee performance, fixed-asset productivity and airport operations. The annual report includes detailed statistical tables that provide quantifiable barometers of industry activity for airport managers, analysts, investors and other aviation stakeholders.

## Policy Briefs, Regulation and Best Practices

ACI produces publications highlighting best practices and policy recommendations. The publications include [policy briefs, and regulation and best practices](https://store.aci.aero/product-category/economics-statistics/policy-briefs/) on matters ranging from taxation and airport ownership to airport charges and slot allocation.

## 

## ACI Asia-Pacific & Middle East Economic Review

The Regional Economics Committee published the ACI Asia-Pacific Economic Review, available to ACI Asia-Pacific & Middle East members. This publication highlights key regional developments and analyses in areas including air traffic, airport economics, airport privatisation, and investments in airport infrastructure.

## **Airport Industry Outlook Asia-Pacific and the Middle East**

This quarterly analytical product serves as an up-to-date snapshot of airport business performance across the region with analyses of the key industry trends. The key objective of this publication is to conduct short-term, fast and high-frequency data collection and analyses, which were especially important for the aviation ecosystem during the pandemic. ACI Asia-Pacific & Middle East jointly develop this publication with Mott MacDonald.
