# Essential Air Service: Illustrating Coming Changes to the Program

# Essential Air Service: Illustrating Coming Changes to the Program

[Transportation & Infrastructure](https://www.taxpayer.net/category/transportation-infrastructure/),  | [Analysis](https://www.taxpayer.net/library/analysis/)

Apr 4, 2013 | 7 min read [| Print Article](#)

The Essential Air Service (EAS) is a federal subsidy program created in the 1970s as part of airline deregulation. Though the program was intended to be temporary, taxpayers across the nation now spend more than $200 million each year so that a privileged few in just 117 communities can be guaranteed convenient air service.

Taxpayers for Common Sense (TCS) has done a comprehensive review of all current Essential Air Service (EAS) program agreements, which are based on proposals made by individual airlines to the Department of Transportation. The airlines lay out the terms they would require to provide service to what would be an otherwise unprofitable market.

**[Visit our Data Center to see the complete data set, some other interesting facts we found reviewing the data, and a map visualization of all EAS airports](/library/article/transportation-data).**

One interesting aspect to consider when looking at the EAS data is which airports are likely to be effected as a result of the air program reauthorization signed into law in 2012. That law changed the EAS eligibility rules to receive subsidized service. At present, to be eligible, an airport or community must1:

1. Be 90 or more miles from the nearest medium or large hub airport.
2. Average 10 or more enplanements per day (this requirement does not apply if the airport is 175 miles or more from a medium or large hub airport).
3. Require a subsidy of less than $1,000 per passenger.
4. Have received subsidized air service between September 30, 2010 and September 30, 2011.

These requirements (in particular #4) have reduced the number of eligible communities to 121. When airline deregulation became law in 1978, it made eligible for subsidized service any community that, at the date of enactment, either received air service or was eligible to receive air service but such service was suspended. As a result, 480 communities (again, not including Alaska or Hawaii) were originally eligible. Now it is 121. At present, 117 of these receive subsidized service.

The first requirement pre-dates the recent changes, and though there are some airports that could be argued are within 90 miles of a hub, any airports this would eliminated have ostensibly been removed from the program already.

The enplanement requirement (#2) and subsidy cap (#3) –new as of the 2012 reauthorization – could potentially pare down the list of subsidized airports in the coming months and years. To date, only one airport – in Ely, Nevada – has lost its service due to these requirements. At the time, Ely had the distinction of the highest per passenger subsidy (a whopping $3,720) of all EAS airports, so it seems appropriate that it would be the first to lose its service. ([See the U.S. DOT doc for this decision](/wp-content/uploads/ported/images/downloads/Ely%20Termination%20Order.pdf))

These nine communities had less than 3,650 enplanements in 2011, and are within 175 miles of a large or medium hub airport. By the new rules passed by Congress, they would not be eligible for future subsidies if they do not get above the 10 enplanements per day threshold:

| EAS Community | Airport | 2011 Enplanements | Nearest Large/Med. Hub | Distance (mi.) to Hub |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Jamestown, NY | Chautauqua County-Jamestown Airport | 3,483 | Greater Buffalo Int'l, NY (M) | 76 |
| Merced, CA | Merced Municipal Airport-Macready Field | 3,181 | San Jose Int'l, CA (M) | 114 |
| Bradford, PA | Bradford Regional Airport | 2,908 | Greater Buffalo Int'l, NY (M) | 76 |
| Athens, GA | Athens-Ben Epps Airport | 1,655 | Hartsfield Int'l, Atlanta, GA (L) | 72 |
| Franklin/Oil City, PA | Venango Regional Airport | 1,284 | Greater Pittsburgh Int'l, PA (L) | 86 |
| Jonesboro, AR | Jonesboro Municipal Airport | 989 | Memphis Int'l, TN (M) | 79 |
| Kingman, AZ | Kingman Airport | 975 | McCarran Int'l, Las Vegas, NV (L) | 103 |
| Macon, GA | Middle Georgia Regional Airport | 917 | Hartsfield Int'l, Atlanta, GA (L) | 81 |
| Jackson, TN | McKellar-Sipes Regional Airport | 484 | Memphis Int'l, TN (M) | 85 |

In addition, there are three communities that require a subsidy of more than $1,000 to support air service at their location. These would also not be eligible:

| EAS Community | Airport | Calculated Subsidy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lewistown, MT | Lewistown Municipal Airport | $1,904.79 |
| Miles City, MT | Miles City Airport-Frank Wiley Field | $1,372.10 |
| Jackson, TN | McKellar-Sipes Regional Airport | $1,187.71 |

At the end of March, Lewistown and Miles city received word that their service is slated to be terminated as a result of their required subsidy level exceeding $1,000. ([See the U.S. DOT doc for this decision](/wp-content/uploads/ported/images/downloads/Lewistown-Miles%20City%20Termination%20Order.pdf))

Though Congress believes these changes to the EAS program solve its greatest ills, the result would be only a tiny cut to the program. Eliminating service at these 11 airports would save $17 million, less than a ten-percent cut in the overall size of the program. Rapid cost escalation in recent years could itself wipe out these potential savings in future years, leaving taxpayers worse off than they are currently.

TCS has been calling for the elimination of EAS for many years, and there is no time like the present to get rid of this wasteful and unnecessary program. We are not alone in our opposition. Last year, during debate over the authorization of the nation’s air program and transportation appropriations bill, several members of Congress called for the program’s elimination, and an amendment to eliminate the EAS program received [bipartisan support](http://clerk.house.gov/evs/2012/roll417.xml) in the House. The Washington Post editorial board [recently stated the EAS program should be zeroed out](http://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/small-town-airports-propped-up-with-200-million/2013/03/08/2cde6ce6-869b-11e2-98a3-b3db6b9ac586_story.html) in favor of funding other, well, more essential federal programs.

Simply put, the EAS program has long outlived its intended purpose and needs to be eliminated.

—

1. None of these requirements apply to Alaska or Hawaii.

Evidence that tempers or refutes the hypothesis that an airport with approximately 500,000 annual passengers generates significant and measurable socioeconomic impacts. Seek contrary evidence and methodological critiques, including: (1) academic and policy studies arguing small airports have low or negligible employment multipliers — e.g., studies on the 'home bias' of regional airports, small airport subsidies, and whether economic impact studies overstate benefits that would occur regardless (attribution and counterfactual problems); (2) evidence on the threshold of passenger throughput or route network density required for airports to attract airlines, sustain connectivity, and produce measurable productivity or agglomeration effects (note that many carriers require far more than 500,000 passengers or specific catchment populations to sustain service); (3) econometric studies using control regions, difference-in-differences, or instrumental variables that find small airports do not cause measurable regional growth — contrast with larger hub airports that do; (4) methodological caveats of input-output multiplier analysis in airport context: leakages, displacement effects, the fact that airports serving tourism may shift spending rather than create it, and the role of existing alternative transport (roads, rail) in making airport impacts marginal; (5) regional context dependence: evidence that impacts vary with urban vs. rural setting, tourism dependence, industrial base, and presence of competing airports within 100-200 km; (6) any data showing that at 500,000 passengers per year the absolute jobs/GDP numbers are tiny relative to regional economies (e.g., jobs per million passengers figures for small airports, compared with regional employment bases). Provide concrete citations, statistics, and links to original peer-reviewed studies and reports.

--- SOURCE 2: Chapter 4 The Role of the Airport in the Local Economy ---
URL: https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/28759/chapter/5

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is Chapter 4 ("The Role of the Airport in the Local Economy") of a 2025 National Academies publication titled "Communicating a Balanced Look at Local Airport Activity and Climate Change." The chapter provides new research to help airports supplement their own economic impact studies when communicating with stakeholders about the tension between economic benefits and climate change concerns. It addresses the question: "Since aviation climate effects are so expensive to abate, what benefits would be lost by curtailing aviation activity?"

Key content includes:
- IATA's 2022 Global Passenger Survey found 75% of passengers "prioritized proximity to airport when choosing where to fly from."
- ACI's national study reports U.S. commercial airports produce total economic output exceeding $1.4 trillion, supporting more than 11.5 million jobs with a payroll exceeding $428 billion, and account for more than 7% of U.S. GDP.
- Economic impact studies measure three types of impacts: direct, indirect, and induced. "Leakage" refers to dollars re-spent outside the region.

Three new measures of economic impacts are presented:
1. Expected additional economic impacts due to growth in activity (marginal jobs, income, and output per additional enplanement at commercial airports; and per additional operation/based jet aircraft at GA airports).
2. Costs to consumers if they made the same trip using another mode of transportation (Full Price of Travel - FPT).
3. Costs to consumers if they made the same trip using another airport.

Key data tables:
- Table 4-1 shows average increase in FPT via alternate mode by hub type: Large hub = 426% time-related, 157% out-of-pocket, 289% FPT, 70% GHG increase; Medium = 360%/125%/241%/56%; Small = 317%/101%/206%/56%; Nonhub = 283%/73%/172%/51%.
- An example: East Coast to Europe via air costs about $800 fare plus $377 time value = $1,177 FPT; via ocean liner = $3,861 FPT, saving $2,684 each way via aviation.
- Table 4-2 lists CO2 emissions factors by mode (well-to-wake), including air travel (short/medium/long-haul for passengers and freight), passenger car, intercity rail, ocean (0.402 kg/passenger mile), truck, and rail.
- Table 4-3 shows FPT increases using an alternate airport: Large hub = 45% time, 15% out-of-pocket, 29% FPT, 13.6% GHG; Medium = 39%/13%/26%/14.3%; Small = 35%/12%/23%/14.4%; Nonhub = 29%/10%/19%/13.9%. Conclusion: local consumers spend on average 19-29% more on FPT basis flying from an alternative airport.
- Table 4-4 shows FPT increases based on alternate airport's hub classification relative to subject airport.
- Table 4-5 shows passengers almost always save time flying locally (e.g., 29 of 29 large hub domestic markets).
- Table 4-6 shows quintile dispersion of FPT increases, greatest for large hubs.

Methodological notes: results are "marginal" impacts not average impacts; marginal impacts typically smaller than average impacts from existing economic impact studies. Alternative mode and alternate airport measures are not available for GA airports due to lack of comparable data. The chapter includes case study examples (Austin, Texas) and notes that airports sometimes are reluctant to link economic activity with climate discussions in communications.
</summary>

"Airports are more than runways and terminals. Airports are powerful engines of economic growth and possibility for local communities across the United States. In Taking America Beyond the Horizon: The Economic Impact of Commercial Service Airports in 2017, we are pleased to announce the total economic output of U.S. commercial airports now exceeds $1.4 trillion, supporting more than 11.5 million jobs with a payroll of more than $428 billion."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://crp.trb.org/acrpwebresource1/the-value-of-my-airport

SUMMARY:
<summary>

This article by Larry Swedroe (published December 5, 2019 on Alpha Architect) explores the global phenomenon of home country bias in investing—the tendency of investors to overweight domestic assets relative to their share of global market capitalization. The article draws on multiple research studies including:

- A 2017 Vanguard study showing strong home country bias across countries. Data showed: US (50% of global market cap, 79% allocated to domestic equities), UK (7% market share, 26% domestic allocation), Japan (7% share, 55% domestic), Canada (3% share, 59% domestic), and Australia (2% share, 67% domestic). The article's central question asks whether home country bias affects stock prices. Victor Haghani and James White of Elm Partners conducted a thought experiment with one large market (US at 50%) and ten small markets (5% each), assuming US investors want 80% domestic allocation and small market investors want 50% domestic allocation. They concluded that home bias creates excess demand for the large US market (pushing it up as much as 60%, from $50 to $80) and a shortfall in smaller markets, reducing expected returns for US equities by about 1.5%. This contradicts active investors' claims that passive investing distorts prices—rather, active home-bias decisions drive the distortion.

Swedroe concludes by noting behavioral biases destroy returns and suggests that believers in market efficiency should accept that all risky assets have similar risk-adjusted returns, eliminating the rationale for home bias. He also notes that US investors whose labor capital is tied to the US economy should consider overweighting foreign markets to offset labor capital risk.

--- SOURCE 1: Comparing Enhanced Models for Evaluating Economic Impact of Airports ---
URL: https://www.preprints.org/manuscript/202305.2200

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This preprint (DOI:10.20944/preprints202305.2200.v1), titled "Comparing Enhanced Models for Evaluating Economic Impact of Airports," compares three approaches for determining the economic contribution of airports in regions with multiple airports, using the three largest airports in São Paulo state, Brazil (SBKP - Viracopos International, SBGR - Governador André Franco Montoro, and SBSP - Deputado Freitas Nobre). The paper was submitted May 26, 2023 and posted May 31, 2023, and is not peer-reviewed. A peer-reviewed version was published in Future Transportation 2023, 3(3), 1124-1146 (DOI:10.3390/futuretransp3030062).

The study applies the Input-Output (IO) analysis method, recommended by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) for assessing airport economic impacts. Because the three airports have overlapping catchment areas, the authors applied three weight factor models to divide the IO air transport economic data: (1) circular buffer model (based on straight-line/Euclidean distance), (2) displacement/travel time model (based on minimum travel time via tools like Google Maps), and (3) Huff's gravitational model (a probabilistic model considering airport attractiveness, travel time, and passenger/air cargo movement).

Methodology: Municipalities within a 200 km radius of the airports were identified. IO tables from Brazil's NEREUS (Center for Regional and Urban Economics of the University of São Paulo) and Federal Government employment/wage data were used to regionalize the IO tables (68 industries). Two average multipliers were determined: generated product and generated income. The three distribution models were then applied.

Key results: 
- SBGR saw ~56% increase in passenger movement (2010-2018); SBSP increased ~47%; SBKP increased nearly 90% (peak in 2014).
- Air cargo at the main terminal (SBGR) grew 67.5% (2010-2018); SBKP grew about 10%; SBSP cargo restricted due to aircraft size limitations.
- With the circular buffer model, every monetary unit invested in SBKP generated 2.5 monetary units, while SBGR and SBSP generated 1.2 units each, indicating SBKP's better geographic/strategic position.
- The travel time model showed SBKP has better accessibility and higher product valuation than SBGR and SBSP.
- The Huff model, which considers airport attractiveness (passenger and air cargo movement), showed SBGR presents higher product generation than SBKP and SBSP, consistent with SBGR concentrating the greatest passenger and cargo movement in the country.
- Across the analyzed period, SBGR showed stability in regional relevance, SBSP had a slight drop, and SBKP gained similar-magnitude increases.

Authors: Ivaciane de Quadra Magalhães (ORCID 0000-0002-1328-0801), Anderson Ribeiro Correia, Michelle Carvalho Galvão da Silva Pinto Bandeira* (ORCID 0000-0001-5399-2451, corresponding author), Mauro Zackiewicz, and Luiz Antonio Tozi (ORCID 0000-0002-4269-1204).

The paper contributes to literature by proposing improved/alternative methodology (using probability distributions as weight factors) for evaluating airport economic and social benefits in multi-airport regions. The authors identified the most suitable model for establishing correlations between airport infrastructure investments and generation of GDP, employment, and added value, concluding that the Huff model's consideration of airport attractiveness factors provides the most realistic analysis.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Evaluating the economic impact of airports is crucial for understanding the benefits they bring to a region. However, when an area has more than one airport, it becomes essential to analyze each airport's contribution to the local economy to make informed investment and policy decisions."

--- SOURCE 3: The effect of airports on regional development: Evidence from the construction of regional airports in Norway ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0739885916301408

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article titled "The effect of airports on regional development: Evidence from the construction of regional airports in Norway" by Eivind Tveter, published in Research in Transportation Economics (Volume 63, August 2017, pages 50-58), as part of a special issue on "The wider economic and social impacts of transport networks: Looking for the empirics" (edited by Bråthen Svein and Moshe Givoni). The paper carries DOI 10.1016/j.retrec.2017.07.001 and has been cited 54 times with 11 policy citations and 103 Mendeley readers.

METHODOLOGY: The study estimates the effect of airports on regional development using the substantial construction of nine regional airports in Norway during 1970-1972 as the source of variation. The effects are estimated using a difference-in-difference design that compares municipalities with a shorter distance to the nearest airport (treated) against three sets of control municipalities: (1) municipalities with regional airports constructed after 1980 (whose travel times are similar to counterfactual travel times for treated areas), (2) municipalities near regional airports constructed well before 1964 (to account for timing correlations with regional growth), and (3) municipalities "just not" affected by the airport constructions (with similar travel times to existing vs. constructed airports, and likely driven by the same regional factors). Outcomes considered are population and employment at the municipality level.

RATIONALE: This paper contributes to the "airport effect" literature by studying changes in airport infrastructure rather than air traffic or usage variables. The author argues this approach offers estimates more likely to have a causal interpretation. The paper also argues that no theory proposes that transport itself (rather than usage) affects local economic development, and since infrastructure is more directly controlled by policymakers, this analysis is more relevant for policy. The study addresses endogeneity/simultaneity bias issues common in prior research, which typically used lagged variables or fixed factors (e.g., hub status) as instruments—often weakly correlated or not credibly excludable.

RESULTS: The results demonstrate a positive but not significant effect on population and employment. Point estimates indicate that population in municipalities near the constructed airports increased by 5% from 1970 to 1980, but the overall imprecision of the estimates makes it impossible to reject the hypothesis that the airports had no regional impacts. Productivity gains (externalities arising from air travel, e.g., through inter-city agglomeration) were not included in this analysis because they are difficult to isolate from direct cost impacts already captured in standard cost-benefit analysis.

CONTEXT: The paper notes the Norwegian air transport market changed considerably since 1970; by 2003, domestic trip rate per capita was almost three times the European average, and by 2015 the trip rate was almost five. JEL classification: H54, O18, R42. Keywords: Air transport, Regional development, Regional airports, Transport infrastructure, Difference-in-difference, Wider economic impacts.

RELATED LITERATURE: The paper is most closely related to Blonigen and Cristea (2015) (also difference-in-difference, but using air travel), and shares empirical strategy elements with Funderburg et al. (2010) on California highway construction. Other related works include Sheard (2014), Brueckner (2003), Percoco (2010), and Green (2007). The article includes 38 references, including works by Baum-Snow (2007), Duranton and Turner (2012), Michaels (2008), Donaldson (railroads), and Donaldson and Hornbeck (2016).

The page also lists citing articles, including Sobieralski (2021) on transportation infrastructure and employment in US MSAs, Lenaerts et al. (2021) on aviation market access, Zhang and Graham (2020) on air transport and economic growth causality, Monterrubio et al. (2020) on airport construction community perceptions in Mexico, and Gibbons and Wu (2021) on airports in China.
</summary>

This is a Wikipedia article on the Essential Air Service (EAS), a U.S. government program enacted to guarantee that small communities previously served by certificated airlines prior to deregulation in 1978 maintain commercial air service. The program aims to maintain a minimal level of scheduled air service to communities that would otherwise not be profitable.

Key facts:
- The program is codified at 49 U.S.C. §§ 41731–41748, administered by the U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT), which subsidizes airlines to serve communities that would not otherwise receive scheduled air service.
- As of June 1, 2015, 159 communities in the US received EAS subsidies: 44 in Alaska, two in Hawaii, and one in Puerto Rico.
- Subsidy levels have increased substantially over time. As of October 2024, program subsidies amounted to $550 million. EAS subsidies have increased by more than 500% since 1997.
- The George W. Bush Administration sought to reduce program costs to $50 million via stricter eligibility criteria and local cost-sharing requirements.

Community eligibility criteria:
- Per the Appropriations Act of 2000, no community within the contiguous 48 states may receive a subsidy greater than $200 per passenger unless the community is more than 210 miles from the nearest large or medium hub airport.

Controversy:

--- SOURCE 8: [PDF] How does the federal government subsidize air service to small ... ---
URL: https://enotrans.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Eno-Aviation-Insights-Question-10.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Eno Center for Transportation Aviation Insight (No. 10, January 31, 2018) explains how the federal government subsidizes air service to small communities through the Essential Air Service (EAS) program. Congress established EAS in 1979 during airline deregulation to subsidize flights to the smallest airports. The program was initially intended to last 10 years but was extended in perpetuity in 1996, and costs have risen significantly since then. With approximately 300 communities receiving subsidized service (of 746 originally eligible), the program distributes roughly $270 million per year.

Key statistics: The busiest EAS airport (Joplin, Missouri) averages fewer than 160 passengers per day, while some airports have fewer than a dozen daily departing passengers. Per-passenger subsidies vary dramatically—from close to zero to several hundred dollars. During FY2016, the highest per-passenger subsidy was Altoona, Pennsylvania at $642 per passenger (3,693 total passengers). McCook, Nebraska had the highest overall subsidy at $778 per passenger.

Program constraints and enforcement issues: Congress imposed limitations including a 70-mile minimum distance from a medium/large hub, a minimum of 10 daily enplanements, and caps on per-passenger subsidies ($200 for communities within 210 miles of a hub, $1,000 for others). U.S. DOT enforced the $200 cap from 1990-2006, causing 39 communities to lose service, but stopped enforcement in 2006. Although DOT announced resumed enforcement in 2014, 26 airports remained above the $200 threshold in FY2016. Since 2006, only one airport has lost service due to the $200 rule, but eight airports lost service due to the $1,000 cap since 2012.

Potential savings and context: Options to reduce EAS costs include increasing the minimum distance requirement, enforcing the per-passenger cap, and enforcing minimum enplanements. A scenario combining a 150-mile minimum distance, the $200 cap, and 10-daily-enplanement enforcement would only save $114.3 million. Notably, the EAS program represents less than two percent of the $16 billion in annual federal aviation spending. The Trump administration's initial 2018 budget proposed cutting the program entirely before settling on a 50 percent reduction. U.S. DOT's criteria for adding new communities include reliability, connections with larger hubs, and community views—but notably do not include cost.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an official U.S. Department of Transportation webpage providing comprehensive information about the Essential Air Service (EAS) program. The EAS program was established by section 419 of the Federal Aviation Act following the Airline Deregulation Act (ADA) of 1978, which removed federal control over fares, routes, and market entry. The program guarantees that communities served by certificated air carriers before deregulation maintain a minimum level of scheduled air service, typically subsidizing two round trips daily with 30- to 50-seat aircraft to large- or medium-hub airports. As of Fall 2024, the Department provides EAS subsidies to 65 communities in Alaska and 112 communities in the 48 contiguous states, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico.

The Civil Aeronautics Board managed the program until January 1, 1985, when the Department of Transportation assumed responsibility. The program, initially authorized for ten years, is now permanently authorized by Congress.

Community eligibility is outlined in 49 U.S.C. § 41731. To remain eligible, communities must maintain an average of 10 enplanements per service day during the most recent fiscal year, though communities more than 175 driving miles from the nearest large or medium hub airport are exempt. EAS communities less than 175 miles from a hub must have an average subsidy per passenger of less than $650, while those farther away must have an average subsidy of less than $1,000 (reduced to $850 effective October 1, 2026). These subsidy requirements do not apply to Alaska and Hawaii. Waivers may be granted for temporary demand declines, but starting October 1, 2026, waivers cannot be provided for more than two consecutive fiscal years or more than five fiscal years within 25 consecutive years. Eligibility criteria were amended in the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (Pub L. No. 118-63, May 16, 2024).

The carrier selection process involves the Department issuing a Request for Proposals (RFP) to all air carriers, with proposals submitted on a sealed "best and final" basis. Under 49 U.S.C. § 41733(c)(1), selection factors include demonstrated reliability, code-share/interline arrangements with larger carriers, community preferences (including views of elected officials), marketing plans, and for Alaska, prior experience providing scheduled air service. Contracts generally run two to four years. Carriers are compensated in arrears on a per-flight-completed basis, with monthly invoices detailing actual service, and only completed flights (take-off and landing at destination) are generally eligible for subsidy. Contact information for the EAS and Domestic Analysis Division is provided, and a list of eligible communities is available at the DOT website.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed academic article by Robert M. McNab (Old Dominion University) published in the Journal of Economic Analysis (2024, Volume 3, Issue 2, pages 134-146). The paper reviews the literature on Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) - highly automated small aircraft and drones for passenger and cargo transport in and around urban areas - and critically examines projections of its economic impact, potential externalities, and equity considerations.

Key points:
- AAM projections vary enormously: total addressable market estimated at $1.5 trillion by 2040 and $9 trillion by 2050 (Morgan Stanley); US annual AAM market projected at $115 billion by 2035; air taxis could account for 12 million passenger enplanements by 2030s and 400 million by 2050.

- The author argues studies assume technologies mature simultaneously, regulatory frameworks adapt rapidly, and ignore displacement effects (where AAM replaces existing transport modalities, reducing employment elsewhere) - many rely on "Say's Law" (supply creates its own demand).
- Equity concerns are largely ignored: horizontal equity (whether similar-income agents receive similar treatment) and vertical equity (how burdens/benefits relate to income) need inclusion. AAM externalities like noise, visual pollution, and reduced property values near vertiports would likely be concentrated in lower-income neighborhoods while benefits accrue to higher-income users.
- The lack of a common AAM definition and failure to specify NAICS codes hinders comparability of studies. Future research should address displacement, equity, and clearly state scope for transparent replication.
- The author concludes projections of AAM economic impact require time, effort, and transparency to more accurately reflect future impacts, otherwise public resources may be misallocated for gains that are unlikely to materialize.
</summary>

**Objective:** The paper compares three approaches to determine individual airport economic contributions and identify their social and economic benefits. The study considers three weight factors for the input-output basic model recommended by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO).

**Methodology:** The three distribution models used as weights for IO analysis were:
1. **Circular Buffer Model** - deterministic model based on Euclidean (straight-line) distance within a 200 km radius of each airport
2. **Travel/Displacement Time Model** - deterministic model using minimum travel time (calculated via Google Maps) instead of straight-line distance
3. **Huff's Gravitational Model** - probabilistic model considering airport attractiveness (e.g., passenger numbers) and distance decay

The analysis was applied to the three largest airports in São Paulo state, Brazil, due to their proximity: Viracopos International Airport (SBKP), Governador André Franco Montoro Airport (SBGR), and Deputado Freitas Nobre Airport (SBSP). - A noted limitation was that the most recent Brazilian IO matrix available was from 2015 (2018 via NEREUS updates), a common global delay issue

The study fills a gap in literature by proposing improvements to methods for evaluating airports' economic and social benefits, enabling better prediction of returns on airport infrastructure investments for government and private sector decision-makers, particularly regarding correlations between airport infrastructure investments and GDP, employment, and added value generation.

URL: https://www.eca.europa.eu/lists/ecadocuments/insr14_21/insr14_21_en.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The European Court of Auditors (ECA) published a special report on 16 December finding that EU-funded investments in airports provide poor value for money. On 11 May 2026, the European Commission launched a public consultation (open until 11 June 2026) on draft new Guidelines on State aid in the air transport sector, which will replace the 2014 Aviation Guidelines. The key proposed changes include:

**Operating aid restrictions:** From April 2027, operating aid will only be permitted for airports handling up to 1 million passengers during a 5-year transitional period (until 3 April 2032). A stronger environmental dimension is introduced, requiring credible decarbonisation plans for capacity-increasing investments, with aid intensity bonuses (up to 20%) for sustainability-related investments, remote regions, and infrastructure supporting zero-emission aircraft or ground-based electrical equipment.

**Extended catchment area:** The catchment area is extended from 100 km (or 60 minutes travel) to a radius of 150 km, unless the journey time by road, sea, or rail exceeds 90 minutes, broadening the competition analysis around subsidised airports. The Commission proposes offsets for certain situations (e.g., routes involving maritime transport without daily return service or air transport are not considered the same catchment area).

**Start-up aid abolished:** The draft completely abolishes start-up aid for launching new routes from regional airports, as the Commission considers that airlines must bear the risks and costs of launching new routes themselves in a fully liberalised market. De minimis aid remains available, capped at EUR 300,000 per airline per country over a three-year period (registered centrally from 1 January 2026).

**Other changes:** The draft omits the previous methodology on airport incentives to airlines (which had been applied in some fifty cases since 2014), and introduces new monitoring mechanisms requiring ex post evaluations for aid schemes exceeding EUR 150 million per year or EUR 750 million total.

The new rules are scheduled to come into force in April 2027. The tightening of rules counterbalances a more favourable regime planned for airports handling up to 500,000 passengers per year, though the authors note this will be ineffective without an appropriate regulatory framework to encourage airlines to launch routes from less attractive airports. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by John L. Crompton (Texas A&M University), published in the Journal of Travel Research (Vol. 45, August 2006, pp. 67-82), argues that most economic impact studies are commissioned to legitimize a political position rather than to search for economic truth. The author contends that these studies are typically driven by sponsors' desires to demonstrate their positive contribution to community prosperity, and that this political motivation frequently leads to "mischievous practices" that breach integrity requirements.

The article's conceptual framework posits that economic impact analyses should measure the net economic change in incomes of host residents resulting from out-of-town visitor spending. Crompton emphasizes that money invested by city councils belongs to residents, not the council, so the key measure is revenue accruing to residents rather than direct tax collections.

The author illustrates the political nature of such studies using the contentious Arlington, Texas, debate over public funding for a Dallas Cowboys stadium. Four economic studies commissioned by different factions produced wildly divergent results: (1) $238M/year for Arlington (City of Arlington), (2) $346M/year for Dallas County (property developer), (3) $51M/year for Irving (City of Irving), and (4) a projected loss of $290.5-325.3 million (opponents). Study 4 used a 30-year timeframe while others reported annual figures. Supporters spent $10 million on the referendum campaign (with $6 million from the Cowboys) versus only $45,000 raised by opponents.

Crompton documents ten mischievous procedures commonly used in these studies:
1. **Including local residents** (the most frequent practice) - Local expenditures represent recycling of existing money, not new economic growth, yet many studies include them. Examples include the Miami-Dade County bond program ($680.3M) and National Assembly of Local Arts Agencies study claiming arts are a "$36.8 billion industry."
2. **Inappropriate aggregation** - Changing geographic units of analysis alters who counts as visitors vs. locals. The Florida state parks study summed county-level impacts ($273M) but when aggregated, most expenditures became local.
3. **Inclusion of time-switchers and casuals** - Visitors who would have come anyway should be excluded.
4. **Abuse of multipliers** - Including improper compounding, emphasizing sales multipliers (which produce numbers 2+ times larger than income measures but are meaningless for policy), mischievous employment multipliers (Baltimore Ravens study claimed 1,170 full-time jobs from a team with 71 full-time employees playing only 10 home games), and failure to use capture rates (only retail margins should be multiplied, not total retail spending).
5. **Ignoring costs borne by the local community** - Studies report only benefits, ignoring costs like traffic congestion, road accidents, vandalism, and police costs.

Crompton notes consultants protect their reputations through extensive qualifying statements in reports and cover letters that shift responsibility for assumptions to sponsors, accepting "assumptions provided by the City and the developer" without critique. These qualifiers receive no visibility in ensuing publicity.

The author notes two legitimate situations for including local expenditures: "deflected impact" (when events keep residents home who would otherwise spend money elsewhere) and "significance analysis" (measuring importance rather than net economic impact). However, significance analyses become mischievous when presented as economic impact studies.

Crompton concludes that consultants are essentially "the exact equivalent of an expert witness in a lawsuit who comes to testify in support of the side that is paying the expert's bill," and that a consulting organization failing to deliver expected numbers rarely receives repeat business.
</summary>

The multiplier effect refers to how economic benefits from tourism multiply throughout a local economy.

The video identifies five types of tourism multipliers, first categorized by Dieke and Jenkins in 1997:
1. Sales/transaction multiplier - increases in sales (e.g., hotel rooms, tours, flights), including both direct sales and indirect sales (e.g., farmers supplying restaurants serving tourists).
2. Output/production multiplier - increases in goods and services produced (e.g., more hotel rooms, shows, or boat trips available), regardless of whether they are actually sold.
3. Income multiplier - multiplied incomes, such as a part-time worker going full-time due to tourism growth, and the resulting spending ripple effect on local businesses.
4. Employment multiplier - more tourism creates more jobs, both directly (e.g., hotel waiters) and indirectly (e.g., construction workers who build hotels or road maintenance workers).
5. Official/government revenue multiplier - official statistics showing government revenue from tourism that can be reinvested (e.g., in hospitals or schools). However, not all tourism revenue is officially recorded (e.g., unregistered drivers or informal vendors), and some suggest actual economic benefits may be up to double the official figures.

The multiplier works through three types of expenditure:
- Direct tourism expenditure (tourist spending on tourism goods/services).
- Indirect tourism expenditure (e.g., government spending on roads tourists use).
- Induced tourism expenditure (spending that wouldn't occur without tourism, e.g., a waiter spending his increased wages on his family).

The video emphasizes the importance of sustainable destination management and warns against economic leakage, where money spent at foreign-owned hotel chains (e.g., Hilton) or on imported products (e.g., Coca-Cola, international alcohol brands) leaves the destination country, whereas buying locally produced goods keeps money in the local economy.

--- SOURCE 18: Modeling Airport Choice Using a Latent Class Logit Model ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2226-4310/10/8/703

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed open-access article published in the MDPI journal "Aerospace" (Volume 10, Issue 8, Article 703, DOI: 10.3390/aerospace10080703) titled "Modeling Airport Choice Using a Latent Class Logit Model," by Luigi dell'Olio (Universidad de Cantabria, Spain), Andrés Rodríguez (Universidad de Cantabria), and Silvia Sipone (Universidad de Burgos). It was submitted July 12, 2023, revised August 6, 2023, accepted August 8, 2023, and published August 10, 2023.

**Purpose:** The study investigates traveler behavior in choosing between nearby (competing) airports, examining whether airport choice depends on user characteristics, trip purpose (leisure vs. business), trip circumstances (traveling with family, children, partner, or friends), presence of low-cost airlines, and number of transfers/direct connections.

**Methodology:** The researchers designed a stated preference survey (using an efficient design methodology per Rose and Bliemer, implemented with NGENE software) and estimated a latent class logit model. A pilot survey of 49 users informed efficient scenario design. The final survey was conducted in two cities in northern Spain, comparing Seve Ballesteros Airport in Santander (influence area ~280,000 inhabitants) and Bilbao Airport (~900,000 inhabitants), located ~105 km apart by road. The survey presented 12 possible scenarios (6 leisure, 6 business), with respondents given 4 scenarios based on their travel purpose. Each scenario offered three alternatives: nearest airport (A1), farthest airport (A2), or the option not to travel (A3). Notably, including the "not travel" option was a novelty designed to avoid biasing results. The final survey was completed by 393 respondents, yielding 1,572 observations.

**Key Results:** The model identified two latent classes of travelers with very different behavior:
- **Class 1 (90% probability):** More price-sensitive travelers (mostly tourism/travelers who perceive travel costs, access costs, and access times more negatively). Traveling with a partner reduces utility of both airports.
- **Class 2 (10% probability):** Higher-income or business travelers who are less price-sensitive, weigh the number of transfers from the nearest airport more negatively (transfers perceived less negatively from A2 than A1), and are more than twice as attracted by low-cost airlines at the nearest airport. For class 2, the "not travel" option is barely considered.

The model achieved a very high McFadden Pseudo R-squared fit of 0.542. Most parameters were statistically significant at 95% confidence, except CHILDREN (A2) and ACCOST (A1) in class 1, and CON (A3) in class 2.

**Conclusions & Policy Recommendations:** Key findings include that minimizing transfers is generally valued positively; traveling with family/partner/children tends to favor choosing the nearest airport; low-cost airlines and direct connections are important attractors. Policy recommendations for airport operators and transport authorities include: (1) service differentiation including premium services to attract class 2 users who prioritize comfort and efficiency; (2) encouraging low-cost airlines and more direct flights to reduce transfers; (3) improving public transport connections and reducing access costs to improve airport accessibility; and (4) improving direct connections between nearby airports to facilitate mutual use and create healthy competition that could lower fares.

**Funding:** The research was funded by the Margarita Salas Grant financed with NextGenerationEU funds from the European Union through the "Plan de Recuperación Transformación y Resiliencia." The article had 5 citations and 4,808 views at time of access, with an Altmetric score of 3.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The main conclusion of this study is that we can identify two main classes of users, with the probability of belonging to class 1 being 90% and that of belonging to class 2 being 10%. Despite this difference, as class 2 are a minority (10% of users), their behavior and preferences can have a significant impact on airport and airline strategies.", "It is shown that there are two classes of users who have different travel behavior, and that the perception of certain variables influences the choice of the nearest or furthest airport depending on the type of trip.", "As a novelty, unlike other studies, the logit model incorporates the option of not traveling (A3). Incorporating this option is not trivial since its omission may bias the results of the models by forcing the respondent to choose between one option (A1) or another (A2), when option A3 is a very real option as shown, especially in the case of class 1 users.", "Overall, it is clear from the results that in order to improve the competitiveness of nearby airports, it is undoubtedly important to have low-cost airlines with as many direct connections as possible and that these should be alternatives to the connections from the furthest airport.", "Class 2 unites higher income users because of the lower weight they attribute to the cost of travel and the cost of access to the furthest airport; these passengers may be less price-sensitive and more attracted by factors such as comfort and efficiency."

<summary>
This appendix (CAP 1135 Appendix F) evaluates whether Stansted Airport Limited (STAL) faces a competitive constraint from marginal passengers switching away from the airport following an airport charge increase. The assessment supplements constraints imposed by airlines switching marginal services.

Key findings:
- Airport charges represent only ~10-20% of airline variable costs, meaning a 10% charge increase would raise fares by only 1-2% even if fully passed through. Airfares may not fully reflect airport charges, muting passenger exposure.
- Marginal passengers at Stansted are unlikely to switch in significant numbers in response to a 5-10% airport charge increase.

Passenger characteristics:
- ~96% of Stansted's 17.4 million passengers travel by surface access.
- Approximately 80% of passengers at Gatwick, Luton and Stansted have surface travel times of at most ~90 minutes.
- 68% of Stansted's passengers travel to/from districts where its catchment overlaps with at least one other London airport; 47% travel to/from a four-way overlap district (mainly central London); only 11% originate from districts covered solely by Stansted.
- Passengers by journey purpose: VFR (46%), holiday (40%), business (14%). Holiday passengers are most cost-sensitive; business passengers most time-sensitive.
- Location and surface access is the most common reason for airport choice (36%); cost is the second most common for Stansted.
- Stansted passengers fly predominantly short-haul (93%), with 7% domestic and virtually no long-haul. There is 83% route overlap for domestic routes and 66% for short-haul routes with other London airports.
- Econometric analysis of easyJet panels found signs of airline competition across London airports, but competition at the same airport appears stronger than across different airports.

Critical loss analysis:
- A 5-10% increase in aeronautical charges (from £7.22/passenger) would generate £6.3m-£12.6m in additional revenue.
- Critical loss of passengers estimated at 0.6-0.7 million (5% increase) and 1.2-1.4 million (10% increase).
- Implied critical demand elasticities range from 0.68 to 0.79.
- The likely airport charge elasticity of demand is 0.2 to 0.6, below the critical threshold, implying STAL could profitably increase charges.
- If STAL achieved a £1 structural increase in variable non-aeronautical revenue per passenger, the critical elasticity would fall to 0.62-0.73.
- Using Ryanair aircraft assumptions (68% of Stansted passengers, 189-seat Boeing 737-800s, 82% load factor), withdrawal of 2-4 based aircraft would be sufficient to prevent a profitable price increase.

Stakeholder context: MAG (STAL's owner) disputed the CAA's analysis, arguing it ignored airline switching alongside passenger switching, inbound passenger substitution opportunities, substitution to Southend and London City, different passenger types, and that historical data from the BAA common-ownership era may be outdated. The CAA maintained that its analysis, including NAPALM modelling and choice-modelling approaches, adequately addresses these concerns.

--- SOURCE 20: Passenger winners and losers in the multi-airport system era: Evidence from Beijing tracking individual travel activities ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0965856425002241

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice (Volume 199, September 2025, Article 104596), titled "Passenger winners and losers in the multi-airport system era: Evidence from Beijing tracking individual travel activities." Authors: Fan Xiao, Huihui Mo, Jiaoe Wang, Frédéric Dobruszkes, and Meicheng Xiong. The article is open access under a Creative Commons license.

The study investigates the impacts of Beijing's multi-airport system (MAS), which includes Beijing Capital International Airport (PEK) and Beijing Daxing International Airport (PKX), on passenger travel utility. The researchers used an innovative approach leveraging an extensive dataset of online check-in data to track individual travel activities of passengers departing from Beijing, addressing data limitations from previous studies regarding observed passenger origins.

Key findings:
1. Ground-side access times are important determinants that provide accurate forecasts for passengers' airport choice in Beijing's multi-airport system.
2. A south-north pattern exists in airport choice, with more passengers favoring PEK in northern areas.
3. At the intraregional scale, the MAS benefits residents of South Beijing, while those living in North Beijing are more likely to be negatively affected.
4. At the inter-regional level, the Beijing MAS has benefited passengers traveling to large airports in the Yangtze River Delta and the Chengdu-Chongqing region, as well as small airports in remote areas.

The methodology included binary probit and logit models for airport choice, catchment area analysis using the Huff model, and Pearson correlation analysis (in appendices). The study includes 10 figures and 6 tables, examining passenger distribution from 1980-2022 and spatial distribution of population density in Beijing.

Keywords: Multi-airport region, Airport choice, Catchment area, Accessibility, Beijing.

The study has been cited once by a 2026 Transport Policy article on door-to-door intercity efficiency and distributional analysis of travel costs by plane, train, and automobile. The article contributes to understanding the multifaceted impact of MAS on regional mobility, offering insights for urban planners and policymakers.
</summary>

"Identified a south-north pattern in airport choice, with more passengers favoring PEK in northern areas." "Ground access time is a key factor influencing airport selection in Beijing's multi-airport system." Finally, at the inter-regional level, the Beijing MAS has benefited passengers traveling to large airports in the Yangtze River Delta and the Chengdu-Chongqing region, as well as small airports in remote areas."
