--- SOURCE 1: World's Busiest Airports: Atlanta Holds, Asia Climbs. Strong Demand while Asia-Pacific Growth Reshape the Rankings | ACI World ---
URL: https://aci.aero/2026/07/15/worlds-busiest-airports-atlanta-holds-asia-climbs-strong-demand-while-asia-pacific-growth-reshape-the-rankings

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 15 July 2026, ACI World released the 2026 ACI World Airport Traffic Dataset, confirming global air travel reached 9.8 billion passengers in 2025, approaching the 10 billion threshold. The dataset covers 2,817 airports across more than 180 countries and territories, showing global passenger traffic rose 3.7% over 2024 and 6.5% above 2019 levels. The world's 20 busiest airports handled 1.59 billion passengers (16% of global travelers).

Asia-Pacific airports led ranking shifts. Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KUL) was the biggest mover, rising from 26th to 20th place with 63.4 million passengers (+11% YoY). Shanghai Pudong (PVG) climbed from 10th to 5th with 84.9 million passengers (+10.7%), driven by visa policy easing and China's aviation market reopening. Guangzhou Baiyun (CAN) fell to 57th in 2022 after topping the table in 2020, but returned to 9th in 2025.

Atlanta (ATL) retained the No. 1 position with 106.3 million passengers despite a 1.6% decline. Dubai (DXB, 95.2 million, +3.1%) held second and Tokyo Haneda (HND, 91.7 million, +6.7%) third, both closing the gap on Atlanta. Five of the top 20 airports are US-based, mostly domestic hubs (80-95% domestic traffic), with LAX the exception at 68% domestic.

Global air cargo exceeded 131 million metric tonnes in 2025, up 3.3% YoY and 7.4% above 2019, driven by e-commerce and supply chain restructuring. The top 20 cargo airports handled nearly 41% of global volumes. Hong Kong (HKG) retained the top cargo ranking with 5.1 million metric tonnes. Memphis (MEM) dropped from 3rd to 6th after losing the US Postal Service contract, with volumes falling 20.9%.

Global aircraft movements exceeded 103.1 million in 2025, up 2.0%, nearing pre-2019 levels. Chicago O'Hare (ORD) claimed the top spot with 857,000 movements (+10.5%), displacing Atlanta (ATL) which had led since 2020. Dallas/Fort Worth (DFW) held 3rd with 743,000 movements.

ACI World Director General Justin Erbacci commented: "Global air travel is approaching a historic milestone, but record demand is also exposing growing pressures on capacity. The planning and investment decisions made today will determine whether aviation can meet the demands of the next generation of travellers."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Global air travel is approaching a historic milestone, but record demand is also exposing growing pressures on capacity. The planning and investment decisions made today will determine whether aviation can meet the demands of the next generation of travellers." — ACI World Director General Justin Erbacci, "In 2025, global air travel reached 9.8 billion passengers, bringing the industry closer than ever to the 10 billion-passenger threshold", "Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KUL) was the biggest mover in the top 20, rising six places from 26th in 2024 to 20th in 2025", "Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) retained the No. 1 position with 106.3 million passengers in 2025, despite a year-on-year decline of 1.6%", "Memphis International Airport (MEM) dropped from 3rd to 6th after losing the US Postal Service contract in late 2024, with volumes falling 20.9%"

--- SOURCE 3: ACI World releases global airport traffic forecasts as long-term demand growth continues to reshape aviation | ACI World ---
URL: https://aci.aero/2026/01/28/aci-world-releases-global-airport-traffic-forecasts-as-long-term-demand-growth-continues-to-reshape-aviation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 28 January 2026, from Montreal, Airports Council International (ACI) World released its World Airport Traffic Forecasts (WATF) 2025–2054, described as the industry's most comprehensive and authoritative outlook on global airport traffic. Key forecast figures include 10.2 billion passengers in 2026 and 18.8 billion by 2045.

Sustained Growth Outlook: The long-term outlook is firmly positive, with global passenger traffic demand projected to more than double by the mid-2040s, driven primarily by emerging and developing markets. However, this growth is increasingly accompanied by challenges including capacity constraints and insufficient investment risks.

Call for Collective Action: ACI World Director General Justin Erbacci warned that long-term growth is not guaranteed without coordinated action. He called for accelerated investment in airport infrastructure, airspace capacity, and operational resilience, along with strengthened collaboration across airports, airlines, governments, regulators, and industry partners. Erbacci noted that capacity constraints could create operational bottlenecks affecting passenger journey quality, while insufficient investment would result in missed economic development opportunities—noting aviation contributes 3.9% of global GDP (per ATAG).

About the WATF: The WATF 2025–2054 provides a comprehensive 30-year outlook covering passenger traffic, air cargo, and aircraft movements across 176 markets. It uses advanced machine-learning models to deliver highly accurate, transparent forecasts to support data-driven planning and investment decisions.

About ACI: ACI is the trade association of the world's airports, a federated organization comprising ACI World, ACI Africa, ACI Asia-Pacific and Middle East, ACI EUROPE, ACI Latin America and the Caribbean, and ACI North America. As of January 2025, ACI serves 830 members operating 2,181 airports in 170 countries. The Executive Summary of the forecast is available for download.

Contact details: Sabrina Guerrieri, Director of Communications at ACI World, is the media contact (mediarelations@aci.aero, +1 514 373 1254). ACI World is headquartered at 1500-800 rue du Square Victoria, Montréal, Québec H3C 0B4, Canada.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The forecast sends a clear signal to the global aviation community: long-term growth is not guaranteed without coordinated action," said ACI World Director General Justin Erbacci. "To accommodate rising demand, the industry must accelerate investment in airport infrastructure, airspace capacity, and operational resilience, while strengthening collaboration across airports, airlines, governments, regulators, and industry partners.", "Ensuring the sector can sustainably absorb future demand growth is therefore not only an industry priority, but a global economic imperative.", "Without collective action, capacity constraints jeopardize the industry's ability to meet the projected demand and create operational bottlenecks, directly affecting the quality and reliability of the passenger journey."

URL: https://dwuconsulting.com/dwu-ai/eas

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This DWU AI article (April 2026) analyzes the FY2027 budget proposal to eliminate Essential Air Service (EAS), a program that has been continuously funded since its creation in the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 (49 U.S.C. §§ 41731–41746) — now 48 years old, despite being characterized as "temporary" by Congress. 

**Program Overview:** DOT subsidizes air carriers to provide minimum service (typically two round trips daily with 30-50 seat aircraft) to eligible communities connecting to large/medium hubs. As of fall 2024, DOT subsidized 65 Alaskan communities and 112 in the contiguous 48 states, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico, with total reach cited as 177 communities across all states plus Puerto Rico (as of Oct 2025). Eligibility requires averaging at least 10 enplanements per service day (~3,650/year), unless located more than 175 driving miles from a hub. Per-passenger subsidy caps: $1,000 (decreasing to $850 effective Oct 1, 2026, under FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024) for communities 175+ miles from a hub; $650 for those closer. Alaska and Hawaii are exempt from distance criteria and caps.

**Carriers:** Four carriers hold ~41% of the program's ~$512 million in annual contracts: SkyWest ($84.7M), Contour ($58.3M), Southern Airways/Mokulele ($48.1M), Alaska Airlines ($17.1M for five Southeast Alaska routes). JetBlue ($10.4M) and Breeze ($8.0M) each held one contract in FY2024.

**Costs:** Per-passenger subsidies range from $6.26 (Joplin, MO) to $1,905 (Lewistown, MT, serving Billings). For 38 lower-48 communities within 150 miles of a hub, average all-in round trip cost was $427, with federal subsidies covering 46%.

**Geographic Distribution:** Alaska accounts for 65 of 177 communities (37%), including communities with no road access (e.g., Adak, Petersburg, Gustavus). Michigan hosted 9 airports (most in lower 48) at $17.6M total cost. 104 of 177 EAS airports are designated Economic Development Areas (EDAs) for FY2025.

**FY2027 Budget Proposal:** Released April 3, 2026, the White House proposal eliminates $372 million of discretionary EAS funding, citing "out of control" spending and "half-empty" flights. It would set discretionary appropriations at $142M plus ~$174M in mandatory overflight fee revenue (under 49 U.S.C. §41742(b)), totaling ~$316M — a ~54% reduction from FY2026's ~$688M.

**Historical Pattern:** Congress has rejected every EAS cut proposal since 1978. The FY2026 budget (released May 2, 2025) proposed a $308M cut (~52%); Congress rejected it and enacted $514M in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (Feb 3, 2026), with language preventing abrupt contract termination. The House Appropriations Committee stated this protected service to 56 communities the budget would have eliminated. Both Obama and first-term Trump administrations proposed EAS cuts that Congress consistently rejected; funding levels have varied and individual communities were removed for failing thresholds, but the program has never been eliminated through appropriations.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an official U.S. Department of Transportation webpage providing comprehensive information about the Essential Air Service (EAS) program. The EAS program was established by section 419 of the Federal Aviation Act following the Airline Deregulation Act (ADA) of 1978, which removed federal control over fares, routes, and market entry. The program guarantees that communities served by certificated air carriers before deregulation maintain a minimum level of scheduled air service, typically subsidizing two round trips daily with 30- to 50-seat aircraft to large- or medium-hub airports. As of Fall 2024, the Department provides EAS subsidies to 65 communities in Alaska and 112 communities in the 48 contiguous states, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico.

The Civil Aeronautics Board managed the program until January 1, 1985, when the Department of Transportation assumed responsibility. The program, initially authorized for ten years, is now permanently authorized by Congress.

Community eligibility is outlined in 49 U.S.C. § 41731. To remain eligible, communities must maintain an average of 10 enplanements per service day during the most recent fiscal year, though communities more than 175 driving miles from the nearest large or medium hub airport are exempt. EAS communities less than 175 miles from a hub must have an average subsidy per passenger of less than $650, while those farther away must have an average subsidy of less than $1,000 (reduced to $850 effective October 1, 2026). These subsidy requirements do not apply to Alaska and Hawaii. Waivers may be granted for temporary demand declines, but starting October 1, 2026, waivers cannot be provided for more than two consecutive fiscal years or more than five fiscal years within 25 consecutive years. Eligibility criteria were amended in the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (Pub L. No. 118-63, May 16, 2024).

The carrier selection process involves the Department issuing a Request for Proposals (RFP) to all air carriers, with proposals submitted on a sealed "best and final" basis. Under 49 U.S.C. § 41733(c)(1), selection factors include demonstrated reliability, code-share/interline arrangements with larger carriers, community preferences (including views of elected officials), marketing plans, and for Alaska, prior experience providing scheduled air service. Contracts generally run two to four years. Carriers are compensated in arrears on a per-flight-completed basis, with monthly invoices detailing actual service, and only completed flights (take-off and landing at destination) are generally eligible for subsidy. Contact information for the EAS and Domestic Analysis Division is provided, and a list of eligible communities is available at the DOT website.
</summary>

<summary>
This article from Taxpayers for Common Sense (TCS), a nonpartisan government watchdog, analyzes the Essential Air Service (EAS) program and the impact of changes made by the 2012 federal air program reauthorization. The EAS is a federal subsidy program created in the 1970s during airline deregulation that was intended to be temporary but now costs taxpayers over $200 million annually to guarantee air service for 117 communities. 

Following the 2012 reauthorization, new eligibility rules were established for subsidized service: communities must be 90+ miles from a medium/large hub, average 10+ daily enplanements (unless 175+ miles from a hub), require a subsidy under $1,000 per passenger, and have received subsidized service between September 30, 2010 and September 30, 2011. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Eno Center for Transportation Aviation Insight (No. 10, January 31, 2018) explains how the federal government subsidizes air service to small communities through the Essential Air Service (EAS) program. Congress established EAS in 1979 during airline deregulation to subsidize flights to the smallest airports. The program was initially intended to last 10 years but was extended in perpetuity in 1996, and costs have risen significantly since then. With approximately 300 communities receiving subsidized service (of 746 originally eligible), the program distributes roughly $270 million per year.

Key statistics: The busiest EAS airport (Joplin, Missouri) averages fewer than 160 passengers per day, while some airports have fewer than a dozen daily departing passengers. Per-passenger subsidies vary dramatically—from close to zero to several hundred dollars. During FY2016, the highest per-passenger subsidy was Altoona, Pennsylvania at $642 per passenger (3,693 total passengers). McCook, Nebraska had the highest overall subsidy at $778 per passenger.

Program constraints and enforcement issues: Congress imposed limitations including a 70-mile minimum distance from a medium/large hub, a minimum of 10 daily enplanements, and caps on per-passenger subsidies ($200 for communities within 210 miles of a hub, $1,000 for others). U.S. DOT enforced the $200 cap from 1990-2006, causing 39 communities to lose service, but stopped enforcement in 2006. Although DOT announced resumed enforcement in 2014, 26 airports remained above the $200 threshold in FY2016. Since 2006, only one airport has lost service due to the $200 rule, but eight airports lost service due to the $1,000 cap since 2012.

Potential savings and context: Options to reduce EAS costs include increasing the minimum distance requirement, enforcing the per-passenger cap, and enforcing minimum enplanements. A scenario combining a 150-mile minimum distance, the $200 cap, and 10-daily-enplanement enforcement would only save $114.3 million. Notably, the EAS program represents less than two percent of the $16 billion in annual federal aviation spending. The Trump administration's initial 2018 budget proposed cutting the program entirely before settling on a 50 percent reduction. U.S. DOT's criteria for adding new communities include reliability, connections with larger hubs, and community views—but notably do not include cost.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Enplanements: FAA Definition, Meaning & Airport Data ---
URL: https://dwuconsulting.com/dwu-ai/enplaned-passengers

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Enplanements: FAA Definition, Meaning & Airport Data

This is a DWU AI reference guide (July 2026) examining enplaned passenger definitions, classifications, and reporting across federal data systems (T-100, DB1B/DB1C, FAA Air Carrier Activity Information System/ACAIS, and airport-reported sources). Enplaned passengers — passengers boarding aircraft at an airport — are the primary traffic metric in U.S. airport finance, driving AIP grant apportionment (49 USC §47114), hub classification, PFC collections (49 USC §40117), and cost per enplaned passenger (CPE) calculations.

### Key Facts & Definitions
- **Enplanement definition:** One passenger boarding one aircraft at an airport. For federal purposes (T-100/ACAIS), enplanements principally count revenue passengers. Example: A traveler boarding in Atlanta, connecting in Dallas, and deplaning in LA generates two revenue enplanements (ATL and DFW).
- **Revenue vs. nonrevenue:** Revenue passengers are those for whom the carrier receives commercial remuneration (paid tickets, loyalty redemptions, corporate discounts, vouchers, barter). Nonrevenue passengers include airline employees, pass interchange passengers, FAM trips, air marshals, NTSB/FAA investigators, disaster relief personnel. T-100 and FAA ACAIS report revenue passengers only; airport reports often include both, causing 1–5% discrepancies.
- **Round trips:** A round trip generates two enplanements — one at each boarding airport.

### Reporting Systems
- **T-100:** 100% census of revenue passenger boardings (14 CFR Part 241 for U.S. carriers; Part 217 for foreign carriers). Answers "how many passengers boarded at this airport."
- **DB1B/DB1C (DB1C effective Q2 2024):** 10% sample of domestic airline tickets capturing full origin-destination itineraries; used for O&D vs. connecting analysis and market-share/fare studies. Not to be summed with T-100.
- **ACAIS:** Publishes official annual enplanement totals (T-100 plus Air Taxi survey data) for hub classification and AIP entitlements.
- **FAA Form 5100-127** line 16.1 collects airport's total fiscal-year enplanements (including nonrevenue), tracked in the Compliance Activity Tracking System (CATS).

### Passenger Classifications (Three Independent Ways)
1. **Revenue vs. Nonrevenue** (detailed categories listed above)
2. **O&D vs. Connecting:** O&D passengers begin/end trips at the airport, generating stronger non-aeronautical revenue (parking, rental car, ground transportation). Connecting passengers generate less of this revenue; concession spend depends on layover/terminal design. O&D further segmented into Visitor (home outside catchment) vs. Resident (home within catchment) — a local market-study convention, not federal reporting.
3. **International vs. Domestic:** International passengers generate additional fees and CBP processing requirements.

### Hub Classification
FAA classifies airports by share of total U.S. commercial enplanements into four categories: Large Hub (≥1.00%), Medium Hub (0.25%–0.999%), Small Hub (0.05%–0.249%), Non-Hub (<0.05%). Under CY 2024 data, the U.S. has 31 large hubs and 32 medium hubs (63 L/M total). Hub class determines AIP entitlement funding.

### PFC Details
PFC collections are capped at $4.50 per chargeable passenger (14 CFR Part 158, §158.9 exclusions include nonrevenue passengers and frequent-flier award coupons). PFC authority extends to all commercial service airports regardless of hub class.

### 2025–2026 Updates
- Preliminary indicators suggest 2025 U.S. airport passenger traffic approached or exceeded 2019 levels; FAA released preliminary CY2025 data June 26, 2026; final data expected late August 2026.
- FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-63, Section 712) revised AIP apportionment formulas affecting non-primary commercial and GA airports.
- DCA received 10 additional daily slot exemptions (five slot pairs) awarded by DOT December 2024.
- EWR operations capped at 72 hourly operations (36 arrivals + 36 departures) through October 30, 2027.

### Why Airport Data Disagrees with FAA Data
Four sources: (1) scope (system vs. terminal/authority reporting); (2) nonrevenue inclusion; (3) timing (airport data in weeks vs. FAA lag of 2–3 months); (4) audit/reconciliation adjustments. FAA CY 2024 Passenger Boarding Data (ACAIS) is the apples-to-apples comparison source.

### Data Sources
FAA passenger boarding data at faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/passenger_allcargo_stats/; DWU Consulting maintains T-100 and monthly traffic dashboards at dwuconsulting.com/info/data/t100 and /info/data/monthly-traffic.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"An enplanement is one passenger boarding one aircraft at an airport. For federal regulatory purposes (FAA Passenger Boarding data / ACAIS, and the underlying T-100 traffic data), enplanements principally count revenue passengers — those for whom the carrier receives commercial remuneration."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Airport Categories | Federal Aviation Administration ---
URL: https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/categories

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) webpage from the U.S. Department of Transportation that explains airport categories as defined by law. It identifies approximately 14,400 private-use (closed to the public) and 5,000 public-use (open to the public) airports, heliports, and seaplane bases in the United States. About 3,300 of these public-use facilities are included in the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS) and may be considered for Airport Improvement Program (AIP) funding.

The law categorizes airports by type of activities, including:
- **Commercial Service**: Publicly owned airports with at least 2,500 annual enplanements and scheduled air carrier service. Primary airports (with more than 10,000 annual enplanements) are further classified by hub size: Large Hub (1%+ of annual U.S. commercial enplanements), Medium Hub (0.25-1.0%), Small Hub (0.05-0.25%), Nonhub (less than 0.05% but more than 10,000 enplanements), and Nonprimary Commercial Service Nonhub (2,500-10,000 annual enplanements with scheduled passenger service).
- **Reliever**: Designated by the Secretary of Transportation to relieve congestion at commercial service airports and provide general aviation access to the community.
- **General Aviation**: A public-use airport without scheduled service or with scheduled service of less than 2,500 passenger boardings each year.

The FAA also developed five categories for airports serving general aviation (based on their role in the system): National (support access to national/international markets with high levels of jet and multiengine activity), Regional (connect communities to regional/national markets in metropolitan areas), Local (provide access to markets within a State/region, mostly piston aircraft), Basic (links communities to the national airport system with minimal infrastructure, often a single runway or helipad), and Unclassified (in NPIAS with limited activity).

Contact information: Federal Aviation Administration, 800 Independence Avenue, SW, Washington, DC 20591, phone 866.835.5322 (866-TELL-FAA). The criteria are detailed in FAA Order 5090.5 and Appendix C of the Current Published NPIAS.
</summary>

<summary>
This article, published by GlobalAir.com (a press release dated Sep. 1, 2016, updated Mar. 10, 2021), serves as a beginner's guide to how the FAA classifies public-use airports in the United States, based on the author's experience taking an Airport Management course. The FAA has recognized public-use airports eligible for federal funding since 1970 through the National Airport Systems Plan (NASP), which included approximately 3,200 airports. In 1982, the Airport and Airway Act led to the creation of the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS), which included 3,411 airports as of 2008. The article breaks down the main NPIAS airport classifications:

**1. Primary Airports** – Public-use airports enplaning at least 10,000 passengers annually. This accounts for less than 3 percent of the nation's total airports, with only 383 airports in this category in 2008.

**2. Commercial Service Airports** – Any airport accommodating scheduled air carrier service by a certified airline. Of the 770 million passengers who flew in the US in 2009, practically all went through commercial service airports. The FAA recognized 522 such airports in 2008.

**3. General Aviation (GA) Airports** – Airports with fewer than 2,500 annual enplaned passengers, or those used exclusively by private business aircraft not providing commercial passenger service. Though over 13,000 airports technically fit this description, only those in the NPIAS are counted; there is usually at least one GA airport in the NPIAS per county, and airports with more than 10 based aircraft located more than 20 miles from the nearest NPIAS airport are also included. A total of 2,564 airports held this classification in 2008.

- **Large hubs**: at least 1% of total annual passenger enplanements (30 airports in 2008, handling 70% of all US passenger enplanements)
- **Medium hubs**: between 0.25% and 1% of annual enplanements (37 airports in 2008)
- **Small hubs**: between 0.05% and 0.25% of annual enplanements (72 airports in 2008)
- **Nonhubs**: more than 10,000 annual enplanements but less than 0.05% of the annual total

The author encourages readers to look up their favorite airports to see what hub type they fall under and whether they are classified as primary or commercial service.

URL: https://mesotech.com/pages/npias-acip-nextgen-awos

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Mesotech International, a manufacturer of Automated Weather Observing Systems (AWOS), explains how airports can secure Federal funding for AWOS systems by understanding federal programs. In September 2019, the Federal government combined the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS) and the Airports Capital Improvement Plan (ACIP) into a single order (Order 5090.5), making ACIP a subset of NPIAS and the primary financial planning tool for the Airport Improvement Program (AIP).

Key context: Weather caused over 69% of delays exceeding 15 minutes between 2008-2013, totaling over 10 million lost minutes in 2013 alone. An hour-long delay costs air carriers between $1,400 and $4,500 depending on aircraft class, plus $35/hour for personal travelers and $63/hour for business travelers.

**NPIAS**: Identifies over 3,000 existing and proposed airports in the National Airspace System. Only airports listed in NPIAS qualify for AIP grants. To qualify, airports must be open to the public and publicly owned, or privately owned but designated as a reliever or with scheduled service and at least 2,500 annual enplanements. The most recent NPIAS publication (released September 30, 2022, covering 2023-2027) includes 3,287 existing airports and 8 proposed airports, with $62.4 billion in AIP-eligible projects (a 43% increase, or nearly $19 billion, from two years prior). Of these, 98% (3,232) are publicly owned. Bringing aging airports up to modern FAA design standards accounts for 20% of anticipated funding needs (~$12.4 billion), including weather reporting equipment like AWOS for NextGen compliance.

**ACIP**: An internal FAA document produced annually by the Airport Improvement Program Branch, based on reports from nine Regional Offices (New England, Eastern, Southern, Great Lakes, Southwest, Northwest Mountain, Western-Pacific, and Alaskan Regions). It prioritizes critical airport development and serves as the criteria for AIP grant distribution. Projects must qualify under both AIP guidelines and NPIAS-ACIP criteria.

**NextGen**: Initiated in 2007 by the FAA, this modernization program aims to increase safety, efficiency, capacity, and resilience of the NAS, reduce aviation's environmental impact, and manage air traffic through Trajectory Based Operations. All major components are planned to be in place by 2025. The NextGen Weather Program predicts that more accurate weather data could prevent as many as 2/3 of weather delays and cancellations.

**CSS-Wx**: The Common Support Services – Weather program will be the single provider of weather data within the NAS, with sensors inputting data from AWOS and ASOS systems via the Weather Messaging Switching Center Replacement (WMSCR). The NextGen Weather Processor centrally produces weather products for dissemination. The program was scheduled for operation in 2023 and offers benefits including consistent weather information, increased NAS weather access, and reduced interface/development/infrastructure costs.

The article concludes that purchasing, upgrading, or replacing an AWOS system meets the development category criteria for the 2023-2027 NPIAS and is eligible for AIP grants. Mesotech's Airport Weather Advisor® product has over 25 years of experience and services all USAF fixed weather base systems.
</summary>

This document is the Compilation of Case Studies (Volume) from ACRP Project 03-58, "Measuring and Understanding the Relationship between Air Service and Regional Economic Development," prepared for the Airports Cooperative Research Board (TRB) by InterVISTAS Consulting, the University of North Carolina at Greensboro, Amy Kvistad Design, and Hubpoint Strategic Advisors (dated Jan. 3, 2022). It is a companion to ACRP Web-Only Document 53 (the guide), ACRP WebResource 12, and the Contractor's Technical Report.

The project includes 14 case studies illustrating the connection between air service and regional economic development, divided into two sections: (1) Passenger Air Service case studies and (2) Air Cargo and Air Freight case studies. The document argues that traditional airport economic impact studies are limited because they only measure activity "on airport properties or that is tied directly to airport operations" and fail to capture how air service facilitates economic activity "beyond the fence" (i.e., how air service is critical for other regional employers and industries).

Section I covers ten passenger air service case studies: Atlanta, Greater Austin, Columbia (Missouri), Des Moines, Fresno, Green Bay, Piedmont Triad (GSO), Greater Miami, Raleigh-Durham, Reno-Tahoe, San Diego, and Charles M. Schulz Sonoma County. Section II covers air cargo airports: Allentown-Lehigh Valley (ABE) and Huntsville (HSV).

The first detailed case study (Atlanta) is provided in full. Key findings include:
- Metro Atlanta is the economic hub of the American southeast, home to 16 Fortune 500 companies (Delta, Coca-Cola, Home Depot, UPS) and ranks 3rd nationally for Fortune 1000 headquarters; over 70% of the Fortune 1000 have a presence there.
- Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) is the world's busiest airport, handling 2,700 arrivals/departures and 275,000 passengers daily, with nonstop service to 150 domestic and 75 international destinations.
- Delta Air Lines dominates ATL, carrying 74% of total passengers in 2019 (78% with regional affiliates) and 58% of O&D traffic.
- Freight is mostly truck (83%) and rail (17%) by tonnage, with under 1% by air, but air cargo handles high-value, time-sensitive goods; ATL handled over 600,000 metric tons of cargo in 2019 (40% domestic, 60% international).
- Between 2008-2019, the region's population grew 16% to 6.9 million, employment rose 23% (838,000 jobs), and per capita income rose 38% to nearly $53,000; the region produced $442.1 billion in GDP in 2019 (11th among MSAs).
- Major employment growth sectors 2008-2019 included health care (+32%, +70k jobs), transportation and warehousing (+28%, +32k jobs), accommodations/food service (+25%), professional/scientific/technical services (+25%), and management of companies (+24%).
- The freight and logistics sector accounts for about $514.8 billion of economic output (38% of total regional output).
- The Information Technology location quotient for Atlanta is 3.37, indicating unusually high concentration.
- ATL ranked 12th in the world and 3rd in the U.S. in 2019 on the IATA Connectivity Index; the index weights air service by the size of destination airports (ATL gets weight 1.0, while London Heathrow gets 0.90), meaning ATL is a critical connectivity enabler for its own and other regional economies.
- O&D traffic rose from 31 million to 40 million annually (2008-2019), while total passenger traffic rose from 88 million to almost 108 million; flight numbers fell 8% (from 475k to 436k) due to aircraft upgauging, with average seats per departing flight rising 24% to 145.
- The region is also a top location for film/video production and a growing technology and logistics hub, employing ~136,000 warehouse/distribution workers within a 45-minute drive of ATL.

This is a confidential Oxera Consulting report (September 23, 2024) prepared for ACI EUROPE, UAF, ADV, RAA, and Assaeroporti, analyzing the profitability of regional airports in the EU context of state aid rules.

**Key Context:**
- Under the EU's 2014 Aviation State Aid Guidelines, regional airports with traffic between 200,000 and 3 million passengers per year (mppa) could receive operating aid for a transitional period. This was originally 10 years (until April 2024), then extended by 3 years to April 2027 due to COVID-19 and the energy crisis.
- After April 2027, operating aid will no longer be allowed for airports above 200,000 passengers per year (ppa), except under the General Block Exemption Regulation (GBER) for smaller airports.

**Current State Aid Rules (Table 2.1):**
- Airports >3mppa: no operating aid allowed
- Airports 700,000–3mppa: max 50% of operating funding gap (2009–13 period)
- Airports 200,000–700,000ppa: max 80% of operating funding gap
- Airports <200,000ppa: 100% of operating losses and reasonable profit via GBER (no phase-out)

**Empirical Findings on Break-Even Thresholds:**
- Studies indicate airports generally need 500,000 to 1 million passengers per year to break even—significantly higher than the 200,000ppa threshold underpinning GBER
- Specific break-even thresholds from studies: 1mppa (UK, Poland, EU), 800,000ppa (Europe/GAP), 750,000ppa (Europe/Bubalo), 700,000ppa (Europe/Lear et al.), 500,000ppa (Spain, Europe), 460,000ppa (Europe/Adler et al.)
- The Commission's own 2020 fitness check acknowledged many airports below 1mppa would be unlikely to cover operating costs by 2024; a supporting study found more than 30% of airports between 200,000–700,000ppa and 62% of airports below 200,000ppa would likely fail to cover operating costs by 2024
- About 90% of airports in the sample were below 1mppa, with a majority unlikely to break even

**COVID-19 and War in Ukraine Impacts:**
- EU passenger numbers declined 73% in 2020 vs 2019; European airport revenues declined by ~€33.6bn (-68.8%) in 2020
- Regional airports recovered faster than hubs (90% of fully recovered airports by 2022), mainly due to leisure traffic rebound
- Smaller regional airports (<700,000ppa) recovered much more slowly than larger regional airports
- As of June 2024, only 53% of European airports had recovered to 2019 traffic levels; total European passenger traffic was just 0.4% above pre-pandemic levels, with air connectivity still 14% below pre-pandemic levels
- The war in Ukraine affected airports unevenly, particularly in Bulgaria, Czechia, Finland, Latvia, and Slovenia

**Report Structure:**
1) Introduction and background on state aid rules
2) Overview of state aid rules and relationship between airport size and profitability
3) Analysis of regional airports' financial position based on case studies (passenger trends, aeronautical/non-aeronautical revenues, operating costs, profitability metrics including EBITDA and EBIT)
4) Conclusions and policy recommendations

The report's key concern is whether the extended transitional period to 2027 will be sufficient for regional airports to achieve operational cost coverage, given empirical evidence showing break-even thresholds exceed the Commission's 200,000ppa assumption.

This November 2023 report by the Grand Valley State University Seidman Center assesses the economic impact of the Rapid City Regional Airport (RAP) on Pennington County, South Dakota. The study, funded by RAP and the City of Rapid City, found that the airport supports approximately 2,877 jobs and generates $456 million in annual economic activity for Pennington County, with a fiscal impact of $2.2 million for the county.

The analysis used the IMPLAN input-output economic modeling software and covered five primary areas: commercial visitors, general aviation (GA) visitors, airport operations, capital investments, and business tenants. Commercial visitor impact was derived from an intercept survey of 8,836 responses (7,537 usable) conducted October 2022–October 2023 via Qualtrics, finding that 63.2% of passengers were nonlocal, spending roughly $197 per person per day, totaling $153 million in direct spending. Commercial visitors supported 1,439 jobs and $188M in output. General aviation spending (estimated via a benefit transfer model) supported 543 jobs and $58M in output, with $44.8M in direct spending. Airport operations supported 43 jobs and $4.6M in output, based on RAP's 33 full-time equivalent jobs and $4.1M operating budget. Capital investments—using a five-year average of $4.5M annually from 2018–2022 (total $22.4M)—supported 56 jobs and $7.8M in output. Business tenants (approximately 18 tenants, with 423 direct workers) supported 796 jobs and $196M in output.

RAP is South Dakota's second busiest airport, ranked 149th nationally, with 338,458 enplaned passengers in 2022 served by five airlines on seven nonstop routes (American, United, Allegiant, Delta, and Sun Country). The airport recorded 37,228 general aviation flights in 2022. RAP recently received a $10.9 million Bipartisan Infrastructure Law Grant to fund phase one of a $52 million renovation (terminal expansion, baggage, and TSA relocation), which alone is projected to support 99 jobs and $13.7 million in economic output.

Compared to its 2020 study (in 2023 dollars), RAP's total direct spending rose from $205M to $295M, economic output grew from $337M to $456M, and employment increased from 2,869 to 2,877. The report also compares RAP favorably to similarly sized airports like Trenton-Mercer, Baton Rouge Metro, South Bend, and Fort Wayne, noting RAP generates relatively strong impact per passenger. Key industries impacted include air transportation, hotels/lodging, and food services.

The economic activity at and facilitated by airports contributed around 5% of Australia’s gross domestic product (GDP) and supported around 6% of full time equivalent (FTE) jobs in 2022. Beyond commercial aviation services, airports also provide critical infrastructure and services to support a range of general aviation activity. Airports, particularly secondary metro airports, are key to providing the infrastructure necessary for the training of new pilots, facilitating 337,000 training hours in 2022.
Additionally, airports provide the infrastructure necessary to support medical and emergency response operations, aerial work and charter services. These are crucial to supporting Australia’s regions, providing support for primary industries and connecting workers across the country. While the COVID-19 pandemic brought significant challenges for the airport sector, it also highlighted their crucial importance. Indeed, airports facilitated the complex logistics of vaccines and medical equipment, while also serving as key hubs for emergency response operations. In 2022, airports reported that activity at Australia’s airports had recovered to 72% of 2019 levels, with scheduled air transport services increasing as travel restrictions ease. Domestic travel is forecast to make a full recovery to 2019 levels in 2023, while international travel is forecast to recover in 2025. Taking Flight: The economic and social contribution of Australia’s airports The role of the Australian Airports Association The Australian Airports Association is the national peak body that represents the interests of more than 340 airports and aerodromes, as well as more than 150 corporate members and aviation sector stakeholders, across Australia. The AAA is a crucial advocate for effective national policies relating to airport activities that maximise the transport experience for passengers and freight movements, support and promote a prosperous and competitive aviation sector, and connect communities and industry.
The intention of this report is to stand as an information resource for the Australian Airports Association on the importance of Australia’s airports and the nature of their economic and social contribution to Australia. The analysis seeks to move beyond the core quantitative findings, to cover broader insights from industry participants and to discuss strategic implications, opportunities and challenges for the future of Australia’s airport industry.
Scope of the analysis The 2018 analysis established a robust analytical framework for measuring the various components of the contribution of Australia’s airports. The same analytical framework has been drawn on to underpin the analysis in this report to ensure comparability and transparency of findings over time.
The core analytical components of the research cover: • A quantitative assessment of the direct and indirect economic contribution of Australia’s airports, capturing airport operational and broader precinct activities, facilitated tourism and trade • Case studies and qualitative insights to demonstrate the broader social contribution of Australia’s airports in facilitating workforce connectivity, enabling flight training, medical and emergency response services, and supporting local communities • Passenger and movement forecasts of airport activity, as well as industry insights on future challenges and opportunities • A profile of airport workforces, covering demographics, skills, qualifications and actions taken by airports to support career development.
In addition, the report outlines structure, linkages and operating models of Australia’s airports, as well as recent levels and types of investment undertaken to support operational growth. In this report, the term ‘airport’ is used broadly to cover the full range of flight activity and regulated operations. For transparency and consistency with the use of this report, the ‘airport’ population captured in this analysis is consistent with the AAA’s airport membership base.
Data sources The study draws on a range of public data sources including Tourism Research Australia (TRA) visitation data, Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) census, labour force, and industry publications, Airservices Australia general aviation data and Bureau of Infrastructure, Transport and Regional Economics (BITRE) aviation statistics. The data was cleansed, cross referenced across the multiple sources, validated and used to estimate the economic contribution of Australia’s airports in value added and employment terms. All data sources, published reports and academic research drawn on are referenced throughout the report.
Australia’s network of airports play a crucial role in connecting communities, enabling economic activity, promoting social inclusion, and supporting medical, emergency response services and other general aviation activities.
Project context This project Deloitte Access Economics was engaged by the Australian Airports Association (AAA) to undertake an update of a report produced in 2018: Connecting Australia: The economic and social contribution of Australia’s airports, The objective of this study is to provide the Australian Airports Association with a contemporary evidence base on the economic and social contribution Australia’s airports makes to the national economy and community.
This report examines not only the significant economic contribution of Australia’s network of airports, but also their role in connecting communities, facilitating labour, industry and trade links, enabling social inclusion, supporting medical services, emergency response services and other general aviation activities. Survey of airports A further data source for the analysis was a bespoke survey of airports developed by Deloitte and distributed by the AAA. The survey was used to capture contemporary information about airports’ financial performance, workforce profile, and perceptions of future challenges and opportunities. Responses to this survey were the key data input to estimating the economic contribution of airport core operational activities, as well as the workforce profiling and demand outlook. In total, 32 airports completed the survey. Respondents include 7 of 10 major airports, as well as a mix of large regional, minor regional, remote and secondary metro airports. Figures from the survey were scaled and weighted to the airport population profile and used to underpin the core operational activity component of the economic contribution analysis. The survey methodology, sampling outcomes and scaling and weighting approach are detailed further in Appendix A: Survey overview and B: Economic contribution framework.

Taking Flight: The economic and social contribution of Australia’s airports Australia has a vast airport network, servicing both regular public transport and general aviation needs from remote desert mines to thriving cities. Airports provide the infrastructure, labour and service requirements to facilitate both commercial travel and trade, and general aviation needs covering a range of activities to support both industry and the community, including flight training, medical and emergency response services, own use business charters, and aerial work such as crop monitoring and spraying or aerial surveying and mapping. In 2022, the AAA’s airport members transported 117 million passengers 1 and facilitated freight exports worth $51 billion. 2 Australia’s airport network is diverse, ranging from international gateway airports in major cities to regional community airports scattered around the country. In this report airports have been classified into four distinct categories: • Major: The largest airport in each state and territory capital city, as well as Cairns and Gold Coast which act as major tourist hubs • Large regional: Airports with passenger volumes above 100,000, not including the major airports • Minor regional and remote: Airports outside of major cities with passenger volumes lower than 100,000, including non-SAT airports • Secondary metro: Non-major airports in capital cities, primarily fulfilling general aviation requirements for the metro area, such as flight training and medical and emergency response services.
More details on the airport population captured in this analysis are available in Appendix A: Survey overview.
Austalia’s airports domestic passenger activity has been mapped in Figure 2.1. Overall, 90% of airports with SAT are outside of major cities, however 84% of passenger traffic goes through the major airports.2 The wide geographic distribution of airports ensures connectivity, accessibility and support for all Australian regions and communities.
In this report, the economic contribution of airports covers four components of airport activity: core airport operational activity, precinct activity of onsite businesses, facilitated freight and facilitated tourism. This report also focuses on crucial the social benefits that airports enable.
Airports benefit their communities in many ways other than the broadly recognised passenger and freight transport activity. Many airports, particularly those in regional and remote areas, operate on low margins or with the support of government funding to ensure crucial services such as regular domestic airfreight, emergency and medical response, and industry aerial support, among other benefits, are available for their local communities and regions.
Case studies are presented to demonstrate the broader role of airports in supporting local communities through connectivity and medical and emergency response support, as well as supporting industry needs, such as aerial work and connection to workforce. Australia’s diverse network of airports keeps the country connected, providing crucial infrastructure to support travel demands, industry activity, and medical and emergency response services.

Taking Flight: The economic and social contribution of Australia’s airports Australia’s airports make a crucial contribution to the social fabric and welfare of their local communities. Though airports’ social contribution can be, in many cases, difficult to quantify in monetary terms, the broader services enabled and supported by airports are highly valued by local communities.
Airports enable the connection of individuals, families and industries across and throughout the globe. In Australia, airports are crucial for overcoming geographical challenges that are caused by the vastness and remoteness of many parts of Australia. Additionally, airports allow for the efficient delivery of goods and rapid response to emergencies that cannot necessarily be achieved without aviation.
Emergency support and remote air freight Airports provide the infrastructure necessary to facilitate a range of emergency response services, such as fire services, the Royal Flying Doctor Service (RFDS), Police air services and State Emergency Service (SES). These services support all parts of Australia, however, regional and remote areas are the focus, as they often are out of reach of rapid road-based response services.
Airports provide infrastructure that is crucial in emergency response and management. For example, aircraft are used to quickly identify bushfires, and can then be used for early response, or control in areas that are difficult to access. Regional airports enable this, by providing infrastructure dedicated to emergency support, such as high flow water pumps and dedicated hangars. For example, Cessnock Airport played a crucial role in the 2019/20 bushfires by supporting helicopter water bombers with its bushfire designed water storage facilities.1 Medical services are also supported by aircraft, with organisations such as the Royal Flying Doctor Service, relying on the support of aircraft to be able to deliver crucial medical services and supplies to anyone in Australia at any time. Aeromedical services require airports to have specialised staff and rapid responses so that aircraft can be operational, fuelled and ready to fly. The RFDS relies on airports of all sizes, which both allow them to get as close to remote communities as possible and deliver them to state-of-the-art medical facilities in capital cities.
Connecting individuals The primary role of airports is to connect people. 28% of Australia’s population is born overseas, 48% have at least a parent who is born overseas, and many have close family in cities other than where they live.2 Airports create an option for people to remain connected with family and friends across Australia and overseas. Airports in Australia act as a bridge between Australia’s cities and towns, particularly for those that are separated by large distances, where other transport methods would be prohibitive such as Sydney to Perth. Within Australia, airports can help bridge the gap between cities, regional and remote regions, thereby enhancing labour mobility, regional tourism, economic prosperity and the vibrancy of regional and remote life.
Community support and non-aeronautical services Many airports work with the local community to provide social support through both aviation and non-aviation services. For example, Port Hedland airport runs recycling on waste that is collected in its airport and uses the proceeds to sponsor local community organisations. Bankstown Airport is the “largest and most complex emergency medical services base in Australia”,3 and as such has provided large amounts of in-kind support to a variety of emergency medical services organisations such as the RFDS. Part of this is enabled by the airports’ partnerships with the broader community, such as its relations with other on-precinct businesses. Bankstown Airport has improved community amenity in its product offering, which has increased its interaction with the broader community. As part of this, the airport has worked with a number of businesses to expand the scope of its 300 hectare precinct. This has involved the construction of facilities such as an entertainment precinct that allows for a greater interaction between aviation and non-aviation customers.
Aviation skill training The aviation industry relies on a highly skilled workforce to keep travellers and cargo safe and affordable. Airports and other aviation professionals are critical for the provision of practical training options for pilots, aircraft engineers, mechanics, cabin crew, air traffic control and other airport operational roles. Secondary metro airports are particularly key in the training of pilots, providing infrastructure for small planes and other training facilities. Many, such as Bankstown, have relations with tertiary institutions that offer commercial aviation degrees.
Skill training is also important in the context of emergency services, where small airports play a key role. Airports such as Western Australia’s Djarindjin Airport allow for RFDS pilots to practice landing, in all conditions, in a typical rural environment that would be part of their day-to-day roles.
The social importance of Australia’s airports is demonstrated throughout the report via a suite of case studies.

Taking Flight: The economic and social contribution of Australia’s airports Major 71% Large regional 13% Minor regional and remote 15% Major 84% Large regional 11% Minor regional and remote 5% There was a dramatic decrease in the number of passengers and flights across Australia’s airports during the COVID-19 pandemic. While there has been a remarkable recovery in 2022, passengers and movements are still below 2019 levels.
Aviation activity and recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic The airport sector was highly affected by COVID-19, with demand dropping dramatically from March 2020 as airlines cancelled flights due to COVID lockdowns. While some domestic flights continued, international travel almost came to a standstill following the international travel ban preventing international tourists, immigrants and university students from travelling to Australia and Australians from leaving the country without an exemption. In 2019, 164 million revenue passengers passed through Australia’s airports, with 121 million (74%) of them being domestic passengers and 43 million being international (26%).
Major airports serviced a large majority of aircraft movements and passengers, accounting for 82% of domestic travellers, 98% of all international passengers and 87% of overall travellers.2 Major airports typically accommodate larger aircraft, which can be seen by their smaller share of aircraft movements in Chart 2.2. relative to their share of total passengers. In 2022, while airport traffic had recovered from the lows seen in the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic, Australia’s airports were still operating below 2019 traffic levels, as seen in Chart 2.1. Across 2022, domestic passenger traffic was at 82% of 2019 levels, compared to the 45% of 2019 levels observed in the international segment.3 The trajectory of the post-COVID-19 recovery has varied across airport types. In 2022, major airports, who have a higher portion of international travel, were operating at 70% of 2019 passenger levels. While this was partially driven by the slower recovery of international travel, major airports also recorded a relatively weaker domestic market recovery, operating at 80% of their 2019 levels in 2022. Comparatively, large regional and minor regional and remote airports recorded the strongest recovery of passengers, reaching 91% and 90%, respectively, of their 2019 levels in 2022.4 As travel patterns and behaviour trends continue to evolve post recovery, airports have responded by focussing on and delivering a holistic experience. Airports are striving to meet heightened traveller expectations around quality of service relating to connectivity, fast security, and onsite facilities and amenities. To maintain pace with the increasing and evolving demand, airports are investing to increase and improve capacity and the traveller experience. Terminals have to be kept at a high standard to ensure passengers are satisfied and safe. Runways must have enough capacity to meet demand and accommodate required aircraft sizes. Recent trends in investment activity of Australia’s airports are explored further on the next page.

Airport operating performance during recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic In terms of airport operating performance, the decrease in passengers and aircraft movements during the COVID-19 pandemic resulted in lower airport revenues, while recent high inflation has put pressure on operating costs. All categories of airports, except for secondary metro airports, recorded lower revenues in 2022 than 2019, as seen in chart 2.3. However, costs across most airport categories now exceed 2019 levels. As a result, many airports, particularly Minor regional and remote airports operating within reasonably tight budget bounds, reported an operating loss in 2022.
While major airports tend to operate efficiently and serve a diverse range of industries, large regional and Minor regional and remote airport performance is more dependent on the industry they primarily serve. As a result, the pandemic more heavily impacted tourism focused airports, such as those in coastal regions, lowering revenue opportunities while operating costs still needed to be met. Conversely, airports in regions with a strong resource sector recorded higher revenues than 2019 on the back of greater FIFO and trade activity as commodity prices strengthened.
As seen in chart 2.3, for all airport categories except secondary metro airports, revenue has decreased since 2019. Likewise, for all airports but major airports costs have increased. Broadly speaking, for secondary metro airports general aviation activity has continued throughout the pandemic. In particular, medical and emergency services were fundamental to community support and the vaccine rollout at critical stages the pandemic. Pilot training activities, while scaled back, continued to operate to some extent during the pandemic. Industry specific aerial work, such as crop monitoring and land surveillance, still needed to occur and as such, airports concentrated on servicing this type of activity were relatively resilient over the pandemic.
Additionally, a significant portion of secondary metro airport revenues comes from hangar rentals and in-precinct leases – ranging from airside services, warehousing and logistics to retail centres such as Direct Factory Outlets to community entertainment complexes - which remained relatively stable during the pandemic, compared to SAT activity, providing further support for secondary metro airports throughout the pandemic. This helped contribute to their relative revenue resilience since 2019. Taking Flight: The economic and social contribution of Australia’s airports Secondary metro airports provide crucial infrastructure in metropolitan areas to support flight training operations, thereby building Australia’s qualified pilot workforce, and ensuring major airports can focus on scheduled commercial activity.
Australia’s major airports are designed to support larger aircraft and a high volume of passengers, and generally do not invest in facilities or have capacity to support light aircraft and general aviation activity. Indeed, in June 2023, Melbourne Airport recorded no aircraft landings under 7 tonnes, and only half a percent of Sydney Airport’s aircraft movements were under 7 tonnes.1 In contrast, secondary metro airports are specialised in supporting light aircraft activity, crucial for flight training, general aviation and aeromedical operations, among other services. In 2022, 87% of Australia’s aviation students were studying at a university that partners with a secondary metro airport, and these students rely on metropolitan airports for their practical training.2 As shown in Figure 2.2, secondary metro airports support more aircraft movements than the main passenger airports in their respective metropolitan areas, collectively accounting for 38% of Australia’s aircraft movements.3 Each year 600 flight pilots attending schools such as the University of New South Wales and Sydney Flying College, are trained across Bankstown and Camden airports. Bankstown Airport’s south runway is dedicated to flight training operations, with other runways also open to flight schools. Flight training services are particularly critical right now due to qualified commercial pilot labour shortages, exacerbated by COVID-19 as pilots brought forward retirement plans.3 The NSW government has estimated that Australia will need an additional 11,000 pilots by 2038, with specialised aviation labour shortages likely to be further increased due to high international demand for Australian trained pilots.4 Australia’s flight schools provide a small but crucial part of Australia’s international student market, with 34% of Australia’s aviation students not having Australian citizenship in 2020.5 In 2022, 337,000 training hours were enabled by Australia’s airports,6 however, this activity is still down 20% on pre-pandemic levels. Flight training operations not only help to build commercial pilot workforce capabilities but open up a range of alternate career pathways for participants, including aircraft engineers and mechanics, air traffic control and airport operations roles.

Now, more than ever, airports are investing to enhance service quality and expand capacity. With evolving customer preferences and service expectations following the COVID-19 pandemic, strategic investment is a crucial consideration for effective airport operations. Chart 2.5 shows that major airports have made significant recent capital investments, with approximately $210 million per airport in the past three years.1 While to a smaller scale, investments by large regional and secondary metro airports have also been notable, with indications of significant capital injections towards runway development at large regional airports and a focus on investing in property and infrastructure at secondary metro airports, based on the survey responses received. Reported average investment levels at minor regional and remote airports were relatively modest in comparison, with these airports instead tending to focus on servicing their communities within available capacity conditions.
That said, the significant recent investment appears remarkable given the coinciding low demand conditions due to the pandemic. However, the decline in demand provided the opportunity to minimise the use of airport capital, allowing efficient upgrade conditions for runways and terminals. Runway spending represented the largest area of spending of for major and large regional airports. Airports tend to upgrade runways, or build additional runways, to allow for larger aircraft, more aircraft, and safer landing conditions. Higher levels of investment in runway development reveal a competitive market environment; that is, an airport that is investing to increase capacity of flights reduces the revenue it could raise from controlling capacity, indicating the airport is being led by competitive pressures from other airports or travel means.2 Further, airports are increasingly looking at how they can reach net zero, with most setting targets of between 2035 and 2040.3 One way airports have done this is by looking at sustainable materials, such as stone Airports are investing to boost competitiveness, meet passenger demand and experience expectations, and operate more sustainably.
Strategic investment by Australia’s airports Investing in sustainability at Sunshine Coast Airport Sunshine Coast Airport has made significant investments towards becoming Australia’s first carbon neutral airport. This resulted in the Airport achieving “Level 3+ Neutrality” under the Airport Carbon Accreditation management programme. Since 2012, Sunshine Coast Airport has recorded a 28% reduction in diesel consumption, 15% reduction in food waste, 27% reduction in energy consumption, 40% reduction in emissions, and a 10% reduction in water consumption, all of which came alongside strong financial success.5 To achieve these significant improvements in sustainability, Sunshine Coast Airport has invested in energy reduction, waste elimination, water and carbon offset initiatives. For example, the Airport increased the energy efficiency of its air conditioning system and automated their operations to be responsive to flight schedules and temperature throughout the day. The Airport also installed solar powered composting that has the capacity to compost 945 litres of waste per week, preventing it from going to landfill. Water consumption was reduced by implementing urban sensitive land design to reduce irrigation and to harvest rainwater from the terminal roof for use in amenities and landscaping.
Additionally, Sunshine Coast Airport has invested in 1,435 Australian Gold Standard Carbon offsets to negate their remaining carbon emissions. This has helped the Airport to achieve the top sustainability accreditation, which has helped its engagement with local community and branding.

The economic contribution of Australia’s airports Economic contribution analysis Economic contribution studies provide a snapshot of the contribution of a company or industry at a particular point in time. This section estimates the contribution of Australia’s airports to the economy in calendar year 2022. The headline contribution metrics are: • Gross Value Added (GVA)- the contribution of Australia’s airports to Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
• Full Time Equivalent (FTE) Jobs- the number of FTE employees supported by Australia’s airports.
The analysis measures both direct and indirect value of Australia’s Airports. The direct contribution demonstrates the returns contributed from direct labour and capital inputs associated with Airport activity. While the indirect contribution captures the supply chain activity associated with the demand for goods and services generated from other sectors of the economy. The economic contribution analysis in this report is consistent with the Australian National Accounting framework. Specifically, the analysis was underpinned by the Deloitte Access Economics’ Regional Input-Output Model, containing multipliers derived from the ABS’ Input-Output, supply and use, tables.
The economic contribution of airport facilitated tourism was underpinned by a Tourism Satellite Account (TSA) framework. The TSA framework is conceptually similar and draws on the ABS Input-Output Tables, but accounts for the unique, consumption based characteristics of the tourism industry. Further details on the analytical approach are provided in Appendix B: Economic contribution framework and Appendix C: Tourism contribution framework.
Australia’s airports contribute to the economy in a variety of ways This report estimates the direct and indirect value of four key components of airport associated activity: • Core airport activities: similar to the way the economic contribution of a standard business would be estimated, this component examines the profitability, employment and expenditure of the airports themselves. The survey of airports is the primary data input for these estimates.
• Airport precinct activities: this component measures the activity that take place in broader airport precincts, including supporting businesses, retail activity, airport hotels and commercial offices. These estimates are primarily derived from ABS census employment figures, supplemented by the survey of airports. • Facilitated tourism: airports facilitate almost all of Australia’s international tourists, and approximately a quarter of domestic tourism. This component measures the contribution of airport-facilitated expenditure by tourists to the economy. Tourism Research Australia (TRA) figures are the primary inputs to this modelling.
• Facilitated freight: air freight enables safe, quick and efficient trade in perishable and high-value goods. This component measures the contribution of air-facilitated trade. A custom ABS data request is the main data source for this section. The headline results for each of these components are presented in figure 3.1. The aviation industry was still impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic at the time of this study, with ongoing border restrictions, travel hesitancy and supply chain issues being significant factors. As a result, these estimates are likely conservative, and do not represent a ‘typical’ year of operations. Core airport activity $4.2 billion in value added 10,700 FTE Jobs Air-facilitated tourism $34.9 billion in value added 263,100 FTE Jobs Airport precincts $23.2 billion in value added 161,300 FTE Jobs Air freight $42.9 billion in value added 260,000 FTE Jobs $4,000 Contribution per international visitor 13% Air freight share of Australia’s exports by value 91,800 Direct employees on airport precincts Figure 3.1: Economic contribution of Australia’s airports, 2022 Source: Deloitte Access Economics 83% Share of direct economic contribution from major airports 16 © 2023 Deloitte Access Economics Pty Ltd. All rights reserved.
Taking Flight: The economic and social contribution of Australia’s airports 0% 5% 10% 15% 20% 25% 30% 35% Major Non major In 2022, the core activities of Australia’s airports contributed $4.2 billion in value added to the Australian economy and supported 11,000 full time equivalent jobs.
Contribution of core airport activities Operational contribution, 2022 3,700 Direct FTE employment supported by airport core activities Chart 3.2: Airport cost structure, by airport type, 2022 Chart 3.1: Direct employees and gross value added (GVA) of airport core operations, 2022 Source: Deloitte Access Economics Australia’s airports are significant contributors to the economy and employment. In 2022, 3,700 FTE jobs were directly supported by core airport activities. This captures those employed by airports and involved in the day-to-day operations and management of the business, such as ground staff, management, marketing and administration. Major airports are highly productive, capital-intensive operations, thereby returning significant value relative to their labour requirement. In 2022, the ten major airports directly contributed more than $2.7 billion in value added to the economy, equating to $1.2 million in value added per direct employee, more than six times as much as the national average of $176,300 value added per employee across all industries.1 Of this contribution, more than 83% was contributed by the 10 major airports, with a further 11% being contributed by 33 large regional airports. This means that over 94% of the contribution of airport core operations came from just 43, or 23% of all airports in Australia. These airports are structurally different to the smaller airports that have less traffic, fewer employees and lower revenues. While smaller airports do not make a substantial economic contribution from core activities, they are nevertheless vitally important to their communities- providing a rapid, reliable link to the rest of Australia for freight, emergency and medical services. This contribution is not captured in the calculation of a traditional economic contribution study but makes a substantial impact on the communities that benefit.
Airports contribute indirectly to the economy through the purchase of intermediate goods and services to facilitate their operations. In 2022, the indirect contribution of airports was $967 million in value added to the national economy, supporting 7,100 FTE jobs. Most operational expenditure requirements of airports flows to the services and utilities, security and property sectors- the key services required to carry out the day-to-day operations of the airport (Chart 3.2). The result of this upstream activity is two indirect FTE jobs supported for every direct FTE employee. This reflects the unique nature of major airports’ business operations- providing a workplace for a range of labour-intensive businesses and organisations that deliver aviation allied services under contractual arrangements with airports.

This report, prepared by Deloitte Access Economics for the Australian Airports Association (AAA) in November 2023, examines the economic and social contribution of Australia's airports. It is an update of a 2018 report titled "Connecting Australia."

**Key Findings:**
- In 2022, Australia's airports contributed $105 billion in value added (VA) to the national economy, supporting 690,000 full-time equivalent (FTE) jobs.
- Airport activity contributed approximately 5% of Australia's GDP and supported around 6% of FTE jobs (more than 1 in 20 jobs).
- The economic contribution comprises four components:
  - Core airport activities: $4.2 billion VA, ~11,000 FTE jobs
  - Airport precinct activities: $23.2 billion VA, 161,300 FTE jobs (91,800 direct employees on airport precincts)
  - Facilitated tourism: $34.9 billion VA, 263,100 FTE jobs ($28 billion from 110 million domestic visitor nights, $14.2 billion from 3.4 million international visitors, ~$4,000 contribution per international visitor)
  - Facilitated freight: $42.9 billion VA, 260,000 FTE jobs (914,000 tonnes of international freight valued at $138 billion)
- Air freight represents 13% of Australia's exports by value.
- Major airports (10 total) contributed 83% of the direct economic contribution, generating $1.2 million VA per direct employee (compared to national average of $176,300).

**COVID-19 Recovery:**
- Airport activity recovered to 72% of 2019 levels in 2022; domestic passenger traffic was at 82% of 2019 levels, international at 45%.
- Major airports operated at 70% of 2019 passenger levels; large regional at 91% and minor regional/remote at 90%.
- Domestic travel forecast to fully recover to 2019 levels in 2023; international travel forecast to recover in 2025.
- All airport categories except secondary metro airports recorded lower revenues in 2022 than 2019, while costs exceeded 2019 levels for most categories.
- Secondary metro airports showed relative revenue resilience due to stable general aviation activity (medical/emergency services, pilot training, aerial work) and property/hangar rental income.

**Airport Network and Social Contributions:**
- Australia has a diverse network of 340+ AAA-member airports, classified as major, large regional, minor regional/remote, and secondary metro airports.
- 90% of airports with scheduled air transport are outside major cities, but 84% of passenger traffic goes through major airports.
- Social contributions include: emergency response infrastructure (supporting Royal Flying Doctor Service, Rural Fire Service, SES, police air services), community connectivity, medical services, flight training, and workforce development.
- Secondary metro airports provided infrastructure for 337,000 flight training hours in 2022 (down 20% from pre-pandemic levels). Australia needs an additional 11,000 pilots by 2038.
- 87% of Australia's aviation students study at universities partnering with secondary metro airports; 34% of aviation students were non-citizens in 2020.

**Investment and Sustainability:**
- Major airports invested approximately $210 million per airport over the past three years, with runways the largest spending area.
- Airports are setting net-zero targets between 2035 and 2040, using sustainable materials like stone mastic asphalt in runway construction.
- Sunshine Coast Airport achieved "Level 3+ Neutrality" (Australia's first carbon neutral airport) with 40% reduction in emissions since 2012.

**Case Studies Highlighted:**
- Bankstown Airport: third busiest airport in Australia, home base for NSW Air Ambulance, NSW Police Aviation Command, RFDS, and Rural Fire Service; operates a 300-hectare precinct with entertainment, sports, retail, and industrial facilities.
- Sunshine Coast Airport: carbon neutrality achievements.
- Port Hedland Airport: connecting the Pilbara workforce (FIFO).
- Dubbo Airport: emergency response support.
- Djarindjin Airport (Western Australia): supporting medical services in remote conditions.

**Methodology:**
The analysis used the Deloitte Access Economics Regional Input-Output Model with ABS Input-Output tables, Tourism Satellite Account framework, a bespoke survey of 32 airports, and data from Tourism Research Australia, ABS, BITRE, and Airservices Australia.
