This webpage contains the full text of Title 49, Subtitle VII, Part B, Chapter 471 (AIRPORT DEVELOPMENT), Subchapter I (AIRPORT IMPROVEMENT) of the United States Code, specifically covering sections 47101 through 47106. It is hosted on GovRegs, a U.S. Code reference site, with navigation and a table of contents listing sections 47101 through 47146 of Chapter 471.

**§ 47101 (Policies):** Establishes the federal policy that safe airport and airway system operation is the highest aviation priority. Key policies include: minimizing noise impacts on communities, giving special emphasis to developing reliever airports, facilitating cargo hub airports, encouraging intermodal connections, promoting airport projects that increase capacity, ensuring fees are reasonable and airports are self-sustaining (without creating surpluses beyond airport needs), converting former military air bases to civil use, and encouraging innovative technology (including in-pavement lighting and runway incursion prevention devices). It also establishes a National Transportation Policy goal of developing a national intermodal transportation system, and addresses capacity expansion/noise abatement (reducing noncompatible land uses), consistency with air commerce and safety policies, adequacy of navigation aids, maximum use of safety facilities (including electronic/visual vertical guidance on runways, grooving/friction treatment, precision approach systems, runway incursion prevention devices, etc.), and intermodal planning (requiring coordination with state and local officials, and consultation with the Secretary of the Interior and EPA on projects significantly affecting natural resources). Last amended by Pub. L. 118-63, May 16, 2024.

**§ 47102 (Definitions):** Defines key terms including: "air carrier," "airport" (includes heliports), "airport development" (extensive list of eligible activities including constructing/repairing airports, acquiring navigation aids, safety/security equipment, snow removal equipment, aircraft deicing equipment, terminal development, zero-emission vehicle conversions, power supply reliability improvements, natural disaster resilience improvements, cybersecurity compliance, unleaded aviation fuel infrastructure, and hydrogen fueling systems), "airport hazard," "airport planning," "commercial service airport" (at least 2,500 passenger boardings/year with scheduled service), "general aviation airport," "large hub airport" (≥1.0% of passenger boardings), "medium hub airport" (0.25%-1.0%), "small hub airport" (0.05%-0.25%), "nonhub airport" (<0.05%), "primary airport" (>10,000 boardings/year), "public airport," "public-use airport," "reliever airport," "passenger boardings," "sponsor," "State," and "terminal development."

**§ 47103 (National plan of integrated airport systems):** Requires the Secretary of Transportation to maintain "the national plan of integrated airport systems," which shall include the kind and estimated cost of eligible airport development needed for a safe, efficient, integrated system. The plan must meet civil aeronautics needs, national defense requirements, and USPS needs, and be published every 2 years. The Secretary of Defense must make domestic military airports available for civil use to the extent possible. Also requires a detailed statement listing airports not in compliance with grant assurances (with circumstances, timeline, and corrective actions).

**§ 47104 (Project grant authority):** Authorizes the Secretary to make project grants from the Airport and Airway Trust Fund to maintain a safe and efficient nationwide system of public-use airports. Obligations may be incurred as amounts are apportioned under section 47114. This grant authority expires after September 30, 2028, except for certain remaining or recovered amounts.

**§ 47105 (Project grant applications):** Specifies that applications may be submitted by a sponsor or by a State (with written consent of airport sponsors) and requires sponsors to consult with affected airport users. Applications must describe the project, may only propose projects for public-use airports in the national plan, must comply with prescribed standards, and must follow the Secretary's prescribed form. Also addresses State standards for airport development at nonprimary airports (including pavement standards), certification of compliance, and preventive maintenance requirements (sponsors must have an effective pavement maintenance-management program for pavement replacement/reconstruction applications).

**§ 47106 (Project grant application approval):** Authorizes the Secretary to approve project grant applications only if satisfied that: the project is consistent with local public agency plans, contributes to carrying out the subchapter, adequate funding exists for non-federal project costs, the project will be completed without unreasonable delay, and the sponsor has authority to carry it out. For airport development grants, the sponsor must hold (or acquire) good title to landing/takeoff areas, community interests must be fairly considered, and necessary approach lighting must be provided. Environmental requirements include public hearing opportunities for projects involving airport/runway location or major runway extension, and require a finding of no feasible alternative when projects significantly affect natural resources. The Secretary may withhold approval (with a hearing and a 180-day finding deadline) for violations, and affected persons may seek judicial review in federal courts of appeals.

# 49 U.S. Code § 47102 - Definitions

* [U.S. Code](#tab_default_1)
* [Notes](#tab_default_2)
* [Authorities (CFR)](#tab_default_3)

[prev](/uscode/text/49/47101 " Policies") | [next](/uscode/text/49/47103 " National plan of integrated airport systems")

In this subchapter—

(1)

“[air carrier](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1066333662-465961836&term_occur=999&term_src=)” has the meaning given such term in section 40102.

(2) “[airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=)”—

(A) means—

(i)

an area of land or water used or intended to be used for the landing and taking off of aircraft;

(ii)

an appurtenant area used or intended to be used for [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) buildings or other [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) facilities or rights of way; and

(iii)

[airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) buildings and facilities located in any of those areas; and

(B)

includes a heliport.

(3) “[airport development](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1343304346-465961834&term_occur=999&term_src=)” means the following activities, if undertaken by the [sponsor,](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1998892262-1559914943&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) owner, or operator of a [public-use airport:](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1682421198-1559914947&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)

(A) constructing, repairing, or improving a [public-use airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1682421198-1559914947&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102), including—

(i)

removing, lowering, relocating, marking, and lighting an [airport hazard](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1377433863-465961833&term_occur=999&term_src=);

(ii)

preparing a plan or specification, including carrying out a field investigation; and

(iii)

a secondary runway at a [nonhub airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1814514611-1559914976&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) that is equivalent in size and type to the primary runway of such [airport.](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)

(B) acquiring for, or installing at, a [public-use airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1682421198-1559914947&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)—

(i)

a navigation aid or another aid (including a precision approach system) used by aircraft for landing at or taking off from the [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=), including preparing the site as required by the acquisition or installation;

(ii)

safety or security equipment, including explosive detection devices, universal access systems, and emergency call boxes, the Secretary requires by regulation for, or approves as contributing significantly to, the safety or security of individuals and property at the [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) and integrated in-pavement lighting systems for runways and taxiways and other runway and taxiway incursion prevention devices;

(iii)

equipment to remove snow, to measure runway surface friction, or for aviation-related weather reporting, including closed circuit weather surveillance equipment and fuel infrastructure for such equipment to remove snow if the [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) is located in Alaska;

(iv)

firefighting and rescue equipment at an [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) that serves scheduled passenger operations of [air carrier](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1066333662-465961836&term_occur=999&term_src=) aircraft designed for more than 9 passenger seats;

(v)

aircraft deicing equipment and structures (except aircraft deicing fluids and storage facilities for the equipment and fluids);

(vi)

interactive training systems;

(vii)

windshear detection equipment that is certified by the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration;

(viii)

stainless steel adjustable lighting extensions approved by the Administrator;

(ix)

engineered materials arresting systems as described in the Advisory Circular No. 150/5220–22 published by the Federal Aviation Administration on August 21, 1998, including any revision to the circular;

(x)

replacement of baggage conveyor systems, and reconfiguration of terminal baggage areas, that the Secretary determines are necessary to install bulk explosive detection devices; except that such activities shall be eligible for funding under this subchapter only using amounts apportioned under section 47114; and

(xi)

a medium intensity approach lighting system with runway alignment indicator lights.

(C) acquiring an interest in land or airspace, including land for future [airport development](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1343304346-465961834&term_occur=999&term_src=), that is needed—

(i)

to carry out [airport development](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1343304346-465961834&term_occur=999&term_src=) described in subclause (A) or (B) of this clause; or

(ii)

to remove or mitigate an existing [airport hazard](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1377433863-465961833&term_occur=999&term_src=) or prevent or limit the creation of a new [airport hazard](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1377433863-465961833&term_occur=999&term_src=).

(D)

acquiring land for, or constructing, a burn area training structure on or off the [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) to provide live fire drill training for aircraft rescue and firefighting personnel required to receive the training under regulations the Secretary prescribes, including basic equipment and minimum structures to support the training under standards the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration prescribes.

(E)

relocating an air traffic control tower and any navigational aid (including radar) if the relocation is necessary to carry out a [project](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-309310695-1559914973&term_occur=999&term_src=) approved by the Secretary under this subchapter or under section 40117.

(F)

constructing, reconstructing, repairing, or improving an [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=), or purchasing capital equipment for an [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=), if necessary for compliance with the responsibilities of the operator or owner of the [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) under the [Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990](/topn/americans_with_disabilities_act_of_1990) ([42 U.S.C. 12101](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/12101) et seq.), the [Clean Air Act](/topn/air_pollution_control_act) ([42 U.S.C. 7401](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/7401) et seq.), and the [Federal Water Pollution Control Act](/topn/clean_water_act) ([33 U.S.C. 1251](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/33/1251) et seq.), except constructing or purchasing capital equipment that would benefit primarily a revenue-producing area of the [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) used by a nonaeronautical business.

(G)

acquiring land for, or work necessary to construct, a pad suitable for deicing aircraft before takeoff at a [commercial service airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1154669962-465961830&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102), including constructing or reconstructing paved areas, drainage collection structures, treatment and discharge systems, appropriate lighting, paved access for deicing vehicles and aircraft, and including acquiring glycol recovery vehicles, but not including acquiring aircraft deicing fluids or constructing or reconstructing storage facilities for aircraft deicing equipment or fluids.

(H)

routine work to preserve and extend the useful life of runways, taxiways, and aprons at [nonhub airports](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1814514611-1559914976&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) and [airports](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) that are not [primary airports](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-132244653-1559914974&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102), under guidelines issued by the Administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration.

(I)

constructing, reconstructing, or improving an [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=), or purchasing nonrevenue generating capital equipment to be owned by an [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=), for the purpose of transferring passengers, cargo, or baggage between the aeronautical and ground transportation modes on [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) property.

(J)

constructing an air traffic control tower or acquiring and installing air traffic control, communications, and related equipment at an air traffic control tower under the terms specified in section 47124(b)(4).

(K)

work necessary to construct or modify [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) facilities to provide low-emission fuel systems, gate electrification, and other related air quality improvements at a [commercial service airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1154669962-465961830&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102).

(L) a [project](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-309310695-1559914973&term_occur=999&term_src=) by a [commercial service airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1154669962-465961830&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) for the acquisition of [airport-](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)owned vehicles or ground support equipment equipped with [low-emission technology](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1730747724-1559914978&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) if the vehicles are;

(i)

used exclusively on [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) property; or

(ii)

used exclusively to transport passengers and employees between the [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) and the [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=)’s consolidated rental car facility or an intermodal surface transportation facility adjacent to the [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=).

(M)

construction of mobile refueler parking within a fuel farm at a nonprimary [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) meeting the requirements of section [112.8](/cfr/text/40/112.8) of title 40, Code of Federal Regulations.

(N)

[terminal development](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-957481367-1559914941&term_occur=999&term_src=) under section 47119(a).

(O)

acquiring and installing facilities and equipment to provide air conditioning, heating, or electric power from terminal-based, nonexclusive use facilities to aircraft parked at a public use [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) for the purpose of reducing energy use or harmful emissions as compared to the provision of such air conditioning, heating, or electric power from aircraft-based systems.

(P)

an on-[airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) [project](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-309310695-1559914973&term_occur=999&term_src=) to improve reliability and efficiency of the power supply of the [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) or meet current and future electrical power demand and to prevent power disruptions to the airfield, passenger terminal, and any other [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) facilities, including the acquisition and installation of electrical generators, renewable energy generation and storage infrastructure (including necessary substation upgrades to support such infrastructure), separation of the [airport’](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=)s main power supply from its redundant power supply, the construction or modification of [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) facilities to install a microgrid (as defined in section 641 of the [United States Energy Storage Competitiveness Act of 2007](/topn/united_states_energy_storage_competitiveness_act_of_2007) ([42 U.S.C. 17231](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/17231))), and smart glass (including electrochromic glass).

(Q)

converting or retrofitting vehicles and ground support equipment into eligible zero-emission vehicles and equipment (as defined in section 47136) and for acquiring, by purchase or lease, eligible zero-emission vehicles and equipment.

(R)

predevelopment planning, including financial, legal, or procurement consulting services, related to an application or proposed application for an exemption under section 47134.

(S)

acquisition of advanced digital construction management systems and related technology used in the planning, design and engineering, construction, and maintenance of [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) facilities when such systems or technologies are acquired to carry out a [project](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-309310695-1559914973&term_occur=999&term_src=) approved by the Secretary under this subchapter.

(T) improvements, or planning for improvements (including monitoring equipment or services), that would be necessary to sustain commercial service flight operations or permit the resumption of such flight operations following a natural disaster (including an earthquake, flooding, high water, wildfires, hurricane, storm surge, tidal wave, tornado, tsunami, wind driven water, sea level rise, tropical storm, cyclone, land instability, or winter storm) at—

(i)

a [primary airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-132244653-1559914974&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102); or

(ii)

a nonprimary [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) that is designated as a Federal staging area or incident support base by the Administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

(U)

a [project](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-309310695-1559914973&term_occur=999&term_src=) to comply with rulemakings and recommendations on [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) cybersecurity standards from the aviation rulemaking committee convened under section 395 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024.

(V)

reconstructing or rehabilitating an existing crosswind runway (regardless of the wind coverage of the primary runway) if the reconstruction or rehabilitation of such crosswind runway is in the most recently approved [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) layout plan of the [sponsor.](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1998892262-1559914943&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)

(W) constructing or acquiring such [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=)-owned infrastructure or equipment, notwithstanding revenue producing capability of such infrastructure or equipment, as may be required for—

(i)

the on-[airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) distribution or storage of unleaded aviation gasoline for piston-driven aircraft, including on-[airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) construction or expansion of pipelines, storage tanks, low-emission fuel systems, and [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=)-owned fuel trucks providing exclusively unleaded aviation fuels (unless the Secretary determines that an alternative fuel may be safely used in such fuel truck for a limited time); or

(ii)

fueling systems for type certificated hydrogen-powered aircraft.

(X)

constructing, reconstructing, or rehabilitating a taxiway or taxilane that serves non-exclusive use aeronautical facilities, including aircraft storage facilities, except for the 50 feet of pavement immediately in front of an ineligible building.

(Y)

any other activity (excluding [terminal development](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-957481367-1559914941&term_occur=999&term_src=)) that the Secretary concludes will reasonably improve the safety of the [airport.](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)

(4)

“[airport hazard](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1377433863-465961833&term_occur=999&term_src=)” means a structure or object of natural growth located on or near a [public-use airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1682421198-1559914947&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102), or a use of land near the [airport,](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) that obstructs or otherwise is hazardous to the landing or taking off of aircraft at or from the [airport.](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)

(5) “[airport planning](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1904599278-465961832&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)” means planning as defined by requirements the Secretary prescribes and includes—

(A)

[integrated airport system planning](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-118297868-465961828&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) and catchment area analyses;

(B)

developing an environmental management system;

(C)

developing a plan for recycling and minimizing the generation of [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) solid waste, consistent with applicable [State](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-80204913-1559914942&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) and local recycling laws, including the cost of a waste audit; and

(D)

assessing current and future electrical power demand for [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) airside and landside activities.

(6)

“[amount made available under section 48103](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-690941907-465961831&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)” or [“amount newly made available”](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-55755367-465961831&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) means the amount authorized for grants under [section 48103](/uscode/text/49/48103) as that amount may be limited in that year by a subsequent law, but as determined without regard to grant obligation recoveries made in that year or amounts covered by section 47107(f).

(7)

“[commercial service airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1154669962-465961830&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)” means a [public airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-553176556-1559914948&term_occur=999&term_src=) in a [State](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-80204913-1559914942&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) that the Secretary determines has at least 2,500 [passenger boardings](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-22777679-1559914975&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) each year and is receiving scheduled passenger aircraft service.

(8) “[general aviation airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1577308292-465961829&term_occur=999&term_src=)” means a [public-use airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1682421198-1559914947&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) that is located in a [State](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-80204913-1559914942&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) and that, as determined by the Secretary—

(A)

does not have scheduled service; or

(B)

has scheduled service with less than 2,500 [passenger boardings](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-22777679-1559914975&term_occur=999&term_src=) each year.

(9) “[integrated airport system planning](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-118297868-465961828&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)” means developing for planning purposes information and guidance to decide the extent, kind, location, and timing of [airport development](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1343304346-465961834&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) needed in a specific area to establish a viable, balanced, and integrated system of [public-use airports,](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1682421198-1559914947&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) including—

(A)

identifying system needs;

(B)

developing an estimate of systemwide development costs;

(C)

conducting studies, surveys, and other planning actions, including those related to [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) access, needed to decide which aeronautical needs should be met by a system of [airports](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102); and

(D)

standards prescribed by a [State](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-80204913-1559914942&term_occur=999&term_src=), except standards for safety of approaches, for [airport development](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1343304346-465961834&term_occur=999&term_src=) at nonprimary [public-use airports.](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1682421198-1559914947&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)

(10)

“[landed weight](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1897489294-1559914980&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)” means the weight of aircraft transporting only cargo in intrastate, interstate, and foreign air transportation, as the Secretary determines under regulations the Secretary prescribes.

(11)

“[large hub airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-427568955-1559914979&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)” means a [commercial service airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1154669962-465961830&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) that has at least 1.0 percent of the [passenger boardings.](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-22777679-1559914975&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)

(12)

“[low-emission technology](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1730747724-1559914978&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)” means technology for vehicles and equipment whose emission performance is the best achievable under emission standards established by the Environmental Protection Agency and that relies exclusively on alternative fuels that are substantially nonpetroleum based, as defined by the Department of Energy, but not excluding hybrid systems or natural gas powered vehicles.

(13)

“[medium hub airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-517178251-1559914977&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)” means a [commercial service airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1154669962-465961830&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) that has at least 0.25 percent but less than 1.0 percent of the [passenger boardings.](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-22777679-1559914975&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)

(14)

“[nonhub airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1814514611-1559914976&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)” means a [commercial service airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1154669962-465961830&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) that has less than 0.05 percent of the [passenger boardings.](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-22777679-1559914975&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)

(15) “[passenger boardings](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-22777679-1559914975&term_occur=999&term_src=)”—

(A)

means, unless the context indicates otherwise, revenue [passenger boardings](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-22777679-1559914975&term_occur=999&term_src=) in the United [States](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-80204913-1559914942&term_occur=999&term_src=) in the prior calendar year on an aircraft in service in air commerce, as the Secretary determines under regulations the Secretary prescribes; and

(B)

includes passengers who continue on an aircraft in international flight that stops at an [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) in the 48 contiguous [States,](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-80204913-1559914942&term_occur=999&term_src=) Alaska, or Hawaii for a nontraffic purpose.

(16)

“[primary airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-132244653-1559914974&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)” means a [commercial service airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1154669962-465961830&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) the Secretary determines to have more than 10,000 [passenger boardings](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-22777679-1559914975&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) each year.

(17)

“[project](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-309310695-1559914973&term_occur=999&term_src=)” means a [project](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-309310695-1559914973&term_occur=999&term_src=), separate [projects](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-309310695-1559914973&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102) included in one [project grant](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1541646677-1559914971&term_occur=999&term_src=) application, or all [projects](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-309310695-1559914973&term_occur=999&term_src=) to be undertaken at an [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) in a fiscal year, to achieve [airport development](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1343304346-465961834&term_occur=999&term_src=) or [airport planning.](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1904599278-465961832&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)

(18)

“[project cost](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-880893044-1559914972&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)” means a cost involved in carrying out a [project.](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-309310695-1559914973&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)

(19)

“[project grant](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1541646677-1559914971&term_occur=999&term_src=)” means a grant of money the Secretary makes to a [sponsor](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1998892262-1559914943&term_occur=999&term_src=) to carry out at least one [project.](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-309310695-1559914973&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)

(20) “[public agency](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-811202972-1559914949&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)” means—

(A)

a [State](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-80204913-1559914942&term_occur=999&term_src=) or political subdivision of a [State](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-80204913-1559914942&term_occur=999&term_src=);

(B)

a tax-supported organization;

(C)

an Indian tribe or pueblo; or

(D)

the Republic of the Marshall Islands, Federated [States](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-80204913-1559914942&term_occur=999&term_src=) of Micronesia, and Republic of Palau.

(21) “[public airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-553176556-1559914948&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)” means an [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) used or intended to be used for public purposes—

(A)

that is under the control of a [public agency](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-811202972-1559914949&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102); and

(B)

of which the area used or intended to be used for the landing, taking off, or surface maneuvering of aircraft is publicly owned.

(22) “[public-use airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-1682421198-1559914947&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102)” means—

(A)

a [public airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-553176556-1559914948&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102); or

(B) a privately-owned [airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-991666997-465961835&term_occur=999&term_src=) used or intended to be used for public purposes that is—

(i)

a [reliever airport](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-690872647-1559914946&term_occur=999&term_src=title:49:subtitle:VII:part:B:chapter:471:subchapter:I:section:47102); or

(ii)

determined by the Secretary to have at least 2,500 [passenger boardings](/definitions/uscode.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=49-USC-22777679-1559914975&term_occur=999&term_src=) each year and to receive scheduled passenger aircraft service.

This webpage presents the full text of 49 U.S. Code § 47102 - Definitions, which is part of the U.S. Code chapter on airport and airway improvement programs (subchapter covering airport grants). The section defines 28 key terms used throughout the subchapter.

Key definitions include:
- **Airport**: An area of land or water used for landing/taking off of aircraft, appurtenant areas for facilities, and airport buildings; includes heliports.
- **Airport development**: A comprehensive list of eligible activities including constructing/repairing public-use airports, acquiring navigational aids, installing safety/security equipment (explosive detection devices, emergency call boxes, in-pavement lighting), snow removal equipment, firefighting equipment, deicing equipment, windshear detection, implementing ADA, Clean Air Act, and Federal Water Pollution Control Act compliance, deicing pads, terminal development, low-emission fuel systems, air quality improvements, electrical power reliability projects, zero-emission vehicle conversion, disaster-recovery improvements, cybersecurity compliance projects, crosswind runway rehabilitation, unleaded aviation gasoline infrastructure, and hydrogen fueling systems.
- **Airport hazard**: A structure or natural growth near a public-use airport that obstructs or is hazardous to aircraft landing/taking off.
- **Commercial service airport**: A public airport with at least 2,500 passenger boardings per year receiving scheduled passenger service.
- **General aviation airport**: A public-use airport without scheduled service or with less than 2,500 annual passenger boardings.
- **Hub airport classifications**: Large hub (≥1.0% of passenger boardings), medium hub (0.25%–1.0%), small hub (0.05%–0.25%), and nonhub (<0.05%).
- **Primary airport**: Commercial service airport with more than 10,000 passenger boardings per year.
- **Passenger boardings**: Revenue passenger boardings in the U.S. in the prior calendar year, including international flight passengers stopping for nontraffic purposes.
- **Public agency**: States, political subdivisions, tax-supported organizations, Indian tribes/pueblos, and the Marshall Islands, Federated States of Micronesia, and Palau.
- **Public airport**: Under control of a public agency with publicly owned landing areas.
- **Reliever airport**: Designated to relieve congestion at commercial service airports.
- **Sponsor**: A public agency or private airport owner applying for financial assistance.
- **State**: Includes U.S. states, DC, Puerto Rico, Virgin Islands, American Samoa, Northern Mariana Islands, and Guam.
- **Terminal development**: Development of passenger terminal buildings, gates, access roads, walkways, and passenger/baggage moving vehicles.

The section was enacted July 5, 1994 (Pub. L. 103-272) and has been amended numerous times through May 16, 2024 (Pub. L. 118-63, the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024), which added provisions for unleaded aviation fuel infrastructure, hydrogen fueling systems, and cybersecurity compliance. The page includes historical revision notes detailing the statutory sources for each definition.

This is a Quizlet flashcard set titled "Airport Management Chapter 1," created by user Gemini101ify, containing 60 terms related to airport management fundamentals. The set covers the U.S. airport system, key definitions, regulatory bodies, and aviation organizations.

Key data points about the U.S. airport system:
- Approximately 19,000 civil landing areas exist in the United States
- Approximately 5,200 public-use airports exist
- About 3,400 airports are included in the NPIAS (National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems)
- Approximately 522 are "commercial service" airports in the NPIAS (accommodating at least 10,000 annual enplanements)
- Approximately 2,500 are "general aviation" airports in the NPIAS
- NPIAS "primary airports" accommodate at least 10,000 annual commercial passenger enplanements
- "Large Hub" airports enplane at least 1.0% of total U.S. enplanements; "Medium Hub" 0.25%-0.99%; "Small Hub" 0.05%-0.24%; "Non-Hub" less than 0.05%
- The largest number of NPIAS airports are classified as General Aviation
- A Reliever airport requires a local population of at least 500,000 OR at least 100 based aircraft or at least 25,000 itinerant operations (the answer given is at least 100 based aircraft or at least 25,000 itinerant operations)
- Cargo is NOT a category of airports in the NPIAS (categories are Commercial Service, General Aviation, and Reliever)

Key organizations and regulations:
- Civil aviation in the U.S. is administered through the Department of Transportation (DOT); the FAA oversees civil aviation
- The FAA is responsible for the certification of airports serving commercial air carriers
- ICAO (International Civil Aviation Organization) provides international standards; founded in 1944 with approximately 190 member countries
- NASP (National Airport System Plan) was created in 1982
- FAR Part 91: General Operating and Flight Rules; FAR Part 139: certification of airports; FAR Part 150: Airport Noise and Compatibility Planning; FAR Part 1: definitions and abbreviations
- Transportation Security Regulations fall under 49 CFR - Transportation
- AOPA represents general aviation pilots; ALPA represents airline pilots; ACI-NA is the "voice of airports"; IATA assesses international airports for service quality; NASAO represents state DOT aviation offices

Key definitions:
- Enplanement: number of passengers that board an aircraft; Deplanement: passengers that deplane
- Transfer passenger: counted twice (deplaning and enplaning)
- Aircraft operation: takeoff/landing; Based aircraft: aircraft based at an airport
- Itinerant operation: takes off at one airport, lands at another; Local operation: takes off and lands at same airport
- Airport activity measured by enplanements at commercial service airports and operations at GA airports
- U.S. airports typically owned/operated by states, cities, municipalities
- Basic utility airports designed to accommodate General Aviation
- FAA Airport District Offices (ADOs) ensure compliance with FAA regulations
- Reliever airports relieve congestion at commercial airports to allow more GA access

Fact-checked by Grok 7 months ago

# FAA airport categories

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) categorizes U.S. airports through the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS), a congressionally mandated program that identifies approximately 3,300 public-use airports vital to the national air transportation system out of nearly 19,000 total airports (including about 5,000 public-use and 14,400 private-use facilities).[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1) These categories classify airports based on their operational roles, passenger enplanements, cargo volumes, and contributions to aviation infrastructure, encompassing **commercial service airports**, **cargo service airports**, **reliever airports**, and **general aviation airports** to guide federal funding, planning, and safety standards.[[[2]](#ref-2)](#ref-2) Commercial service airports are publicly owned facilities with scheduled passenger service and at least 2,500 annual enplanements; they divide into **primary** (≥10,000 enplanements) and **nonprimary** (2,500–9,999 enplanements) subtypes.[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1) Primary commercial service airports are further subdivided by hub status relative to total U.S. enplanements: **large hubs** (≥1%, such as Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson with over 36 million enplanements in 2021), **medium hubs** (0.25%–1%), **small hubs** (0.05%–0.25%), and **nonhub primaries** (<0.05% but ≥10,000 enplanements).[[[3]](#ref-3)](#ref-3) Nonprimary commercial service airports, often smaller regional facilities, support local air travel without qualifying as hubs.[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1) Cargo service airports prioritize freight operations, defined by handling more than 100 million pounds of annual landed cargo weight, and may overlap with commercial service categories to facilitate [logistics](/page/Logistics) for industries like [e-commerce](/page/E-commerce) and [manufacturing](/page/Manufacturing).[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1) Reliever airports, which can be publicly or privately owned, are specifically designated to reduce congestion and enhance access at nearby larger commercial airports by accommodating [general aviation](/page/General_aviation) traffic.[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1) General aviation airports form the largest group, comprising about 88% of NPIAS facilities, and serve non-scheduled, non-commercial flights such as private, business, and recreational aviation with fewer than 2,500 annual enplanements or no scheduled passenger service.[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1) They are assigned functional roles based on activity levels, based aircraft, and infrastructure per FAA guidelines: **national** (high-volume facilities supporting national and international markets), **regional** (connecting regional economies and metro areas), **local** (serving state or community needs, often with piston-engine aircraft), **basic** (minimal amenities for essential local access), and **unclassified** (limited operations without defined roles).[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1) This classification ensures balanced development across the aviation network, with categories influencing eligibility for Airport Improvement Program grants and safety certifications under 14 CFR Part 139.[[[2]](#ref-2)](#ref-2)

## Overview

### Purpose and Scope

[The Federal Aviation Administration](/page/Federal_Aviation_Administration) (FAA) establishes airport categories to fulfill its statutory responsibility under 49 U.S.C. § 47102 for developing and maintaining a safe, efficient, and integrated system of public-use airports that supports the national air transportation network. This categorization framework prioritizes safety by enforcing standardized infrastructure and operational protocols, enhances efficiency through optimized capacity and connectivity, and promotes accessibility to ensure equitable service for commercial, cargo, and [general aviation](/page/General_aviation) activities across the [United States](/page/United_States). By aligning with the Department of Transportation's goals of safety, economic strength, equity, climate stewardship, and operational excellence, the system guides infrastructure investments to meet evolving aviation demands while minimizing environmental impacts.[[[4]](#ref-4)](#ref-4)[[[5]](#ref-5)](#ref-5) The scope of FAA airport categories is explicitly limited to public-use airports documented in the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS), which identifies 3,287 existing facilities and projects 5 additional nonprimary airports by [fiscal year](/page/Fiscal_year) 2029, totaling 3,292 airports under the 2025–2029 planning period. Public-use airports, defined as those available for unrestricted access by the general public regardless of ownership, contrast sharply with the approximately 14,852 private-use airports that remain outside this framework unless they qualify for public designation based on [accessibility](/page/Accessibility) and service criteria. The NPIAS serves as the comprehensive federal blueprint for these airports, estimating development needs over a 20-year horizon while focusing on near-term priorities within the 5-year report cycle.[[[4]](#ref-4)](#ref-4)[[[5]](#ref-5)](#ref-5) Through categorization, the FAA influences key aspects of airport management, including eligibility for federal grants via the Airport Improvement Program (AIP) and Bipartisan Infrastructure Law funding, adherence to safety standards like runway safety areas and lighting, and operational requirements such as [aircraft rescue and firefighting](/page/Aircraft_rescue_and_firefighting) capabilities. This approach ensures targeted [resource allocation](/page/Resource_allocation) to sustain [infrastructure](/page/Infrastructure) integrity and public service without prescribing granular details on individual airport roles or metrics.[[[4]](#ref-4)](#ref-4)[[[5]](#ref-5)](#ref-5)

### Key Definitions and Legislation

The [Federal Aviation Administration](/page/Federal_Aviation_Administration) (FAA) defines a commercial service [airport](/page/Airport) as a publicly owned [airport](/page/Airport) in a state that has at least 2,500 passenger boardings (enplanements) each calendar year and receives scheduled passenger service.[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1) This definition, codified in 49 U.S.C. § 47102(7), distinguishes these airports from non-commercial facilities by emphasizing their role in scheduled air carrier operations.[[[6]](#ref-6)](#ref-6) A primary airport, in contrast, refers to a subset of commercial service airports that collectively account for 99 percent of the nation's annual passenger enplanements, with each individual primary [airport](/page/Airport) having at least 10,000 enplanements per year.[[[7]](#ref-7)](#ref-7) These airports are further subdivided by hub status—large, medium, small, or nonhub—based on their share of total U.S. enplanements, as outlined in 49 U.S.C. § 47102(16).[[[8]](#ref-8)](#ref-8) This categorization ensures that federal resources prioritize facilities handling the majority of commercial air traffic. The legislative foundation for FAA airport categorizations stems from the [Federal Aviation Act of 1958](/page/Federal_Aviation_Act_of_1958), which established the FAA as an independent agency to regulate [civil aviation](/page/Civil_aviation) safety and [airspace](/page/Airspace) use, laying the groundwork for standardized airport oversight.[[[9]](#ref-9)](#ref-9) Building on this, the Airport and Airway Improvement Act of 1982 (as amended) created the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS) and the Airport Improvement Program (AIP), mandating the inclusion of qualifying public-use airports in a national system based on their service levels and enplanement data to guide federal funding and development.[[[10]](#ref-10)](#ref-10) Terminology has evolved to better reflect diverse airport roles, particularly for general aviation facilities. In 2012, the FAA's report *General Aviation Airports: A National Asset* updated classifications by introducing categories such as national, regional, local, basic, and unclassified for nearly 3,000 [general aviation](/page/General_aviation) airports, using criteria like location, based aircraft, and operations to highlight their contributions beyond commercial service.[[[11]](#ref-11)](#ref-11) This framework refined earlier NPIAS groupings, emphasizing economic and community impacts without altering primary commercial definitions.[[[12]](#ref-12)](#ref-12)

## Primary Commercial Service Airports

### Hub Size Classifications

Primary commercial service airports, which account for at least 10,000 annual passenger enplanements, are further subdivided by the [Federal Aviation Administration](/page/Federal_Aviation_Administration) (FAA) into hub size categories based on their proportion of total U.S. commercial enplanements.[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1) These classifications help prioritize infrastructure investments, funding allocations, and planning within the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS).[[[8]](#ref-8)](#ref-8) The FAA recalculates these categories annually using certified enplanement data from the previous calendar year.[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1) As of calendar year 2023 data used in the 2025–2029 NPIAS, there are 31 large hubs, 33 medium hubs, 74 small hubs, and 252 nonhub primary airports, for a total of 390 primary commercial service airports.[[[13]](#ref-13)](#ref-13) The categories are defined as follows:

| Hub Category | Enplanement Threshold | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Large Hub | At least 1% of total U.S. annual enplanements (9,448,913 based on 944,891,353 total in 2023) | Represents major national and international gateways handling the highest traffic volumes. There are 31 such [airports](/page/List_of_airports_in_Armenia).[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1)[[[13]](#ref-13)](#ref-13) |
| Medium Hub | 0.25% to 0.999% of total U.S. annual enplanements (2,362,273 to 9,448,912 based on 2023 total) | Serves as regional connectors with significant but not dominant traffic. There are 33 such [airports](/page/List_of_airports_in_Armenia).[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1)[[[13]](#ref-13)](#ref-13) |
| Small Hub | 0.05% to 0.249% of total U.S. annual enplanements (472,445 to 2,362,272 based on 2023 total) | Focuses on local and regional service with moderate passenger volumes. There are 74 such [airports](/page/List_of_airports_in_Armenia).[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1)[[[13]](#ref-13)](#ref-13) |
| Nonhub Primary | At least 10,000 but less than 0.05% of total U.S. annual enplanements (10,000 to 472,444 based on 2023 total) | Includes smaller commercial [airports](/page/List_of_airports_in_Armenia) providing [essential air service](/page/Essential_Air_Service) to communities. There are 252 such [airports](/page/List_of_airports_in_Armenia).[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1)[[[13]](#ref-13)](#ref-13) |

Large hubs, such as Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) with 50,950,068 enplanements in 2023, dominate U.S. [air travel](/page/Air_travel) by facilitating extensive domestic and international connections.[[[14]](#ref-14)](#ref-14) In contrast, nonhub primary airports, like many regional facilities serving smaller populations, support localized commercial operations without qualifying as hubs.[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1) These distinctions ensure that FAA resources address varying operational scales while maintaining a balanced national airport network.[[[8]](#ref-8)](#ref-8)

### Criteria for Primary Designation

The designation of an airport as a primary commercial service airport by the [Federal Aviation Administration](/page/Federal_Aviation_Administration) (FAA) hinges on achieving at least 10,000 annual passenger enplanements, as defined under 49 U.S.C. § 47102(16).[[[15]](#ref-15)](#ref-15) This threshold ensures that primary airports collectively account for approximately 99 percent of all U.S. passenger enplanements, focusing federal resources on facilities handling the vast majority of commercial air traffic.[[[8]](#ref-8)](#ref-8) Enplanements are calculated as the total number of revenue passengers boarding [aircraft](/page/Aircraft) at the airport, including both originating passengers and those making connections or transfers, based on data reported by air carriers.[[[16]](#ref-16)](#ref-16) The FAA conducts an annual review to determine primary status, utilizing enplanement data submitted by U.S. air carriers through the Department of Transportation's Air Carrier Activity Information System, primarily derived from Form 41 reports.[[[17]](#ref-17)](#ref-17) To qualify, an [airport](/page/Airport) must also be publicly owned and receiving scheduled passenger air service, aligning with the statutory definition of a commercial service [airport](/page/Airport) under 49 U.S.C. § 47102(7), which requires a minimum of 2,500 annual enplanements for any commercial service designation.[[[15]](#ref-15)](#ref-15) This process allows for dynamic updates to [airport](/page/Airport) categories each year, reflecting changes in air traffic patterns and ensuring eligibility for Airport Improvement Program (AIP) funding and inclusion in the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS).[[[2]](#ref-2)](#ref-2) Historical adjustments to designations have responded to significant disruptions in [air travel](/page/Air_travel). Following the September 11, 2001, attacks, a sharp decline in passenger volumes led to several airports falling below the 10,000-enplanement threshold and losing primary status in subsequent annual reviews, illustrating the FAA's reliance on current-year [data](/page/Data) to adapt classifications amid traffic shifts.[[[17]](#ref-17)](#ref-17) During the [COVID-19 pandemic](/page/COVID-19_pandemic), the FAA temporarily mitigated similar risks by basing 2021 NPIAS classifications on 2019 enplanement [data](/page/Data) rather than the drastically reduced 2020 figures, preventing unwarranted demotions for airports affected by the crisis; this approach was extended through waivers and policy guidance from 2020 to 2022 to stabilize funding entitlements.[[[18]](#ref-18)](#ref-18) In contrast, non-primary commercial service airports maintain scheduled passenger service but record between 2,500 and [10,000](/page/10,000) annual enplanements, qualifying them for limited AIP support while excluding them from the full suite of primary designations.[[[15]](#ref-15)](#ref-15) Once designated as primary, airports may be further subdivided by hub size—such as large, medium, or non-hub—based on their share of national enplanements, though this scaling occurs separately from initial qualification.[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1)

## Non-Primary Airports

### Cargo Service Airports

Cargo service airports are public-use airports that, in addition to any other air transportation services that may be available, are served by [aircraft](/page/Aircraft) providing air transportation of only [cargo](/page/Cargo) with a total annual landed weight exceeding 100 million pounds. Landed weight refers to the weight of [aircraft](/page/Aircraft) transporting only [cargo](/page/Cargo) in intrastate, interstate, and foreign air transportation, as determined by FAA regulations. These airports support freight operations critical to national logistics, and an airport may simultaneously qualify as both a commercial service and a cargo service airport if it meets the respective criteria.[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1) Within the non-primary category, cargo service airports are those that fall below the 10,000 annual passenger enplanement threshold for primary designation but play a significant role in freight [logistics](/page/Logistics), often handling substantial volumes such as over 100 million pounds of [cargo](/page/Cargo) annually. These facilities focus on [cargo](/page/Cargo)-only operations without relying on passenger traffic, enabling efficient handling of goods for industries like [manufacturing](/page/Manufacturing) and distribution. For instance, Perot Field Fort Worth [Alliance](/page/Alliance) Airport (AFW) in [Texas](/page/Texas) exemplifies a non-primary cargo service airport, classified as [general aviation](/page/General_aviation) with minimal enplanements (1,628 passenger enplanements in 2021) yet ranking among the top 20 U.S. [cargo](/page/Cargo) airports by handling over 2.4 billion pounds of landed weight in 2021, primarily serving [FedEx](/page/FedEx) and other freight carriers.[[[19]](#ref-19)](#ref-19)[[[20]](#ref-20)](#ref-20) The criteria for cargo service airport designation are based on annual landed weight data collected through the FAA's Air Carrier Activity Information System (ACAIS), which aggregates reports from air carriers via Form 5100-108 for all-[cargo](/page/Cargo) operations. This excludes weights from passenger-cargo combination flights, focusing solely on dedicated freight aircraft to ensure the airport's primary purpose aligns with [cargo](/page/Cargo) handling. While many prominent [cargo](/page/Cargo) hubs like [Memphis International Airport](/page/Memphis_International_Airport) (MEM), FedEx's global superhub, and Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport (SDF), UPS's primary freight base, are classified as primary due to their passenger volumes alongside massive [cargo](/page/Cargo) throughput (MEM handled approximately 23 billion pounds in 2023), non-primary cargo service airports fill essential gaps in regional supply chains.[[[21]](#ref-21)](#ref-21)[[[22]](#ref-22)](#ref-22) These non-primary cargo service airports are increasingly vital amid e-commerce expansion, facilitating rapid distribution of goods across the U.S. In calendar year 2023, U.S. airports collectively processed nearly 199 billion pounds of all-cargo landed weight, underscoring the sector's scale and its support for just-in-time delivery models. Funding through the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS) aids infrastructure improvements at these airports to accommodate growing freight demands.[[[22]](#ref-22)](#ref-22)[[[2]](#ref-2)](#ref-2)

### Reliever and General Aviation Airports

Reliever airports are facilities designated by the [Federal Aviation Administration](/page/Federal_Aviation_Administration) (FAA) to alleviate congestion at commercial service airports by accommodating [general aviation](/page/General_aviation) traffic and enhancing community access to non-commercial air transportation.[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1) These airports play a critical role in distributing [general aviation](/page/General_aviation) operations away from busier hubs, thereby improving overall system efficiency and safety. The FAA has identified over 250 reliever airports as part of its efforts to manage [airspace](/page/Airspace) demands, with many located near major metropolitan areas.[[[23]](#ref-23)](#ref-23) A prominent example is [Teterboro Airport](/page/Teterboro_Airport) (TEB) in [New Jersey](/page/New_Jersey), which serves as a key reliever for the [New York City](/page/New_York_City) region by handling a high volume of business and private jet traffic.[[[24]](#ref-24)](#ref-24) General aviation (GA) encompasses the operation of civilian [aircraft](/page/Aircraft) for purposes other than scheduled commercial passenger or cargo transport, including personal, business, instructional, and recreational flying.[[[12]](#ref-12)](#ref-12) In [2012](/page/2012), the FAA classified GA airports into five categories—national, regional, local, basic, and unclassified—based on factors such as the number of based [aircraft](/page/Aircraft) (aircraft regularly stationed at the airport) and annual operations (takeoffs and landings). These classifications help prioritize [infrastructure](/page/Infrastructure) needs and [safety](/page/Safety) improvements for the diverse GA network. The criteria emphasize the airports' roles in supporting varying levels of activity, from [international business](/page/International_business) flights to local [training](/page/Training) and [emergency](/page/Emergency) services.

| Category | Key Criteria for Based Aircraft | Key Criteria for Operations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| National | More than 200 average based [aircraft](/page/Aircraft), including 11+ jets | At least 5,000 instrument operations; 20+ international flights; 500+ interstate departures |
| Regional | More than 90 average based [aircraft](/page/Aircraft), including 1+ jet | At least 1,000 instrument operations; 10+ domestic flights over 500 miles |
| [Local](/page/.local) | 15+ based [aircraft](/page/Aircraft) (average 37) | At least 10 instrument operations; 2,500+ passenger enplanements |
| Basic | 10+ based [aircraft](/page/Aircraft) or 4+ helicopters (average 10) | Not applicable; focused on location-specific roles like remote access or emergency support |
| Unclassified | Varies, often low or no based [aircraft](/page/Aircraft) | Varies, typically low activity requiring further assessment |

National GA airports, such as [Van Nuys Airport](/page/Van_Nuys_Airport) in [California](/page/California), handle high-intensity operations exceeding 100,000 annually and serve as gateways for long-distance and international GA flights. In contrast, local and basic GA airports, often exemplified by small municipal strips in rural areas, support community-level flying like [flight training](/page/Flight_training) and agricultural operations with more modest activity levels. Smaller GA airports are generally exempt from FAA Part 139 certification, which applies to larger commercial operations.[[[12]](#ref-12)](#ref-12) Within the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS), reliever and [general aviation](/page/General_aviation) airports form the majority of the roughly 3,300 included facilities, with all relievers and select GA airports prioritized for federal funding to enhance safety, runway conditions, and access for non-scheduled flights.[[[2]](#ref-2)](#ref-2) This focus ensures that GA infrastructure supports economic development, emergency response, and recreational [aviation](/page/Aviation) across the [United States](/page/United_States), representing over 90% of the nation's active [aircraft](/page/Aircraft).[[[12]](#ref-12)](#ref-12)

## Airport Certification Under Part 139

### Certification Classes

Under FAA regulations outlined in 14 CFR Part 139, airports are classified into four categories based on the types of air carrier operations they serve, particularly focusing on scheduled versus unscheduled passenger-carrying operations and the size of the [aircraft](/page/Aircraft) involved.[[[25]](#ref-25)](#ref-25) These classifications determine the scope of [certification](/page/Certification) requirements to ensure safety and operational standards for commercial air service. The system was refined in updates effective May 2, 2023, reclassifying existing certificated airports to better align with air carrier operation types and incorporating [safety management system](/page/Safety_management_system) (SMS) mandates for certain classes, impacting approximately 520 U.S. airports holding Airport Operating Certificates (AOCs).[[[26]](#ref-26)](#ref-26)[[[27]](#ref-27)](#ref-27) **Class I airports** serve scheduled operations of large air carrier [aircraft](/page/Aircraft), defined as those designed for 31 or more passenger seats, and may also accommodate unscheduled operations of large air carrier [aircraft](/page/Aircraft) or scheduled operations of small air carrier [aircraft](/page/Aircraft) (more than 9 but fewer than 31 passenger seats).[[[25]](#ref-25)](#ref-25) These airports, often major hubs like those handling domestic and international flights, must comply with the full spectrum of Part 139 standards, including comprehensive safety protocols. For example, Chicago O'Hare International Airport exemplifies a Class I facility due to its extensive scheduled large-carrier services.[[[26]](#ref-26)](#ref-26) **Class II airports** are certificated for scheduled operations of small air carrier [aircraft](/page/Aircraft) (10 to 30 seats) and unscheduled operations of large air carrier aircraft, but they do not serve scheduled large air carrier operations.[[[25]](#ref-25)](#ref-25) This class imposes heightened operational and safety requirements compared to prior limited [certification](/page/Certification) models, reflecting the mix of regular regional flights and occasional larger unscheduled arrivals. Airports in this category, such as many regional facilities in the Midwest, benefit from tailored standards that address their diverse traffic patterns without the full rigor applied to major hubs.[[[26]](#ref-26)](#ref-26) **Class III airports** are limited to scheduled operations of small air carrier [aircraft](/page/Aircraft) (10 to 30 seats) and do not serve any large air carrier operations, with exceptions for certain Alaskan airports.[[[25]](#ref-25)](#ref-25) These newly emphasized in the 2023 reclassification often include smaller commercial outlets serving commuter routes, requiring specific Part 139 compliance focused on essential safety measures like alternative [aircraft rescue and firefighting](/page/Aircraft_rescue_and_firefighting) options. An example is Tompkins Cortland Community Airport (ITH) in New York, which serves only scheduled small air carrier operations to regional destinations.[[[26]](#ref-26)](#ref-26) **Class IV airports** serve only unscheduled operations of large air carrier [aircraft](/page/Aircraft) (31 or more seats) and do not conduct scheduled large or small air carrier operations.[[[25]](#ref-25)](#ref-25) Due to the infrequent nature of these operations, such as [cargo](/page/Cargo) or [charter](/page/Charter) flights, Class IV airports maintain limited Part 139 requirements but include enhanced standards for handling occasional large-[aircraft](/page/Aircraft) arrivals. Facilities like those supporting ad-hoc [military](/page/Military) or private [charter](/page/Charter)s fall into this category, ensuring basic safety without overburdening low-volume sites.[[[26]](#ref-26)](#ref-26) This classification overlaps briefly with primary commercial service designations, where airports meeting passenger boarding thresholds may require certification regardless of class.[[[1]](#ref-1)](#ref-1)

### Requirements and Operations

All airports certificated under 14 CFR Part 139 must maintain an approved Airport Certification Manual (ACM) that outlines procedures for operations, maintenance, and safety compliance, serving as the foundational document for [certification](/page/Certification) adherence. This manual must be updated as needed and approved by the [Federal Aviation Administration](/page/Federal_Aviation_Administration) (FAA), ensuring standardized practices across certificated facilities. Additionally, all classes are required to implement [wildlife](/page/Wildlife) hazard management programs, including periodic assessments to identify and mitigate risks such as bird strikes, with plans developed if significant [hazards](/page/Hazard) are found. [Emergency](/page/Emergency) planning is mandatory for every certificated airport, requiring a comprehensive Airport [Emergency](/page/Emergency) Plan that addresses incidents like [aircraft](/page/Aircraft) accidents, hazardous material spills, and natural disasters, with regular training and exercises to ensure readiness. Class-specific operational requirements under Part 139 emphasize varying levels of safety infrastructure based on airport scale and traffic. For Classes I and II airports, which handle larger commercial operations, aircraft rescue and firefighting (ARFF) capabilities must meet Indices A through E, determined by the longest aircraft served and average daily departures; for example, Index C requires at least 1,500 pounds of extinguishing agents and response times within three minutes to any runway point. In contrast, Classes III and IV airports, serving smaller operations, are limited to ARFF Index A, providing basic firefighting resources like 500 pounds of dry chemical agents, with allowances for pre-arranged mutual aid agreements to achieve equivalent safety where on-site capabilities are limited. These distinctions ensure resources are scaled appropriately, prioritizing higher-risk environments at larger hubs. Compliance and inspection protocols reinforce operational standards, with certificated airports conducting daily self-inspections of [runways](/page/Runway), [taxiways](/page/Taxiway), and safety areas to detect hazards like debris or lighting failures, maintaining records for at least 12 months. The FAA performs annual audits and unannounced [inspections](/page/Inspection) to verify adherence, including evaluations of runway safety areas—which must be cleared, graded, and drivable by rescue vehicles—and marking standards such as illuminated runway thresholds and taxiway edge lights tailored to the airport's class and night operations. Many [general aviation](/page/General_aviation) (GA) and reliever airports operate without Part 139 certification if they do not meet the enplanement thresholds for air carrier service, such as fewer than 2,500 annual passenger boardings, allowing them to forgo these rigorous standards while adhering to basic FAA safety guidelines. Exemptions may also apply to certain remote or small aircraft-focused facilities, like those in [Alaska](/page/Alaska) serving only aircraft under 12,500 pounds, provided equivalent safety measures are in place. Following the 2023 amendment to Part 139, certificated airports must now implement Safety Management Systems (SMS) to proactively identify and mitigate risks, with phased rollouts completed by 2026 for most facilities; this framework integrates existing requirements like [wildlife management](/page/Wildlife_management) and emergency planning into a broader risk-based approach.[[[28]](#ref-28)](#ref-28) The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (P.L. 118-63) directs the FAA to update Part 139 regulations to require small, medium, and large hub airports to have at least one [emergency medical technician](/page/Emergency_medical_technician) (EMT) on duty during air carrier operations. As of November 2025, the FAA is in the process of rulemaking to implement this EMT requirement, expected to enhance on-site medical response at certificated hub airports. The Act also addresses broader aviation threats, including cybersecurity vulnerabilities and integration of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) through separate FAA programs and updated detection and mitigation policies.[[[29]](#ref-29)](#ref-29)[[[30]](#ref-30)](#ref-30)
