SUMMARY:
<summary>
On 15 July 2026, ACI World released the 2026 ACI World Airport Traffic Dataset, confirming global air travel reached 9.8 billion passengers in 2025, approaching the 10 billion threshold. The dataset covers 2,817 airports across more than 180 countries and territories, showing global passenger traffic rose 3.7% over 2024 and 6.5% above 2019 levels. The world's 20 busiest airports handled 1.59 billion passengers (16% of global travelers).

Asia-Pacific airports led ranking shifts. Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KUL) was the biggest mover, rising from 26th to 20th place with 63.4 million passengers (+11% YoY). Shanghai Pudong (PVG) climbed from 10th to 5th with 84.9 million passengers (+10.7%), driven by visa policy easing and China's aviation market reopening. Guangzhou Baiyun (CAN) fell to 57th in 2022 after topping the table in 2020, but returned to 9th in 2025.

Atlanta (ATL) retained the No. 1 position with 106.3 million passengers despite a 1.6% decline. Dubai (DXB, 95.2 million, +3.1%) held second and Tokyo Haneda (HND, 91.7 million, +6.7%) third, both closing the gap on Atlanta. Five of the top 20 airports are US-based, mostly domestic hubs (80-95% domestic traffic), with LAX the exception at 68% domestic.

Global air cargo exceeded 131 million metric tonnes in 2025, up 3.3% YoY and 7.4% above 2019, driven by e-commerce and supply chain restructuring. Memphis (MEM) dropped from 3rd to 6th after losing the US Postal Service contract, with volumes falling 20.9%.

Global aircraft movements exceeded 103.1 million in 2025, up 2.0%, nearing pre-2019 levels. Chicago O'Hare (ORD) claimed the top spot with 857,000 movements (+10.5%), displacing Atlanta (ATL) which had led since 2020. Dallas/Fort Worth (DFW) held 3rd with 743,000 movements.

URL: https://dwuconsulting.com/dwu-ai/eas

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This DWU AI article (April 2026) analyzes the FY2027 budget proposal to eliminate Essential Air Service (EAS), a program that has been continuously funded since its creation in the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 (49 U.S.C. §§ 41731–41746) — now 48 years old, despite being characterized as "temporary" by Congress. 

**Program Overview:** DOT subsidizes air carriers to provide minimum service (typically two round trips daily with 30-50 seat aircraft) to eligible communities connecting to large/medium hubs. As of fall 2024, DOT subsidized 65 Alaskan communities and 112 in the contiguous 48 states, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico, with total reach cited as 177 communities across all states plus Puerto Rico (as of Oct 2025). Eligibility requires averaging at least 10 enplanements per service day (~3,650/year), unless located more than 175 driving miles from a hub. Per-passenger subsidy caps: $1,000 (decreasing to $850 effective Oct 1, 2026, under FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024) for communities 175+ miles from a hub; $650 for those closer. Alaska and Hawaii are exempt from distance criteria and caps.

**Carriers:** Four carriers hold ~41% of the program's ~$512 million in annual contracts: SkyWest ($84.7M), Contour ($58.3M), Southern Airways/Mokulele ($48.1M), Alaska Airlines ($17.1M for five Southeast Alaska routes). JetBlue ($10.4M) and Breeze ($8.0M) each held one contract in FY2024.

**Costs:** Per-passenger subsidies range from $6.26 (Joplin, MO) to $1,905 (Lewistown, MT, serving Billings). For 38 lower-48 communities within 150 miles of a hub, average all-in round trip cost was $427, with federal subsidies covering 46%.

**Geographic Distribution:** Alaska accounts for 65 of 177 communities (37%), including communities with no road access (e.g., Adak, Petersburg, Gustavus). Michigan hosted 9 airports (most in lower 48) at $17.6M total cost. 104 of 177 EAS airports are designated Economic Development Areas (EDAs) for FY2025.

**FY2027 Budget Proposal:** Released April 3, 2026, the White House proposal eliminates $372 million of discretionary EAS funding, citing "out of control" spending and "half-empty" flights. It would set discretionary appropriations at $142M plus ~$174M in mandatory overflight fee revenue (under 49 U.S.C. §41742(b)), totaling ~$316M — a ~54% reduction from FY2026's ~$688M.

**Historical Pattern:** Congress has rejected every EAS cut proposal since 1978. The FY2026 budget (released May 2, 2025) proposed a $308M cut (~52%); Congress rejected it and enacted $514M in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (Feb 3, 2026), with language preventing abrupt contract termination. The House Appropriations Committee stated this protected service to 56 communities the budget would have eliminated. Both Obama and first-term Trump administrations proposed EAS cuts that Congress consistently rejected; funding levels have varied and individual communities were removed for failing thresholds, but the program has never been eliminated through appropriations.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Wikipedia article on the Essential Air Service (EAS), a U.S. government program enacted to guarantee that small communities previously served by certificated airlines prior to deregulation in 1978 maintain commercial air service. The program aims to maintain a minimal level of scheduled air service to communities that would otherwise not be profitable.

Key facts:
- The program is codified at 49 U.S.C. §§ 41731–41748, administered by the U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT), which subsidizes airlines to serve communities that would not otherwise receive scheduled air service.
- As of June 1, 2015, 159 communities in the US received EAS subsidies: 44 in Alaska, two in Hawaii, and one in Puerto Rico.
- Subsidy levels have increased substantially over time. As of October 2024, program subsidies amounted to $550 million. EAS subsidies have increased by more than 500% since 1997.
- The George W. Bush Administration sought to reduce program costs to $50 million via stricter eligibility criteria and local cost-sharing requirements.

Community eligibility criteria:
- Per the Appropriations Act of 2000, no community within the contiguous 48 states may receive a subsidy greater than $200 per passenger unless the community is more than 210 miles from the nearest large or medium hub airport.
- Per the FAA Modernization and Reform Act of 2012, eligible communities in the contiguous 48 states must either maintain an average of 10 or more enplanements per service day or be located more than 175 miles from the nearest large or medium hub airport (the enplanement requirement can be waived annually by the Secretary of Transportation for temporary declines).
- Pursuant to the Consolidated and Further Appropriations Act of 2015, USDOT must negotiate a local cost share with communities located less than 40 miles from a small hub airport.

Controversy:
- Critics question the economic and environmental efficiency of the service.
- According to a 2006 New York Times article, the subsidy per passenger averaged approximately $74 across the program (excluding Alaska), with some poorly patronized flights receiving subsidies as high as $801 per passenger.
- The program is politically popular in receiving cities, which use scheduled airport service as an economic development selling point, though several subsidized airports are within an hour's drive of an unsubsidized airport.

Denver Air Connection), Cape Air, JetBlue, and American Airlines Group. --- SOURCE 8: Essential Air Service | US Department of Transportation ---
URL: https://www.transportation.gov/policy/aviation-policy/small-community-rural-air-service/essential-air-service

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an official U.S. Department of Transportation webpage providing comprehensive information about the Essential Air Service (EAS) program. The EAS program was established by section 419 of the Federal Aviation Act following the Airline Deregulation Act (ADA) of 1978, which removed federal control over fares, routes, and market entry. The program guarantees that communities served by certificated air carriers before deregulation maintain a minimum level of scheduled air service, typically subsidizing two round trips daily with 30- to 50-seat aircraft to large- or medium-hub airports. As of Fall 2024, the Department provides EAS subsidies to 65 communities in Alaska and 112 communities in the 48 contiguous states, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico.

The Civil Aeronautics Board managed the program until January 1, 1985, when the Department of Transportation assumed responsibility. The program, initially authorized for ten years, is now permanently authorized by Congress.

Community eligibility is outlined in 49 U.S.C. § 41731. To remain eligible, communities must maintain an average of 10 enplanements per service day during the most recent fiscal year, though communities more than 175 driving miles from the nearest large or medium hub airport are exempt. EAS communities less than 175 miles from a hub must have an average subsidy per passenger of less than $650, while those farther away must have an average subsidy of less than $1,000 (reduced to $850 effective October 1, 2026). These subsidy requirements do not apply to Alaska and Hawaii. Waivers may be granted for temporary demand declines, but starting October 1, 2026, waivers cannot be provided for more than two consecutive fiscal years or more than five fiscal years within 25 consecutive years. Eligibility criteria were amended in the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (Pub L. No. 118-63, May 16, 2024).

The carrier selection process involves the Department issuing a Request for Proposals (RFP) to all air carriers, with proposals submitted on a sealed "best and final" basis. Under 49 U.S.C. § 41733(c)(1), selection factors include demonstrated reliability, code-share/interline arrangements with larger carriers, community preferences (including views of elected officials), marketing plans, and for Alaska, prior experience providing scheduled air service. Contracts generally run two to four years. Carriers are compensated in arrears on a per-flight-completed basis, with monthly invoices detailing actual service, and only completed flights (take-off and landing at destination) are generally eligible for subsidy. Contact information for the EAS and Domestic Analysis Division is provided, and a list of eligible communities is available at the DOT website.
</summary>

URL: https://www.taxpayer.net/transportation-infrastructure/essential-air-service-illustrating-coming-changes-to-the-program

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Taxpayers for Common Sense (TCS), a nonpartisan government watchdog, analyzes the Essential Air Service (EAS) program and the impact of changes made by the 2012 federal air program reauthorization. The EAS is a federal subsidy program created in the 1970s during airline deregulation that was intended to be temporary but now costs taxpayers over $200 million annually to guarantee air service for 117 communities. 

Following the 2012 reauthorization, new eligibility rules were established for subsidized service: communities must be 90+ miles from a medium/large hub, average 10+ daily enplanements (unless 175+ miles from a hub), require a subsidy under $1,000 per passenger, and have received subsidized service between September 30, 2010 and September 30, 2011. These rules, particularly the fourth requirement, reduced eligible communities from 480 (originally after deregulation) to 121, with 117 currently receiving service.

To date, only Ely, Nevada has lost service due to the new requirements (it had the highest per-passenger subsidy at $3,720). Nine communities are identified as at risk for having fewer than 3,650 annual enplanements while within 175 miles of a hub (including Jamestown, NY; Merced, CA; Bradford, PA; Athens, GA; Franklin/Oil City, PA; Jonesboro, AR; Kingman, AZ; Macon, GA; and Jackson, TN). Three communities require subsidies over $1,000 per passenger (Lewistown, MT at $1,904.79; Miles City, MT at $1,372.10; and Jackson, TN at $1,187.71), with Lewistown and Miles City slated for service termination.

TCS argues these changes would only save $17 million (less than 10% of the program), which could be wiped out by rapid cost escalation. The organization calls for complete elimination of the EAS program, noting bipartisan support for elimination in the House and a Washington Post editorial board endorsement of zeroing out the program. TCS maintains the program has long outlived its intended purpose.
</summary>

Require a subsidy of less than $1,000 per passenger. 4. Have received subsidized air service between September 30, 2010 and September 30, 2011."

--- SOURCE 10: [PDF] How does the federal government subsidize air service to small ... ---
URL: https://enotrans.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Eno-Aviation-Insights-Question-10.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Eno Center for Transportation Aviation Insight (No. 10, January 31, 2018) explains how the federal government subsidizes air service to small communities through the Essential Air Service (EAS) program. Congress established EAS in 1979 during airline deregulation to subsidize flights to the smallest airports. The program was initially intended to last 10 years but was extended in perpetuity in 1996, and costs have risen significantly since then. With approximately 300 communities receiving subsidized service (of 746 originally eligible), the program distributes roughly $270 million per year.

Key statistics: The busiest EAS airport (Joplin, Missouri) averages fewer than 160 passengers per day, while some airports have fewer than a dozen daily departing passengers. Per-passenger subsidies vary dramatically—from close to zero to several hundred dollars. During FY2016, the highest per-passenger subsidy was Altoona, Pennsylvania at $642 per passenger (3,693 total passengers). McCook, Nebraska had the highest overall subsidy at $778 per passenger.

Program constraints and enforcement issues: Congress imposed limitations including a 70-mile minimum distance from a medium/large hub, a minimum of 10 daily enplanements, and caps on per-passenger subsidies ($200 for communities within 210 miles of a hub, $1,000 for others). U.S. DOT enforced the $200 cap from 1990-2006, causing 39 communities to lose service, but stopped enforcement in 2006. Although DOT announced resumed enforcement in 2014, 26 airports remained above the $200 threshold in FY2016. Since 2006, only one airport has lost service due to the $200 rule, but eight airports lost service due to the $1,000 cap since 2012.

Potential savings and context: Options to reduce EAS costs include increasing the minimum distance requirement, enforcing the per-passenger cap, and enforcing minimum enplanements. A scenario combining a 150-mile minimum distance, the $200 cap, and 10-daily-enplanement enforcement would only save $114.3 million. Notably, the EAS program represents less than two percent of the $16 billion in annual federal aviation spending. The Trump administration's initial 2018 budget proposed cutting the program entirely before settling on a 50 percent reduction. U.S. DOT's criteria for adding new communities include reliability, connections with larger hubs, and community views—but notably do not include cost.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Enplanements: FAA Definition, Meaning & Airport Data ---
URL: https://dwuconsulting.com/dwu-ai/enplaned-passengers

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Enplanements: FAA Definition, Meaning & Airport Data

This is a DWU AI reference guide (July 2026) examining enplaned passenger definitions, classifications, and reporting across federal data systems (T-100, DB1B/DB1C, FAA Air Carrier Activity Information System/ACAIS, and airport-reported sources). Enplaned passengers — passengers boarding aircraft at an airport — are the primary traffic metric in U.S. airport finance, driving AIP grant apportionment (49 USC §47114), hub classification, PFC collections (49 USC §40117), and cost per enplaned passenger (CPE) calculations.

### Key Facts & Definitions
- **Enplanement definition:** One passenger boarding one aircraft at an airport. For federal purposes (T-100/ACAIS), enplanements principally count revenue passengers. Example: A traveler boarding in Atlanta, connecting in Dallas, and deplaning in LA generates two revenue enplanements (ATL and DFW).
- **Revenue vs. nonrevenue:** Revenue passengers are those for whom the carrier receives commercial remuneration (paid tickets, loyalty redemptions, corporate discounts, vouchers, barter). Nonrevenue passengers include airline employees, pass interchange passengers, FAM trips, air marshals, NTSB/FAA investigators, disaster relief personnel. T-100 and FAA ACAIS report revenue passengers only; airport reports often include both, causing 1–5% discrepancies.
- **Round trips:** A round trip generates two enplanements — one at each boarding airport.

### Reporting Systems
- **T-100:** 100% census of revenue passenger boardings (14 CFR Part 241 for U.S. carriers; Part 217 for foreign carriers). Answers "how many passengers boarded at this airport."
- **DB1B/DB1C (DB1C effective Q2 2024):** 10% sample of domestic airline tickets capturing full origin-destination itineraries; used for O&D vs. connecting analysis and market-share/fare studies. Not to be summed with T-100.
- **ACAIS:** Publishes official annual enplanement totals (T-100 plus Air Taxi survey data) for hub classification and AIP entitlements.
- **FAA Form 5100-127** line 16.1 collects airport's total fiscal-year enplanements (including nonrevenue), tracked in the Compliance Activity Tracking System (CATS).

### Passenger Classifications (Three Independent Ways)
1. **Revenue vs. Nonrevenue** (detailed categories listed above)
2. **O&D vs. Connecting:** O&D passengers begin/end trips at the airport, generating stronger non-aeronautical revenue (parking, rental car, ground transportation). Connecting passengers generate less of this revenue; concession spend depends on layover/terminal design. O&D further segmented into Visitor (home outside catchment) vs. Resident (home within catchment) — a local market-study convention, not federal reporting.
3. **International vs. Domestic:** International passengers generate additional fees and CBP processing requirements.

### Hub Classification
FAA classifies airports by share of total U.S. commercial enplanements into four categories: Large Hub (≥1.00%), Medium Hub (0.25%–0.999%), Small Hub (0.05%–0.249%), Non-Hub (<0.05%). Under CY 2024 data, the U.S. has 31 large hubs and 32 medium hubs (63 L/M total). Hub class determines AIP entitlement funding.

### PFC Details
PFC collections are capped at $4.50 per chargeable passenger (14 CFR Part 158, §158.9 exclusions include nonrevenue passengers and frequent-flier award coupons). PFC authority extends to all commercial service airports regardless of hub class.

### 2025–2026 Updates
- Preliminary indicators suggest 2025 U.S. airport passenger traffic approached or exceeded 2019 levels; FAA released preliminary CY2025 data June 26, 2026; final data expected late August 2026.
- FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-63, Section 712) revised AIP apportionment formulas affecting non-primary commercial and GA airports.
- DCA received 10 additional daily slot exemptions (five slot pairs) awarded by DOT December 2024.
- EWR operations capped at 72 hourly operations (36 arrivals + 36 departures) through October 30, 2027.

### Why Airport Data Disagrees with FAA Data
Four sources: (1) scope (system vs. terminal/authority reporting); (2) nonrevenue inclusion; (3) timing (airport data in weeks vs. FAA lag of 2–3 months); (4) audit/reconciliation adjustments. FAA CY 2024 Passenger Boarding Data (ACAIS) is the apples-to-apples comparison source.

### Data Sources
FAA passenger boarding data at faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/passenger_allcargo_stats/; DWU Consulting maintains T-100 and monthly traffic dashboards at dwuconsulting.com/info/data/t100 and /info/data/monthly-traffic.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"An enplanement is one passenger boarding one aircraft at an airport. For federal regulatory purposes (FAA Passenger Boarding data / ACAIS, and the underlying T-100 traffic data), enplanements principally count revenue passengers — those for whom the carrier receives commercial remuneration."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Airport Categories | Federal Aviation Administration ---
URL: https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/categories

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) webpage from the U.S. Department of Transportation that explains airport categories as defined by law. It identifies approximately 14,400 private-use (closed to the public) and 5,000 public-use (open to the public) airports, heliports, and seaplane bases in the United States. About 3,300 of these public-use facilities are included in the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS) and may be considered for Airport Improvement Program (AIP) funding.

The law categorizes airports by type of activities, including:
- **Commercial Service**: Publicly owned airports with at least 2,500 annual enplanements and scheduled air carrier service. Primary airports (with more than 10,000 annual enplanements) are further classified by hub size: Large Hub (1%+ of annual U.S. commercial enplanements), Medium Hub (0.25-1.0%), Small Hub (0.05-0.25%), Nonhub (less than 0.05% but more than 10,000 enplanements), and Nonprimary Commercial Service Nonhub (2,500-10,000 annual enplanements with scheduled passenger service).
- **Reliever**: Designated by the Secretary of Transportation to relieve congestion at commercial service airports and provide general aviation access to the community.
- **General Aviation**: A public-use airport without scheduled service or with scheduled service of less than 2,500 passenger boardings each year.

The FAA also developed five categories for airports serving general aviation (based on their role in the system): National (support access to national/international markets with high levels of jet and multiengine activity), Regional (connect communities to regional/national markets in metropolitan areas), Local (provide access to markets within a State/region, mostly piston aircraft), Basic (links communities to the national airport system with minimal infrastructure, often a single runway or helipad), and Unclassified (in NPIAS with limited activity).

Contact information: Federal Aviation Administration, 800 Independence Avenue, SW, Washington, DC 20591, phone 866.835.5322 (866-TELL-FAA). The criteria are detailed in FAA Order 5090.5 and Appendix C of the Current Published NPIAS.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A June 2026 Government Accountability Office (GAO) report reveals that smaller communities (nonhub airports, handling more than 10,000 annual passenger boardings but less than 0.05% of total U.S. commercial traffic) experienced a 19% decline in average daily departures per route between 2018 and 2024. Over 70% of nonhub airports not receiving Essential Air Service (EAS) support suffered departure losses, while EAS subsidy costs rose 31% from 2018 to 2023.

The decline stems from structural pressures in regional aviation, including pilot and maintenance workforce supply challenges, increased airline operating costs, and heightened airline expectations for revenue guarantees. The Small Community Air Service Development Program (SCASDP) has become less effective as operating costs rise faster than grant amounts can offset.

Stakeholders identified several potential solutions: increasing the aviation workforce supply, supporting other transportation modes (e.g., bus service), supporting new technologies (e.g., electric aircraft), focusing EAS assistance on more remote communities, expanding EAS, and modifying SCASDP. In April 2026, the GAO recommended that the FAA establish and publicly communicate timelines for finalizing two pilot training initiatives provided for in statute; the Department of Transportation agreed with these recommendations. The DOT administers federal programs providing subsidies and grants to help eligible small communities retain a link to the national aviation system.
</summary>

Primary airports must have scheduled commercial airline service with more than 10,000 annual passenger enplanements and comprise less than 15 percent of NPIAS airports (just under 400 airports). They are subdivided into large, medium, small, and nonhub categories based on enplanepercentage compared to national totals. --- SOURCE 8: Beginners’ Guide to Public-Use Airport Classification ---
URL: https://www.globalair.com/articles/beginners-guide-to-public-use-airport-classification/3796

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published by GlobalAir.com (a press release dated Sep. 1, 2016, updated Mar. 10, 2021), serves as a beginner's guide to how the FAA classifies public-use airports in the United States, based on the author's experience taking an Airport Management course. The FAA has recognized public-use airports eligible for federal funding since 1970 through the National Airport Systems Plan (NASP), which included approximately 3,200 airports. In 1982, the Airport and Airway Act led to the creation of the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS), which included 3,411 airports as of 2008. The article breaks down the main NPIAS airport classifications:

**1. Primary Airports** – Public-use airports enplaning at least 10,000 passengers annually. This accounts for less than 3 percent of the nation's total airports, with only 383 airports in this category in 2008.

**2. Commercial Service Airports** – Any airport accommodating scheduled air carrier service by a certified airline. Of the 770 million passengers who flew in the US in 2009, practically all went through commercial service airports. The FAA recognized 522 such airports in 2008.

**3. General Aviation (GA) Airports** – Airports with fewer than 2,500 annual enplaned passengers, or those used exclusively by private business aircraft not providing commercial passenger service. Though over 13,000 airports technically fit this description, only those in the NPIAS are counted; there is usually at least one GA airport in the NPIAS per county, and airports with more than 10 based aircraft located more than 20 miles from the nearest NPIAS airport are also included. A total of 2,564 airports held this classification in 2008.

**4. Reliever Airports** – Designated as "general aviation airports that provide relief to congested major airports." To qualify, an airport must have at least 100 airplanes based there or handle 25,000 itinerant operations.

Primary Airports also have subcategories based on annual enplaned passengers (note: the NPIAS hub definition differs from the airline industry's):
- **Large hubs**: at least 1% of total annual passenger enplanements (30 airports in 2008, handling 70% of all US passenger enplanements)
- **Medium hubs**: between 0.25% and 1% of annual enplanements (37 airports in 2008)
- **Small hubs**: between 0.05% and 0.25% of annual enplanements (72 airports in 2008)
- **Nonhubs**: more than 10,000 annual enplanements but less than 0.05% of the annual total

The author encourages readers to look up their favorite airports to see what hub type they fall under and whether they are classified as primary or commercial service.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 9: The National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS) and the Airports Capital Improvement Plan (ACIP), Next Generation Air Transportation System (NextGen), Airport Improve Program (AIP ) grants for AWOS – Mesotech International ---
URL: https://mesotech.com/pages/npias-acip-nextgen-awos

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Mesotech International, a manufacturer of Automated Weather Observing Systems (AWOS), explains how airports can secure Federal funding for AWOS systems by understanding federal programs. In September 2019, the Federal government combined the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS) and the Airports Capital Improvement Plan (ACIP) into a single order (Order 5090.5), making ACIP a subset of NPIAS and the primary financial planning tool for the Airport Improvement Program (AIP).

Key context: Weather caused over 69% of delays exceeding 15 minutes between 2008-2013, totaling over 10 million lost minutes in 2013 alone. An hour-long delay costs air carriers between $1,400 and $4,500 depending on aircraft class, plus $35/hour for personal travelers and $63/hour for business travelers.

**NPIAS**: Identifies over 3,000 existing and proposed airports in the National Airspace System. Only airports listed in NPIAS qualify for AIP grants. To qualify, airports must be open to the public and publicly owned, or privately owned but designated as a reliever or with scheduled service and at least 2,500 annual enplanements. The most recent NPIAS publication (released September 30, 2022, covering 2023-2027) includes 3,287 existing airports and 8 proposed airports, with $62.4 billion in AIP-eligible projects (a 43% increase, or nearly $19 billion, from two years prior). Of these, 98% (3,232) are publicly owned. Bringing aging airports up to modern FAA design standards accounts for 20% of anticipated funding needs (~$12.4 billion), including weather reporting equipment like AWOS for NextGen compliance.

**ACIP**: An internal FAA document produced annually by the Airport Improvement Program Branch, based on reports from nine Regional Offices (New England, Eastern, Southern, Great Lakes, Southwest, Northwest Mountain, Western-Pacific, and Alaskan Regions). It prioritizes critical airport development and serves as the criteria for AIP grant distribution. Projects must qualify under both AIP guidelines and NPIAS-ACIP criteria.

**NextGen**: Initiated in 2007 by the FAA, this modernization program aims to increase safety, efficiency, capacity, and resilience of the NAS, reduce aviation's environmental impact, and manage air traffic through Trajectory Based Operations. All major components are planned to be in place by 2025. The NextGen Weather Program predicts that more accurate weather data could prevent as many as 2/3 of weather delays and cancellations.

**CSS-Wx**: The Common Support Services – Weather program will be the single provider of weather data within the NAS, with sensors inputting data from AWOS and ASOS systems via the Weather Messaging Switching Center Replacement (WMSCR). The NextGen Weather Processor centrally produces weather products for dissemination. The program was scheduled for operation in 2023 and offers benefits including consistent weather information, increased NAS weather access, and reduced interface/development/infrastructure costs.

The article concludes that purchasing, upgrading, or replacing an AWOS system meets the development category criteria for the 2023-2027 NPIAS and is eligible for AIP grants. Mesotech's Airport Weather Advisor® product has over 25 years of experience and services all USAF fixed weather base systems.

This webpage is Chapter 4 of the FAA's Airport Improvement Program (AIP) Handbook, titled "What AIP funding is available?" It details the legal, structural, and procedural framework governing AIP grant funding for airports.

Key sections covered:

**Legislative Basis (4-1):** The FAA needs both an authorization (the FAA Bill/Reauthorization passed by Congress, defining annual funding levels and giving contract authority) and an annual appropriation (the annual Congress budget) to issue AIP grants. At publication, AIP operated under the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2018 (Public Law 115-141).

**Funding Source (4-2):** AIP funding comes from the Airport and Airway Trust Fund, created by the Airport and Airway Revenue Act of 1970, authorized by 49 USC § 48103 and 26 USC § 9502(c).

**Timing (4-3):** Passenger boardings, entitlements, and cargo landed weight are calculated based on the prior calendar year (e.g., FY 2014 uses calendar year 2012 data).

**AIP Funding Categories (4-4):** Table 4-1 details 12 fund types with calculations differing based on whether AIP funding is below or at/above $3.2 billion annually, including:
- Passenger Entitlement (per enplanement rates from $0.50 to $15.60 depending on threshold; annual minimum $650K-$1M, maximum $22M-$26M)
- Cargo Entitlement (3.5% of total AIP, pro-rated by landed cargo weight)
- Nonprimary Entitlement and State Apportionment
- Alaska Supplemental ($10.67M or $21.35M)
- Small Airport Fund (a calculation, not a set-aside fund)
- Discretionary including Noise/Environmental Set Aside (35% of discretionary, max $300M), MAP Set Aside (4%), Reliever Set Aside (0.66%), C/S/S/N (75%), Pure Discretionary (25%), and Discretionary from Converted Entitlements.

**Airport Types and Eligibility (4-5):** Only public-use NPIAS airports are eligible. Table 4-3 classifies airports into large hub, medium hub, small hub, nonhub primary, three virtual primary scenarios, nonprimary commercial service, general aviation, reliever, and privately-owned public use categories, each with its own funding eligibility.

**Fund Usage Restrictions (4-6, 4-7):** Tables 4-4 and 4-5 specify which airports can use each fund type and which project types are restricted (e.g., terminal buildings, parking lots, revenue-producing facilities generally not allowed; various exceptions apply).

**Fund Expiration (4-8):** Table 4-6 outlines expiration: primary hub airports have 3-year fund life (2 additional years), nonhub primary and nonprimary airports have 4-year life, state apportionment/Alaska supplemental have 3 years, and discretionary funds expire after 1 year.

**Federal Share (4-9):** Table 4-7 details federal cost share by airport type, with a normal 75% share for large/medium hubs, and exceptions including 80% for noise projects, up to 90% in states with large public land amounts and insular areas, a 90% share for two fiscal years after small-to-medium hub transitions, 70% for the private ownership pilot program, and 50% for zero emission pilot projects.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage contains the full text of Title 49, Subtitle VII, Part B, Chapter 471 (AIRPORT DEVELOPMENT), Subchapter I (AIRPORT IMPROVEMENT) of the United States Code, specifically covering sections 47101 through 47106. It is hosted on GovRegs, a U.S. Code reference site, with navigation and a table of contents listing sections 47101 through 47146 of Chapter 471.

**§ 47101 (Policies):** Establishes the federal policy that safe airport and airway system operation is the highest aviation priority. Key policies include: minimizing noise impacts on communities, giving special emphasis to developing reliever airports, facilitating cargo hub airports, encouraging intermodal connections, promoting airport projects that increase capacity, ensuring fees are reasonable and airports are self-sustaining (without creating surpluses beyond airport needs), converting former military air bases to civil use, and encouraging innovative technology (including in-pavement lighting and runway incursion prevention devices). It also establishes a National Transportation Policy goal of developing a national intermodal transportation system, and addresses capacity expansion/noise abatement (reducing noncompatible land uses), consistency with air commerce and safety policies, adequacy of navigation aids, maximum use of safety facilities (including electronic/visual vertical guidance on runways, grooving/friction treatment, precision approach systems, runway incursion prevention devices, etc.), and intermodal planning (requiring coordination with state and local officials, and consultation with the Secretary of the Interior and EPA on projects significantly affecting natural resources). Last amended by Pub. L. 118-63, May 16, 2024.

**§ 47102 (Definitions):** Defines key terms including: "air carrier," "airport" (includes heliports), "airport development" (extensive list of eligible activities including constructing/repairing airports, acquiring navigation aids, safety/security equipment, snow removal equipment, aircraft deicing equipment, terminal development, zero-emission vehicle conversions, power supply reliability improvements, natural disaster resilience improvements, cybersecurity compliance, unleaded aviation fuel infrastructure, and hydrogen fueling systems), "airport hazard," "airport planning," "commercial service airport" (at least 2,500 passenger boardings/year with scheduled service), "general aviation airport," "large hub airport" (≥1.0% of passenger boardings), "medium hub airport" (0.25%-1.0%), "small hub airport" (0.05%-0.25%), "nonhub airport" (<0.05%), "primary airport" (>10,000 boardings/year), "public airport," "public-use airport," "reliever airport," "passenger boardings," "sponsor," "State," and "terminal development."

**§ 47103 (National plan of integrated airport systems):** Requires the Secretary of Transportation to maintain "the national plan of integrated airport systems," which shall include the kind and estimated cost of eligible airport development needed for a safe, efficient, integrated system. The plan must meet civil aeronautics needs, national defense requirements, and USPS needs, and be published every 2 years. The Secretary of Defense must make domestic military airports available for civil use to the extent possible. Also requires a detailed statement listing airports not in compliance with grant assurances (with circumstances, timeline, and corrective actions).

**§ 47104 (Project grant authority):** Authorizes the Secretary to make project grants from the Airport and Airway Trust Fund to maintain a safe and efficient nationwide system of public-use airports. Obligations may be incurred as amounts are apportioned under section 47114. This grant authority expires after September 30, 2028, except for certain remaining or recovered amounts.

**§ 47105 (Project grant applications):** Specifies that applications may be submitted by a sponsor or by a State (with written consent of airport sponsors) and requires sponsors to consult with affected airport users. Applications must describe the project, may only propose projects for public-use airports in the national plan, must comply with prescribed standards, and must follow the Secretary's prescribed form. Also addresses State standards for airport development at nonprimary airports (including pavement standards), certification of compliance, and preventive maintenance requirements (sponsors must have an effective pavement maintenance-management program for pavement replacement/reconstruction applications).

**§ 47106 (Project grant application approval):** Authorizes the Secretary to approve project grant applications only if satisfied that: the project is consistent with local public agency plans, contributes to carrying out the subchapter, adequate funding exists for non-federal project costs, the project will be completed without unreasonable delay, and the sponsor has authority to carry it out. For airport development grants, the sponsor must hold (or acquire) good title to landing/takeoff areas, community interests must be fairly considered, and necessary approach lighting must be provided. Environmental requirements include public hearing opportunities for projects involving airport/runway location or major runway extension, and require a finding of no feasible alternative when projects significantly affect natural resources. The Secretary may withhold approval (with a hearing and a 180-day finding deadline) for violations, and affected persons may seek judicial review in federal courts of appeals.

This is a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) webpage from the U.S. Department of Transportation that explains airport categories as defined by law. --- SOURCE 6: Enplanements: FAA Definition, Meaning & Airport Data ---
URL: https://dwuconsulting.com/dwu-ai/enplaned-passengers

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Enplanements: FAA Definition, Meaning & Airport Data

This is a DWU AI reference guide (July 2026) examining enplaned passenger definitions, classifications, and reporting across federal data systems (T-100, DB1B/DB1C, FAA Air Carrier Activity Information System/ACAIS, and airport-reported sources). Enplaned passengers — passengers boarding aircraft at an airport — are the primary traffic metric in U.S. airport finance, driving AIP grant apportionment (49 USC §47114), hub classification, PFC collections (49 USC §40117), and cost per enplaned passenger (CPE) calculations.

### Key Facts & Definitions
- **Enplanement definition:** One passenger boarding one aircraft at an airport. For federal purposes (T-100/ACAIS), enplanements principally count revenue passengers. Example: A traveler boarding in Atlanta, connecting in Dallas, and deplaning in LA generates two revenue enplanements (ATL and DFW).
- **Revenue vs. nonrevenue:** Revenue passengers are those for whom the carrier receives commercial remuneration (paid tickets, loyalty redemptions, corporate discounts, vouchers, barter). Nonrevenue passengers include airline employees, pass interchange passengers, FAM trips, air marshals, NTSB/FAA investigators, disaster relief personnel. T-100 and FAA ACAIS report revenue passengers only; airport reports often include both, causing 1–5% discrepancies.
- **Round trips:** A round trip generates two enplanements — one at each boarding airport.

### Reporting Systems
- **T-100:** 100% census of revenue passenger boardings (14 CFR Part 241 for U.S. carriers; Part 217 for foreign carriers). Answers "how many passengers boarded at this airport."
- **DB1B/DB1C (DB1C effective Q2 2024):** 10% sample of domestic airline tickets capturing full origin-destination itineraries; used for O&D vs. connecting analysis and market-share/fare studies. Not to be summed with T-100.
- **ACAIS:** Publishes official annual enplanement totals (T-100 plus Air Taxi survey data) for hub classification and AIP entitlements.
- **FAA Form 5100-127** line 16.1 collects airport's total fiscal-year enplanements (including nonrevenue), tracked in the Compliance Activity Tracking System (CATS).

### Passenger Classifications (Three Independent Ways)
1. **Revenue vs. Nonrevenue** (detailed categories listed above)
2. **O&D vs. Connecting:** O&D passengers begin/end trips at the airport, generating stronger non-aeronautical revenue (parking, rental car, ground transportation). Connecting passengers generate less of this revenue; concession spend depends on layover/terminal design. O&D further segmented into Visitor (home outside catchment) vs. Resident (home within catchment) — a local market-study convention, not federal reporting.
3. **International vs. Domestic:** International passengers generate additional fees and CBP processing requirements.

### Hub Classification
FAA classifies airports by share of total U.S. commercial enplanements into four categories: Large Hub (≥1.00%), Medium Hub (0.25%–0.999%), Small Hub (0.05%–0.249%), Non-Hub (<0.05%). Under CY 2024 data, the U.S. has 31 large hubs and 32 medium hubs (63 L/M total). Hub class determines AIP entitlement funding.

### PFC Details
PFC collections are capped at $4.50 per chargeable passenger (14 CFR Part 158, §158.9 exclusions include nonrevenue passengers and frequent-flier award coupons). PFC authority extends to all commercial service airports regardless of hub class.

### 2025–2026 Updates
- Preliminary indicators suggest 2025 U.S. airport passenger traffic approached or exceeded 2019 levels; FAA released preliminary CY2025 data June 26, 2026; final data expected late August 2026.
- FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-63, Section 712) revised AIP apportionment formulas affecting non-primary commercial and GA airports.
- DCA received 10 additional daily slot exemptions (five slot pairs) awarded by DOT December 2024.
- EWR operations capped at 72 hourly operations (36 arrivals + 36 departures) through October 30, 2027.

### Why Airport Data Disagrees with FAA Data
Four sources: (1) scope (system vs. terminal/authority reporting); (2) nonrevenue inclusion; (3) timing (airport data in weeks vs. FAA lag of 2–3 months); (4) audit/reconciliation adjustments. FAA CY 2024 Passenger Boarding Data (ACAIS) is the apples-to-apples comparison source.

### Data Sources
FAA passenger boarding data at faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/passenger_allcargo_stats/; DWU Consulting maintains T-100 and monthly traffic dashboards at dwuconsulting.com/info/data/t100 and /info/data/monthly-traffic.
</summary>

"An enplanement is one passenger boarding one aircraft at an airport. For federal regulatory purposes (FAA Passenger Boarding data / ACAIS, and the underlying T-100 traffic data), enplanements principally count revenue passengers — those for whom the carrier receives commercial remuneration."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: FAA airport categories — Grokipedia ---
URL: https://grokipedia.com/page/FAA_airport_categories

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Grokipedia provides a comprehensive overview of Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) airport categories in the United States. The FAA categorizes airports through the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS), a congressionally mandated program identifying approximately 3,300 public-use airports vital to the national air transportation system out of nearly 19,000 total airports (about 5,000 public-use and 14,400 private-use). Categories classify airports by operational roles, passenger enplanements, cargo volumes, and infrastructure contributions, encompassing commercial service airports, cargo service airports, reliever airports, and general aviation airports.

**Key categories:**
- **Commercial service airports**: Publicly owned facilities with scheduled passenger service and at least 2,500 annual enplanements, divided into primary (≥10,000 enplanements) and nonprimary (2,500–9,999) subtypes.
- **Primary commercial service airports** (at least 10,000 annual enplanements) are subdivided by hub status: large hubs (≥1% of total U.S. enplanements, 31 airports), medium hubs (0.25%–1%, 33 airports), small hubs (0.05%–0.25%, 74 airports), and nonhub primaries (<0.05% but ≥10,000, 252 airports). As of 2023 data used in the 2025–2029 NPIAS, there are 390 total primary commercial service airports.
- **Cargo service airports**: Handle more than 100 million pounds of annual landed cargo weight; example includes Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport with over 2.4 billion pounds in 2021 despite only 1,628 enplanements.
- **Reliever airports**: Designated to reduce congestion at larger commercial airports (over 250 identified); example is Teterboro Airport serving the New York City region.
- **General aviation airports**: Approximately 88% of NPIAS facilities; categorized in 2012 into national, regional, local, basic, and unclassified roles based on based aircraft and operations.

**Part 139 Certification:** Airports are classified into four classes (effective May 2023, affecting ~520 airports with Airport Operating Certificates): Class I (scheduled large air carrier operations), Class II (scheduled small air carrier operations and unscheduled large), Class III (only scheduled small air carrier operations), and Class IV (only unscheduled large air carrier operations). Requirements include Airport Certification Manuals, wildlife hazard management, emergency planning, aircraft rescue and firefighting capabilities (ARFF indices A-E), daily self-inspections, and Safety Management Systems phased in by 2026. The FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 directs the FAA to require at least one EMT on duty at hub airports during air carrier operations, with rulemaking in progress as of November 2025.

**Legal foundation:** Categorization stems from the Federal Aviation Act of 1958 and the Airport and Airway Improvement Act of 1982. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the FAA used 2019 enplanement data for 2021 NPIAS classifications to prevent unwarranted demotions. In 2023, U.S. airports processed nearly 199 billion pounds of all-cargo landed weight.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Enplanements: FAA Definition, Meaning & Airport Data ---
URL: https://dwuconsulting.com/dwu-ai/enplaned-passengers

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Enplanements: FAA Definition, Meaning & Airport Data

This is a DWU AI reference guide (July 2026) examining enplaned passenger definitions, classifications, and reporting across federal data systems (T-100, DB1B/DB1C, FAA Air Carrier Activity Information System/ACAIS, and airport-reported sources). Enplaned passengers — passengers boarding aircraft at an airport — are the primary traffic metric in U.S. airport finance, driving AIP grant apportionment (49 USC §47114), hub classification, PFC collections (49 USC §40117), and cost per enplaned passenger (CPE) calculations.

### Key Facts & Definitions
- **Enplanement definition:** One passenger boarding one aircraft at an airport. For federal purposes (T-100/ACAIS), enplanements principally count revenue passengers. Example: A traveler boarding in Atlanta, connecting in Dallas, and deplaning in LA generates two revenue enplanements (ATL and DFW).
- **Revenue vs. nonrevenue:** Revenue passengers are those for whom the carrier receives commercial remuneration (paid tickets, loyalty redemptions, corporate discounts, vouchers, barter). Nonrevenue passengers include airline employees, pass interchange passengers, FAM trips, air marshals, NTSB/FAA investigators, disaster relief personnel. T-100 and FAA ACAIS report revenue passengers only; airport reports often include both, causing 1–5% discrepancies.
- **Round trips:** A round trip generates two enplanements — one at each boarding airport.

### Reporting Systems
- **T-100:** 100% census of revenue passenger boardings (14 CFR Part 241 for U.S. carriers; Part 217 for foreign carriers). Answers "how many passengers boarded at this airport."
- **DB1B/DB1C (DB1C effective Q2 2024):** 10% sample of domestic airline tickets capturing full origin-destination itineraries; used for O&D vs. connecting analysis and market-share/fare studies. Not to be summed with T-100.
- **ACAIS:** Publishes official annual enplanement totals (T-100 plus Air Taxi survey data) for hub classification and AIP entitlements.
- **FAA Form 5100-127** line 16.1 collects airport's total fiscal-year enplanements (including nonrevenue), tracked in the Compliance Activity Tracking System (CATS).

### Passenger Classifications (Three Independent Ways)
1. **Revenue vs. Nonrevenue** (detailed categories listed above)
2. **O&D vs. Connecting:** O&D passengers begin/end trips at the airport, generating stronger non-aeronautical revenue (parking, rental car, ground transportation). Connecting passengers generate less of this revenue; concession spend depends on layover/terminal design. O&D further segmented into Visitor (home outside catchment) vs. Resident (home within catchment) — a local market-study convention, not federal reporting.
3. **International vs. Domestic:** International passengers generate additional fees and CBP processing requirements.

### Hub Classification
FAA classifies airports by share of total U.S. commercial enplanements into four categories: Large Hub (≥1.00%), Medium Hub (0.25%–0.999%), Small Hub (0.05%–0.249%), Non-Hub (<0.05%). Under CY 2024 data, the U.S. has 31 large hubs and 32 medium hubs (63 L/M total). Hub class determines AIP entitlement funding.

### PFC Details
PFC collections are capped at $4.50 per chargeable passenger (14 CFR Part 158, §158.9 exclusions include nonrevenue passengers and frequent-flier award coupons). PFC authority extends to all commercial service airports regardless of hub class.

### 2025–2026 Updates
- Preliminary indicators suggest 2025 U.S. airport passenger traffic approached or exceeded 2019 levels; FAA released preliminary CY2025 data June 26, 2026; final data expected late August 2026.
- FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-63, Section 712) revised AIP apportionment formulas affecting non-primary commercial and GA airports.
- DCA received 10 additional daily slot exemptions (five slot pairs) awarded by DOT December 2024.
- EWR operations capped at 72 hourly operations (36 arrivals + 36 departures) through October 30, 2027.

### Why Airport Data Disagrees with FAA Data
Four sources: (1) scope (system vs. terminal/authority reporting); (2) nonrevenue inclusion; (3) timing (airport data in weeks vs. FAA lag of 2–3 months); (4) audit/reconciliation adjustments. FAA CY 2024 Passenger Boarding Data (ACAIS) is the apples-to-apples comparison source.

### Data Sources
FAA passenger boarding data at faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/passenger_allcargo_stats/; DWU Consulting maintains T-100 and monthly traffic dashboards at dwuconsulting.com/info/data/t100 and /info/data/monthly-traffic.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"An enplanement is one passenger boarding one aircraft at an airport. For federal regulatory purposes (FAA Passenger Boarding data / ACAIS, and the underlying T-100 traffic data), enplanements principally count revenue passengers — those for whom the carrier receives commercial remuneration."
</key_excerpts>

These are further subdivided into Commercial Service Airports (Large Hub, Medium Hub, Small Hub, Non-Hub) and General Aviation Airports (National, Regional, Local, Basic, Unclassified).

- Local Airports: Account for nearly half of all general aviation flying, used mostly by light piston-engine aircraft and predominantly as flight training centers. About 1,236 exist. - Basic Airports: 668 in the US, often with single runways and limited infrastructure for pleasure flying and training. Criteria include 10+ based aircraft, public or private ownership (not state-owned), and location at least 30 nautical miles from an NPIAS airport.
- Unclassified Airports: 497 nationwide with no set criteria, including decommissioned military airfields, private landing strips, and 'mom and pop' airfields.

Airport classification matters because it indicates what kind of traffic and procedures to expect. Larger regional and national airports require excellent knowledge of aeronautical regulations and procedures, and even smaller local airports demand procedural knowledge. This document from the Metropolitan Council's Imagine 2050 Transportation Policy Plan addresses the need to update airport classifications for the Twin Cities Metropolitan region in Minnesota. It argues that the Metropolitan Council's regional airport classification system has not changed in nearly 50 years, despite significant changes in aviation demand, aircraft technology, and regional growth.

**History of Classifications:**
- 1970s: FAA classifications included Scheduled Air Transport, Transport (General and Basic), Utility (General, Basic-I and II), and Landing Strips
- 1970: First MnDOT State Aviation System Plan (SASP) developed; updated in 1974 (Secondary changed to Intermediate)
- 1972: Metropolitan Council's classifications mirrored FAA's
- 1977: Metropolitan Development Guide debuted the new classification system (Major, Intermediate, Minor, Special Purpose) still in use today, based on aircraft size/weight, users, runway length, and instrument approach capability
- 1980: MN Legislature prohibited upgrading Minor airports to Intermediate status
- 1987: Citizens League report on MSP capacity options
- 1989: Metropolitan Planning Act began "Dual-Track" process
- March 1996: Recommended continued use of MSP and abandoned search for new Major airport
- April 1996: Legislation prohibited MAC from acquiring land for new Major airport; required diverting GA traffic to reliever airports
- 2000: MN Legislature updated statute - regional airports may only be reclassified by law; Minor airports defined solely by maximum runway length of 5,000 feet

**Current Classification Systems:**
- FAA NPIAS: Classifies airports by Hub (Large, Medium, Small, Non-Hub) for primary airports (10,000+ enplanements) and Non-Primary categories (commercial service, reliever, general aviation). MSP is the only Large Hub airport in the region

- STP (the only Intermediate) had only 68 more jet operations than FCM (11,081 vs 11,013) in 2023; FCM on track to exceed STP in 2024
- The three busiest reliever airports (all classified as Minor under METC system) significantly exceed the only Intermediate airport

The document proposes a revised classification framework with categories: Major, Intermediate, Minor-Primary, Minor-Secondary, and Special Purpose. Metrics include system role, critical design aircraft, most demanding users, total annual operations, total annual jet operations, employment within Airport Compatibility Area (3 nautical miles from runway ends), and legislative/community ordinances.

Proposed facilities inventory includes runway length requirements, air traffic control tower presence, and amenities (jet fuel, maintenance, FBO facilities, etc.).

**Regional Impacts:**
The document recommends tracking aircraft noise, Environmental Justice Demographic Index, PM2.5, NO₂, and Ozone impacts on surrounding communities.

**Conclusion:**
The document argues it's time to update the classification system to align with current conditions and forecast growth, and aligns this with Metropolitan Council goals: (1) Equitable and Inclusive region, (2) Healthy and Safe communities, (3) Dynamic and Resilient region.

--- SOURCE 1: Airport Categorisation ---
URL: http://www.airfieldcharts.com/airportcategorisation.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Airfield Charts explains two methods of categorising airports in aviation. The first categorisation determines the largest aircraft an airport can handle, using ICAO and FAA standards. Key systems include the ICAO Rescue Fire-Fighting (RFF) category (based on fuselage length and width), the FAA Airfield Rescue Fire-Fighting (ARFF) category (based on fuselage length only), the Approach Category (letters A-D based on final approach speed), the Aerodrome Reference Code (ICAO number 1-4 for runway length, letter A-F for wingspan and gear track), and the FAA Airplane Design Group (numbers I-VI based on wingspan). A detailed table provides per-aircraft specifications including wingspan, main gear track, fuselage length/width, approach category, aerodrome reference code, and RFF/ARFF categories for aircraft such as the A310, A320, A330, A340, A380, B737, B757, B767, B777, B747, and B787. As an example, a code 4D airport can accept aircraft up to the size of a Boeing 767 or Airbus A310.

The second categorisation assesses how easy or difficult an airport is to fly into and out of. Operators must perform a risk assessment and categorise airports as A, B, or C. Category A airports meet all basic requirements: an approved instrument approach procedure, at least one runway with no performance-limited take-off/landing procedure, published circling minima not higher than 1000ft, and night operations capability. Category B airports do not meet all Category A requirements or need extra considerations (non-standard approach aids, unusual weather, performance limitations, obstructions, etc.). Category C airports pose additional problems for approach, landing, or take-off and require extra considerations beyond Category B. Airfield categorisation is authorised by the Chief Pilot or fleet manager. The page lists 19 Category C airfields in Europe, including Innsbruck (Austria), London City (UK), Narsarsuaq (Greenland), Gibraltar, Tromso (Norway), and several Greek islands (Santorini, Samos, Mikonos, Skiathos). The page contrasts easy airports like Manston (Kent International, UK) with difficult ones like Innsbruck, which sits in a narrow valley with turbulence, poor weather, a short runway, and limited instrument approaches.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
There are two ways of categorising airports. One is to define what size of aircraft the airport has been designed to handle... The other way of categorising an airport is to determine how easy or difficult the airport is to fly into and out of.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: ICAO Aerodrome Reference Code | SKYbrary Aviation Safety ---
URL: https://skybrary.aero/articles/icao-aerodrome-reference-code

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The ICAO Aerodrome Reference Code, included in ICAO Annex 14, is a two-part categorization system that determines whether a particular aircraft can use a particular aerodrome.

**Element 1** is a numeric code based on the Aeroplane Reference Field Length, with four categories:
- Code 1: < 800 m (typical aircraft: DHC-6, Piper PA-31)
- Code 2: 800 m but < 1200 m (typical aircraft: ATR-42, Dash 8 Q300)
- Code 3: 1200 m but < 1800 m (typical aircraft: Saab 340, CRJ-200)
- Code 4: 1800 m and above (typical aircraft: Boeing 737-700, Airbus A-320)

The Aeroplane Reference Field Length is defined as "the minimum field length required for take-off at maximum certificated take-off mass, at sea level, in International Standard Atmosphere conditions in still air and with zero runway slope as documented in the Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM)." Field length is the balanced field length if applicable, or take-off distance otherwise.

**Element 2** is a letter code derived from the most restrictive of either aircraft wingspan or outer main gear wheel span:
- Code A: < 15 m (Piper PA-31, Cessna 404)
- Code B: 15 m but < 24 m (CRJ-200, DHC-6)
- Code C: 24 m but < 36 m (Boeing 737-700, Airbus A-320, Embraer ERJ 190)
- Code D: 36 m but < 52 m (B767 Series, Airbus A-310)
- Code E: 52 m but < 65 m (B777, B787, A330 Family)
- Code F: 65 m but < 80 m (Boeing 747-8, Airbus A-380-800)

Element 2 is often used on its own for detailed airport design and has a parallel but differently defined FAA code called the Airplane Design Group (ADG).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The ICAO Aerodrome Reference Code is a two part categorisation of aircraft types which simplifies the process of establishing whether a particular aircraft is able to use a particular aerodrome.", "Field length means the balanced field length (which is when the take-off distance required is equal to the accelerate-stop distance required) if applicable, or take-off distance in other cases.", "Aeroplane reference field length is defined as 'the minimum field length required for take-off at maximum certificated take-off mass, at sea level, in International Standard Atmosphere conditions in still air and with zero runway slope as documented in the Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM) or equivalent document.'", "Element 2 is often used on its own since it has direct relevance to detailed airport design. It also has a parallel but differently defined code use by the FAA, the Airplane Design Group (ADG)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Airfield Categories | Bytron Aviation Systems ---
URL: https://www.bytron.aero/aviation-news/airfield-categories

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Dan Cook (Bytron Aviation Systems, dated 17 Nov 2025) explains airfield categories (Category A, B, and C airports) used in aviation to define airport complexity, operational requirements, and crew qualification needs, and how the Airfield Watch tool helps monitor METAR, TAF, and NOTAMs effectively.

**Airfield Categories:**
- **Category A:** Most straightforward airports with standard runway lengths, simple approach procedures, minimal terrain/airspace complexity, and well-established infrastructure. No additional crew training or briefing typically required (e.g., Heathrow).
- **Category B:** Require additional crew briefing due to complexities like challenging approach profiles, unusual runway configurations, limited manoeuvring space, surrounding terrain, or restricted airspace. Examples include Florence (FLR), Dubrovnik (DBV), and Lanzarote (ACE).
- **Category C:** Most complex, requiring specific crew training/certification. Features include steep or curved approaches, high terrain, short or sloped runways, complex procedures, and tight noise-restricted corridors. Examples include Innsbruck (LOWI), Madeira (FNC), and Santorini (LGSR).

**Why Categories Matter:**
- Affects flight planning (crew qualification, airport restrictions, weather minima), operational suitability (adapting when conditions exceed crew/aircraft limits), alternates (B and C airports are often unsuitable alternates in marginal weather), and passenger safety/schedule integrity (unexpected NOTAMs or visibility drops cause delays, diversions, extra fuel burn, missed connections).

**Airfield Watch Features:**
- Live METAR & TAF updates, real-time NOTAM alerts with filtering, weather trend analysis, and airport-specific insights
- Monitors cloud ceiling, visibility, RVR, wind speed, and gusts
- Customizable weather minima for Groups of airfields, individual airfields, alternates, en-route alternates, and ETOPS alternates
- Colour-coded graphics (normal, warning, critical weather)
- Critical NOTAM alerts (e.g., runway closures) sent to specific emails
- METAR/TAF forecasting trends to evaluate improving or deteriorating conditions
- Real-time visibility helps dispatchers answer: Is the airport still suitable? Do we need to rebrief crew? Does the flight plan need updating? Is an alternate decision required?

Key testimonials include quotes from Domas Makarevičius (Flight Planning Manager, GetJet Airlines) and Ahmed Hassan (Manager, Operations Control Center) praising the tool's ability to highlight troublesome areas and detect closures early.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"It helps to attract attention to troublesome areas when our team is busy with daily operational tasks" - Domas Makarevičius, Flight Planning Manager, GetJet Airlines, "A volcanic eruption in Italy closed our destination. Luckily, with NOTAM watch, we were the first to know and called the flight back, reducing disruption over all the fleet." - Ahmed Hassan, Manager, Operations Control Center, "Airfield categories define the operational baseline and Airfield Watch ensures your decisions are informed by real-time operational awareness."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Airport Categories | Federal Aviation Administration ---
URL: https://www.faa.gov/airports/planning_capacity/categories

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a webpage from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) titled "Airport Categories," which explains the classification system for airports in the United States. The page reports that there are approximately 14,400 private-use airports and 5,000 public-use airports, heliports, and seaplane bases in the U.S. About 3,300 public-use facilities are included in the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS), and airports in this plan may be considered for Airport Improvement Program (AIP) funding.

The law categorizes airports by type of activities: Commercial Service (publicly owned airports with at least 2,500 annual enplanements and scheduled air carrier service), Reliever (airports designated to relieve congestion at commercial service airports), and General Aviation (public-use airports without scheduled service or with less than 2,500 passenger boardings each year). Commercial service airports are further broken down by hubs: Large Hub (1% or more of annual U.S. commercial enplanements), Medium Hub (0.25-1.0%), Small Hub (0.05-0.25%), Nonhub (less than 0.05% but more than 10,000 enplanements—all categorized as Primary), and Nonprimary Commercial Service Nonhub (2,500-10,000 annual enplanements). Primary airports are commercial service airports with more than 10,000 annual enplanements.

The FAA also developed five categories for general aviation airports (including nonprimary commercial service, relievers, and general aviation) based on existing activity levels: National (support access to national and international markets with high levels of jet activity), Regional (connect communities to regional and national markets, usually in metropolitan areas), Local (supplement local communities within a state or immediate region, mostly piston aircraft), Basic (links community to national airport system with minimal infrastructure), and Unclassified (in NPIAS but with limited activity). The airport roles capture the diverse functions and economic contributions GA airports make to communities and the nation.

The page also provides contact information for the FAA: Federal Aviation Administration, 800 Independence Avenue, SW, Washington, DC 20591, 866.835.5322 (866-TELL-FAA).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"There are approximately 14,400 private-use (closed to the public) and 5,000 public-use (open to the public) airports, heliports, and seaplane bases. Approximately 3,300 of these public-use facilities are included in the National Plan of Integrated Airport Systems (NPIAS).", "An airport is defined in the law as any area of land or water used or intended for landing or takeoff of aircraft including appurtenant area used or intended for airport buildings, facilities, as well as rights of way together with the buildings and facilities.", "Primary airports are a commercial service airport with more than 10,000 annual enplanements (§47102(16)).", "The airport roles capture the diverse functions and economic contributions GA airports make to their communities and the Nation.", "Federal Aviation Administration, 800 Independence Avenue, SW, Washington, DC 20591, 866.835.5322 (866-TELL-FAA)"
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Understanding Airport Classification: A Beginner’s Guide | CAU ---
URL: https://calaero.edu/learn-to-fly/aeronautics/airport-operations/understanding-airport-classification-a-beginners-guide

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from California Aeronautical University provides a beginner's guide to airport classification. It explains that the FAA defines an "airport" as any area of land or water used for aircraft landing/takeoff, including appurtenant buildings, facilities, and rights of way. The FAA categorizes airports into two broad types—"primary" and "nonprimary"—based on the type and frequency of activity. Within these categories are Commercial Service Airports (Large Hub, Medium Hub, Small Hub, Non-Hub) and General Aviation Airports (National, Regional, Local, Basic, Unclassified).

The article details the five general aviation airport categories:
• National Airports (84 in the USA): Large, busy facilities like Teterboro, New Jersey, serving major cities. Criteria include more than 5,000 instrument departures/arrivals, 11+ jet aircraft based, 20+ international flights yearly, 10,000+ passengers, and over 500 million lbs. of cargo yearly.
• Regional Airports (467): Located in metropolitan areas for interstate travel, hosting over a third of all GA flying. Criteria include proximity to a metro area, 10+ flights departing 500+ miles, at least one jet aircraft, and 100+ based aircraft.
• Local Airports (~1,236): Used most by GA, accounting for nearly half of GA flying; predominantly flight training centers with light piston-engine aircraft. Criteria include 2,500+ passengers yearly and 15+ permanently based aircraft.
• Basic Airports (668): Single runways, limited infrastructure, used for pleasure flying and training. Criteria include 10+ based aircraft, public or private ownership, and being at least 30 nautical miles from an NPIAS airport.
• Unclassified Airports (497): No set criteria; includes decommissioned military airfields, private landing strips, and airfields that don't meet other classification standards.

The article concludes that knowing an airport's classification helps pilots anticipate traffic and procedures, and it promotes California Aeronautical University's flight training programs for navigating airports of all sizes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The FAA defines an airport as 'Any area of land or water used or intended for landing or takeoff of aircraft including the appurtenant area used or intended for airport buildings, facilities, as well as rights of way together with the buildings and facilities.'", "According to the FAA, the two main types of airports are 'primary' and 'nonprimary.' The distinction is drawn due to the type of activity conducted at the airport and how frequent arrivals and departures are.", "There are presently 84 national airports in the USA.", "Over a third of all general aviation flying takes place at regional airports.", "Local airports account for nearly half of the general aviation flying performed each year."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Air transport measurement - passengers (avia_pa) ---
URL: https://library.cystat.gov.cy/NEW/AIR_AVNES_A_CY_2020.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the Euro SDMX Metadata Structure (ESMS) reference metadata for EU air transport passenger statistics (avia_pa), compiled by the Department of Civil Aviation Cyprus. It details the methodology, legal framework, and statistical processes for collecting Cyprus air transport data reported to Eurostat.

Key datasets required by EU Regulation 437/2003 (and implementing regulations 1358/2003, 546/2005, 158/2007, and 223/2009) include: A1 (flight stage data on passengers/freight/mail on board, broken down by arrivals/departures, scheduled/non-scheduled services, airlines, and aircraft type), B1 (on flight origin/destination data on passengers carried and freight/mail loaded or unloaded), and C1 (aggregated airport data on total passengers, transit passengers, freight/mail, and aircraft movements).

Classification systems use ICAO codes: airports per document 7910, aircraft per document 8643, and airlines per document 8585 (coded as EU or non-EU). The reference period is calendar year 2020. Statistics cover commercial and civil air traffic at airports with more than 15,000 passenger units annually, located in government-controlled areas of Cyprus. Data have been reported since 2001; direct transit and transfer passenger data available since 2013.

Airport categories defined by the Regulation: Category 0 (less than 15,000 passenger units/year—no reporting obligation), Category 1 (15,000–150,000—report only dataset C), Category 2 (150,000–1.5 million—report A, B, C), and Category 3 (at least 1.5 million—report A, B, C). Units of measure include number of passengers, tonnes (with three decimal places), flights, aircraft movements, and passenger seats available.

Data are published monthly, 120 days (four months) after the reference month, preliminary until annual results are published. Data are not published nationally—only through Eurostat's database. Data transmission occurs no later than six months after the observation period. Data providers submit electronically, collected at individual flight level monthly via airport data systems. Validation involves random checks with corrections requested if errors are found. The metadata was last certified and updated on 04/03/2021. The comment notes that due to COVID-19, 2020 was a bad year for air transport.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The main objective of this statistics is to provide data on the carriage of passengers, freight and mail by commercial air services as well as on civil aircraft movements to or from Community airports, except for flights by State aircraft.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Air transport measurement - passengers (avia_pa) ---
URL: https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/cache/metadata/en/avia_pa_esms.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the Eurostat Reference Metadata (ESMS) document for the "Air transport measurement - passengers" (avia_pa) domain, detailing the statistical concepts, methodologies, and quality processes for air transport data collection and dissemination in the EU.

**Data Overview:** The Air transport domain contains national and international intra/extra-EU data, covering passengers (number of passengers), freight and mail (in 1,000 tonnes), and air traffic data on airports, airlines, and aircraft. Data is collected at airport level and compiled under Regulation (EC) N°1358/2003, implementing Regulation N°437/2003. Airports handling less than 15,000 passenger units annually are excluded. Data is transmitted by EU Member States, EFTA countries, and other reporting countries. Data is disseminated in four sub-domains: passengers, freight and mail, traffic by airports/aircraft/airlines, and regional statistics (by NUTS regions). Statistics based on Regulation 437/2003 are disseminated from reference year 2003 (with some partial data from 1993 onwards).

**Key Statistical Concepts:**
- Three datasets: Flight Stage (A), On Flight Origin/Destination (B), Airport (C)
- Passengers on board: all passengers landing/taking off, including direct transit passengers (counted at arrivals and departures)
- Passengers carried: passengers counted once per flight, excludes direct transit passengers
- Direct transit passengers: continue on same aircraft and same flight number
- Flight Stage vs. OFOD concepts are not directly comparable due to direct transit passenger treatment (illustrated with a New York-London-Paris example)
- Community airport definitions and four airport categories under the Regulation

**Quality and Access:** 
- Compiling agency: European Commission (Eurostat); Eurostat contact address at 5, Rue Alphonse Weicker, L-2920 Luxembourg
- Metadata last certified/posted: 15 October 2025; last update: 2 March 2026
- Most tables updated twice monthly; some (fleet, airport infrastructure, accident, regional) updated annually
- Data quality assessed as high; validation includes codification, format checks, consistency checks, and mirror statistics cross-checking
- Final annual data disseminated 8-9 months after reference period; monthly/quarterly provisional data within 2 weeks of delivery
- Data is comparable over time since 2003; route-level data has dissemination thresholds due to sensitivity
- Users include DG MOVE, DG REGIO, DG COMP, European Court of Auditors, national authorities, universities, and industry
- Double-counting issue when calculating EU passenger/freight totals requires aggregating country totals first
- No confidential information in datasets A1, B1, C1, but airline and route-level details have dissemination restrictions
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Data are compiled following the provisions of the Regulation (EC) N°1358/2003, implementing Regulation N°437/2003 of the European Parliament and of the Council on statistical returns in respect of the carriage of passengers, freight and mail by air."
</key_excerpts>
